convention: x @ w. each fixture declares its own algorithm variant. no external packages are needed to run this companion. """ import math import json from collections import counter def softmax(z): """finite logits -> positive probabilities, using a stable common shift.""" if not z or not all(math.isfinite(v) for v in z): raise valueerror('need nonempty finite logits') m = max(z); e = [math.exp(v-m) for v in z]; total = sum(e) return [v/total for v in e] def bpe_train(words, steps): """toy character bpe, weighted words; lexical tie break, explicit end marker. not a byte-level gpt tokenizer. returned merges are applied in learned order. """ seqs = {tuple(w)+('</w>',): n for w,n in words.items()}; merges=[] for _ in range(steps): counts=counter() for seq,n in seqs.items(): for a,b in zip(seq,seq[1:]): counts[(a,b)]+=n if not counts: break pair=min(counts, key=lambda p:(-counts[p],p)); merges.append(pair) updated={} for seq,n in seqs.items(): merged=bpe_apply(seq,[pair]); updated[merged]=updated.get(merged,0)+n seqs=updated return {'merges':merges,'segmented_words':[(list(s),n) for s,n in seqs.items()]} def bpe_apply(tokens, merges): """apply ranked adjacent pair merges without crossing the supplied sequence.""" tokens=list(tokens) for pair in merges: out=[];i=0 while i<len(tokens): if i+1<len(tokens) and tuple(tokens[i:i+2])==tuple(pair): out.append(tokens[i]+tokens[i+1]);i+=2 else: out.append(tokens[i]);i+=1 tokens=out return tuple(tokens) def rope(x, position, base=10000.): """rotate adjacent coordinate pairs; even dimension, angle p*base^(-2i/d).""" if len(x)%2 or len(x)==0 or base<=0: raise valueerror('even positive width and base required') out=[] for i in range(0,len(x),2): a=position*base**(-i/len(x));c=math.cos(a);s=math.sin(a) out.extend([x[i]*c-x[i+1]*s,x[i]*s+x[i+1]*c]) return out def rmsnorm(x, eps=1e-6, gain=none): """normalize final feature vector by sqrt(mean(square)+eps); no centering.""" if not x or eps<0: raise valueerror('invalid vector/epsilon') gain=[1.]*len(x) if gain is none else gain if len(gain)!=len(x): raise valueerror('gain shape mismatch') d=math.sqrt(sum(v*v for v in x)/len(x)+eps) if d==0: raise valueerror('zero denominator') return [v*g/d for v,g in zip(x,gain)] def matmul(a,b): """rectangular m*n times n*p -> m*p.""" if not a or not b or not a[0] or not b[0] or any(len(r)!=len(a[0]) for r in a) or any(len(r)!=len(b[0]) for r in b) or len(a[0])!=len(b): raise valueerror('matrix shape mismatch') return [[sum(a[i][k]*b[k][j] for k in range(len(b))) for j in range(len(b[0]))] for i in range(len(a))] def swiglu(x,gate,up,down): """swiglu: silu(xw_gate) elementwise xw_up, then w_down; no biases.""" g=matmul(x,gate);u=matmul(x,up) if len(g[0])!=len(u[0]): raise valueerror('gate/up shape mismatch') def silu(v): sig=1/(1+math.exp(-v)) if v>=0 else math.exp(v)/(1+math.exp(v)) return v*sig return matmul([[silu(a)*b for a,b in zip(ga,ua)] for ga,ua in zip(g,u)],down) def parameter_count(vocab,d,ffn,layers,tied=true,gated=false): """bias-free mha decoder, two per-block rms gains and final gain; no learned positions.""" if any(type(v)!=int or v<=0 for v in [vocab,d,ffn,layers]): raise valueerror('positive integer dimensions') return vocab*d*(1 if tied else 2)+layers*(4*d*d+(3 if gated else 2)*d*ffn+2*d)+d def truncate(p, method, value): """explicit deterministic support rules; includes boundary token for top-p/typical.""" if not p or any(v<0 or not math.isfinite(v) for v in p) or abs(sum(p)-1)>1e-8: raise valueerror('pmf required') order=sorted(range(len(p)),key=lambda i:(-p[i],i)) if method=='top-k': if type(value)!=int or not 1<=value<=len(p): raise valueerror('invalid k') keep=order[:value] elif method in ['top-p','typical']: if not 0<value<=1: raise valueerror('mass must be in (0,1]') if method=='typical': h=-sum(v*math.log(v) for v in p if v) order=sorted(range(len(p)),key=lambda i:(abs(-math.log(p[i])-h) if p[i]>0 else math.inf,i)) keep=[];total=0 for i in order: keep.append(i);total+=p[i] if total>=value-1e-15:break elif method=='min-p': if not 0<=value<=1:raise valueerror('ratio must be in [0,1]') keep=[i for i in order if p[i]>=value*max(p)] else: raise valueerror('unknown filter') total=sum(p[i] for i in keep) return {'kept_ids':keep,'retained_mass':total,'probabilities':[p[i]/total if i in keep else 0 for i in range(len(p))]} def sample(p,u): """inverse-cdf draw for supplied uniform variate 0<=u<1; half-open bins.""" if not 0<=u<1 or any(v<0 for v in p) or abs(sum(p)-1)>1e-8:raise valueerror('invalid draw/pmf') total=0 for i,v in enumerate(p): total+=v if u<total:return i return len(p)-1 def beam_fixture(width): """exact supplied two-step beam example; fixed length, no eos/length penalty.""" first={'bright':.5,'sunny':.35,'cold':.15} nexts={'bright':{'outside':.5,'today':.3,'again':.2},'sunny':{'outside':.95,'today':.03,'again':.02},'cold':{'outside':.4,'today':.4,'again':.2}} beams=sorted([(k,math.log(v)) for k,v in first.items()],key=lambda x:(-x[1],x[0]))[:width] candidates=[(prefix+' '+k,score+math.log(v)) for prefix,score in beams for k,v in nexts[prefix].items()] return [(s,math.exp(logp)) for s,logp in sorted(candidates,key=lambda x:(-x[1],x[0]))[:width]] def gnmt_score(logp,length,alpha): """wu length-penalty variant, not the distinct length^alpha convention.""" if length<1:raise valueerror('positive length') return logp/(((5+length)/6)**alpha) def repetition(z,seen,penalty,sign_aware=true): """unique-token penalty; negative seen logits multiplied in sign-aware variant.""" if penalty<=0:raise valueerror('positive penalty') return [v*penalty if sign_aware and v<0 and i in seen else v/penalty if i in seen else v for i,v in enumerate(z)] def contrastive(p,similarity,alpha): """one contrastive-search candidate score; similarity is precomputed max cosine.""" if len(p)!=len(similarity) or not 0<=alpha<=1:raise valueerror('invalid candidate data') scores=[(1-alpha)*a-alpha*b for a,b in zip(p,similarity)] return {'scores':scores,'selected':max(range(len(scores)),key=lambda i:scores[i])} def mirostat_update(mu,surprise_bits,target_bits,eta): """mirostat feedback update only; does not implement full adaptive sampler.""" return mu-eta*(surprise_bits-target_bits) def lora(x,w,b,a,alpha): """row-input orientation b:din*r, a:r*dout; frozen w plus alpha/r ba.""" rank=len(a);delta=matmul(b,a);scale=alpha/rank merged=[[v+scale*d for v,d in zip(row,dr)] for row,dr in zip(w,delta)] base=matmul(x,w);branch=matmul(matmul(x,b),a) return {'delta':delta,'merged':merged,'separate_output':[[v+scale*d for v,d in zip(row,dr)] for row,dr in zip(base,branch)],'merged_output':matmul(x,merged)} def affine_quantize(x,step,zero,qmin,qmax): """dequantization step units; python nearest-even rounding and explicit clipping.""" if step<=0 or qmin>qmax or type(zero)!=int:raise valueerror('invalid quantizer') q=[max(qmin,min(qmax,round(v/step)+zero)) for v in x] return {'codes':q,'reconstructed':[step*(v-zero) for v in q]} def float_decode(sign,exponent,mantissa,ebits,mbits): """ieee-style binary field teaching decoder; not vendor fp8 e4m3fn.""" bias=2**(ebits-1)-1 if sign not in [0,1] or not 0<=exponent<2**ebits or not 0<=mantissa<2**mbits:raise valueerror('invalid fields') if exponent==2**ebits-1:return math.copysign(math.inf,(-1)**sign) if mantissa==0 else math.nan sig=mantissa/2**mbits if exponent==0 else 1+mantissa/2**mbits return (-1)**sign*sig*2.**((1-bias) if exponent==0 else exponent-bias) def gptq_compensate(w,inverse_h,q,quantized): """one constrained quadratic compensation step on the current free coordinates.""" error=w[q]-quantized;denom=inverse_h[q][q] if denom<=0:raise valueerror('positive diagonal required') return [v-error*inverse_h[j][q]/denom for j,v in enumerate(w)] def kl(p,q): """exact categorical kl(p||q), natural logs, defined support behavior.""" if len(p)!=len(q) or abs(sum(p)-1)>1e-8 or abs(sum(q)-1)>1e-8 or any(v<0 for v in p+q):raise valueerror('normalized pmfs') if any(a>0 and b==0 for a,b in zip(p,q)):return math.inf return sum(a*math.log(a/b) for a,b in zip(p,q) if a) def reverse_kl_gradient(z,teacher): """exact finite-support gradient wrt student logits; teacher fixed positive.""" q=softmax(z) if len(z)!=len(teacher) or any(p<=0 or not math.isfinite(p) for p in teacher) or abs(sum(teacher)-1)>1e-8:raise valueerror('matching positive teacher pmf') v=[math.log(a/b) for a,b in zip(q,teacher)];mean=sum(a*b for a,b in zip(q,v)) return [a*(b-mean) for a,b in zip(q,v)] def kd_loss(student,teacher,target,temperature,hard_weight): """classical one-token kd variant: alpha hard ce +(1-alpha) t² forward kl.""" if temperature<=0 or not math.isfinite(temperature) or not 0<=hard_weight<=1 or len(student)!=len(teacher) or not 0<=target<len(student):raise valueerror('invalid kd configuration') p=softmax([v/temperature for v in teacher]);q=softmax([v/temperature for v in student]) hard=-math.log(softmax(student)[target]);soft=temperature**2*kl(p,q) return {'hard_ce':hard,'scaled_kl':soft,'total':hard_weight*hard+(1-hard_weight)*soft} def advantages(rewards,eps=1e-4,sample_std=false): """group-standardized rewards; explicit population/sample denominator.""" n=len(rewards) if not n or eps<0 or sample_std and n<2:raise valueerror('insufficient rewards or invalid epsilon') mean=sum(rewards)/n;std=math.sqrt(sum((v-mean)**2 for v in rewards)/(n-1 if sample_std else n)) if std+eps==0:raise valueerror('zero spread requires positive epsilon or a separate skip rule') return {'mean':mean,'std':std,'advantages':[(v-mean)/(std+eps) for v in rewards]} def clipped_surrogate(ratio,advantage,eps): """ppo/grpo maximization surrogate; loss negates this, before reductions/kl.""" clipped=min(1+eps,max(1-eps,ratio)) return min(ratio*advantage,clipped*advantage) def kl_sample(log_current,log_reference): """per-sample log ratio and nonnegative k3 estimator, for declared current-policy draws.""" d=log_reference-log_current return {'log_ratio':-d,'k3':math.expm1(d)-d} def importance_expectation(target,proposal,values): """exact finite sum under proposal with target/proposal weights; not self-normalized.""" if len(target)!=len(proposal) or len(target)!=len(values):raise valueerror('shape mismatch') if any(v<0 for v in target+proposal) or abs(sum(target)-1)>1e-8 or abs(sum(proposal)-1)>1e-8:raise valueerror('normalized pmfs required') if any(t>0 and p<=0 for t,p in zip(target,proposal)):raise valueerror('missing proposal support') return sum(p*(t/p)*v for t,p,v in zip(target,proposal,values) if p) def cache_bytes(batch,length,layers,kv_heads,head_dim,bytes_per_element): """k plus v storage only; excludes allocator, q, weights, attention workspace.""" return 2*batch*length*layers*kv_heads*head_dim*bytes_per_element def routed_output(x,expert_weights,logits,k,shared_weight=none): """tiny linear experts, softmax scores, top-k selected-renormalized routing.""" p=softmax(logits);selected=sorted(range(len(p)),key=lambda i:(-p[i],i))[:k] mass=sum(p[i] for i in selected);weights=[p[i]/mass for i in selected] outs=[matmul([x],expert_weights[i])[0] for i in selected] y=[sum(a*v[j] for a,v in zip(weights,outs)) for j in range(len(x))] if shared_weight is not none:y=[a+b for a,b in zip(y,matmul([x],shared_weight)[0])] return {'selected':selected,'weights':weights,'output':y} def balance_loss(assignments,router_probabilities,experts,coefficient=1.): """switch-style top-1 auxiliary illustration, not every deepseek balancing variant.""" n=len(assignments);f=[assignments.count(i)/n for i in range(experts)] p=[sum(row[i] for row in router_probabilities)/n for i in range(experts)] return coefficient*experts*sum(a*b for a,b in zip(f,p)) def mtp_alignment(tokens,horizon): """base=next token, depth k target=t+k+1; teacher-forced prefix extends to t+k.""" if type(horizon)!=int or horizon<0:raise valueerror('nonnegative integer depth') return [{'position':t,'visible_through':t+horizon,'target_position':t+horizon+1,'target':tokens[t+horizon+1]} for t in range(len(tokens)-horizon-1)] def weighted_gradient(grads,valid_tokens): """aggregate per-microbatch token-mean gradients into a global valid-token mean.""" total=sum(valid_tokens) if total<=0 or len(grads)!=len(valid_tokens):raise valueerror('invalid microbatches') return [sum(g[j]*n for g,n in zip(grads,valid_tokens))/total for j in range(len(grads[0]))] def majority(votes): """count canonical answer strings, lexical tie break, no correctness guarantee.""" counts=counter(votes) if not counts:raise valueerror('no answers') return min(counts,key=lambda v:(-counts[v],v)) def pass_at_k(n,c,k): """unbiased combinatorial estimator given c successes among n sampled candidates.""" if not 0<=c<=n or not 1<=k<=n:raise valueerror('invalid n,c,k') return 1-(math.comb(n-c,k)/math.comb(n,k) if n-c>=k else 0.) def token_f1(prediction,gold): """toy whitespace/multiset token f1; benchmark normalization is a separate contract.""" p=counter(prediction.split());g=counter(gold.split());overlap=sum((p&g).values()) if not sum(p.values()) or not sum(g.values()):return float(p==g) precision=overlap/sum(p.values());recall=overlap/sum(g.values()) return 2*precision*recall/(precision+recall) if overlap else 0. def mla_content(query,latent,up_key,up_value): """content-only absorption equivalence, one head, no rope or causal mask.""" def transpose(x):return [list(r) for r in zip(*x)] expanded_keys=matmul(latent,up_key) expanded_values=matmul(latent,up_value) scores=matmul(query,transpose(expanded_keys)) absorbed_scores=matmul(matmul(query,transpose(up_key)),transpose(latent)) weights=[softmax([v/math.sqrt(len(query[0])) for v in row]) for row in scores] return {'expanded_scores':scores,'absorbed_scores':absorbed_scores, 'expanded_output':matmul(weights,expanded_values),'absorbed_output':matmul(matmul(weights,latent),up_value)} def speculative_distribution(target,proposal): """exact one-step speculative rejection distribution on a categorical support.""" if len(target)!=len(proposal) or any(v<0 for v in target+proposal) or abs(sum(target)-1)>1e-8 or abs(sum(proposal)-1)>1e-8:raise valueerror('matching categorical pmfs') accepted=[min(p,q) for p,q in zip(target,proposal)];rejection=1-sum(accepted) residual=[max(p-q,0) for p,q in zip(target,proposal)];mass=sum(residual) corrected=[a+rejection*r/mass if mass>0 else a for a,r in zip(accepted,residual)] return {'accepted_mass':sum(accepted),'residual':residual,'final_distribution':corrected} def fp8_finite_values(format_name): """enumerate positive finite e4m3fn or ieee-style e5m2 values; excludes nan/inf.""" if format_name=='e4m3fn':e,m,bias=4,3,7 elif format_name=='e5m2':e,m,bias=5,2,15 else:raise valueerror('unsupported explicit fp8 variant') integer_product*weight_scale*activation_absmax/activation_qmax def storage_bits(weights,bits,metadata_bits_per_block,block_size): """payload plus complete-block metadata; this fixture assumes exactly neural networks ultimately perform enormous numbers of operations on scalar values. but manipulating one scalar at a time would be impossible. so we group scalars into vectors and matrices . 0.1.2 vector a vector is an ordered collection of numbers. for example: x= \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 4\\ 7 \end{bmatrix}. this is a 3-dimensional vector: x\in\mathbb r^3. we can also write: x=(2,4,7). the individual values are components: x_1=2,\qquad x_2=4,\qquad x_3=7. why does an llm need vectors? because a token such as: cat cannot directly participate in operations such as: q=xw_q. we first convert the token into numbers. eventually: \text{cat} \rightarrow \text{token id} \rightarrow \text{embedding vector}. for example: \text{cat} \rightarrow [0.21,-0.53,0.72,\ldots]. that vector contains a learned numerical representation of the token. raschka's book follows precisely this progression from token representations into vector operations and later q/k/v projections. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.1.3 matrix a matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers. for example: a= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2&3\\ 4&5&6 \end{bmatrix}. this has: 2\text{ rows} and 3\text{ columns}. therefore: \boxed{a\in\mathbb r^{2\times3}} the notation m\times n means: m=\text{number of rows} n=\text{number of columns}. why do transformers need matrices? because instead of transforming one token vector at a time, we want to transform an entire sequence simultaneously. suppose: n=4 tokens and embedding dimension: d=8. then the input representation is: x\in\mathbb r^{4\times8}. conceptually: x= \begin{bmatrix} ---x_1---\\ ---x_2---\\ ---x_3---\\ ---x_4--- \end{bmatrix}. each row represents one token. so: \boxed{ \text{rows}=\text{tokens} } and: \boxed{ \text{columns}=\text{features} } this shape convention will appear throughout the entire course. 0.1.4 matrix multiplication suppose: a\in\mathbb r^{m\times n} and b\in\mathbb r^{n\times p}. then: ab\in\mathbb r^{m\times p}. the crucial rule is: \boxed{ \text{inner dimensions must match} } because: (m\times n)(n\times p) \rightarrow (m\times p). example let: a= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4 \end{bmatrix} and: b= \begin{bmatrix} 5&6\\ 7&8 \end{bmatrix}. then: ab= \begin{bmatrix} 1(5)+2(7)&1(6)+2(8)\\ 3(5)+4(7)&3(6)+4(8) \end{bmatrix} so: ab= \begin{bmatrix} 19&22\\ 43&50 \end{bmatrix}. notice what happened. for example: (ab)_{11} = 1(5)+2(7). that is a dot product . so matrix multiplication is essentially a huge collection of dot products. 0.1.5 why this becomes q = xw this is our first major connection. suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} and: w_q\in\mathbb r^{d\times d_k}. then: q=xw_q is legal because: (n\times d)(d\times d_k) gives: \boxed{ q\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k}. } this is not arbitrary notation. the matrix multiplication is doing the following to every token simultaneously : x_i \rightarrow x_iw_q. raschka's book explicitly implements these projections using: \texttt{query = x @ w\_query} and shows that changing the number of columns of the weight matrix changes the dimensionality of the resulting query vector. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) this is the first reason i want you to become comfortable with dimensions before we enter attention. 0.1.6 dot product given: x= \begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ \vdots\\ x_d \end{bmatrix} and: y= \begin{bmatrix} y_1\\ y_2\\ \vdots\\ y_d \end{bmatrix}, their dot product is: \boxed{ x^\top y = \sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i y_i } for example: x= \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 3\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad y= \begin{bmatrix} 4\\ -1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. then: x^\top y = 2(4)+3(-1)+1(2) =8-3+2 =7. why is dot product so important? because it measures alignment/similarity between two vectors. geometrically: x^\top y = \|x\|\,\|y\|\cos\theta. therefore: same direction \theta=0 so: \cos\theta=1. large positive dot product. orthogonal \theta=90^\circ so: \cos\theta=0. dot product: 0. opposite directions \theta=180^\circ so: \cos\theta=-1. negative dot product. this is exactly why attention uses it later we will calculate: s_{ij}=q_i^\top k_j. meaning: how compatible is query i with key j ? so the attention mechanism starts with something extremely simple: \boxed{ \text{query-key compatibility} = \text{dot product} } the nlp-with-transformers book describes attention scores precisely as dot products between query and key vectors and then builds the attention matrix from those scores. (source: nlp_transformer) 0.1.7 dimensions — the rule you must master suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d}. then: w_q\in\mathbb r^{d\times d_k} gives: q=xw_q with: q\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k}. likewise: k=xw_k gives: k\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k}. now: k^\top\in\mathbb r^{d_k\times n}. therefore: qk^\top has shape: (n\times d_k)(d_k\times n) \boxed{ =n\times n. } that n\times n matrix is the attention-score matrix . this is one of the most important dimensional relationships in the entire course. 0.1.8 why n\times n matters suppose: n=4. then: qk^\top = \begin{bmatrix} s_{11}&s_{12}&s_{13}&s_{14}\\ s_{21}&s_{22}&s_{23}&s_{24}\\ s_{31}&s_{32}&s_{33}&s_{34}\\ s_{41}&s_{42}&s_{43}&s_{44} \end{bmatrix}. interpretation: s_{ij} = \text{how much token }i \text{ relates to token }j. therefore: row 1 = what token 1 is interested in row 2 = what token 2 is interested in etc. this is why attention is fundamentally a token-to-token interaction mechanism . 0.1.9 weight parameters vs attention weights this distinction is extremely important and often causes confusion. weight parameters for example: w_q. these are: \boxed{\text{learned during training}} and remain fixed during a particular inference pass. attention weights for example: a_{ij}. these are: \boxed{\text{computed dynamically for the current input}} and can change for every sequence and position. raschka explicitly warns about this distinction: the w matrices are learned model parameters, whereas attention weights determine how strongly the current context vector depends on different input positions. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.1.10 matrix vs tensor a matrix: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} has two dimensions. a batch of sequences: x\in\mathbb r^{b\times n\times d} has three dimensions. where: b=\text{batch size} n=\text{sequence length} d=\text{embedding/model dimension}. so: \boxed{ \text{tensor shape} = (b,n,d) } is what we will normally use in actual pytorch implementations. the nlp-with-transformers source explicitly discusses batch matrix multiplication for attention, where the batch dimension is handled independently for each sequence. (source: nlp_transformer) 0.1.11 why we care about this for the entire course this seemingly basic material will keep reappearing. transformer q=xw_q lora w'=w+ba quantization w\rightarrow\hat w distillation p_{\text{teacher}} \rightarrow q_{\text{student}} rl \pi_\theta(a|s) grpo r_i(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(o_i|q)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i|q)} everything is ultimately built from transformations of numerical objects. 0.1.12 cheatsheet connection from the master sheet: \boxed{ x:(n,d) } \boxed{ w_q:(d,d_k) } \boxed{ q=xw_q:(n,d_k) } \boxed{ qk^\top:(n,n) } the reason these shapes work is exactly the matrix-multiplication rule we just learned. so when you see the transformer equation later, you should not memorize it . you should be able to reconstruct it. 0.1.13 mini numerical transformer example let's make this concrete. suppose: n=3 and: d=2. let: x= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4\\ 5&6 \end{bmatrix}. suppose: w_q= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}. then: q=xw_q so: q= \begin{bmatrix} 1&2\\ 3&4\\ 5&6 \end{bmatrix}. here: d_k=2. therefore: qk^\top will have: 3\times3 entries. for example, if: k=q, then: s_{11} = [1,2] \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = 1^2+2^2 = 5. and: s_{12} = [1,2] \begin{bmatrix} 3\\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = 3+8 = 11. so token 1 has: \boxed{ [5,\;11,\;17] } as its raw similarity scores with the three tokens. this is the first concrete appearance of attention. we have not yet applied: \frac1{\sqrt{d_k}} or: \operatorname{softmax} or: \text{causal masking}. those will be the next concepts. 0.1.14 what we have actually learned we started with: \text{numbers} and reached: \boxed{ \text{token representations} \rightarrow \text{matrix transformations} \rightarrow \text{query/key representations} \rightarrow \text{pairwise token similarities} } the next question is: why should those raw similarities become probabilities? that leads directly to softmax . but before we jump there, we need the probability foundation. master connection our chain so far is: \boxed{ \text{scalar} \rightarrow \text{vector} \rightarrow \text{matrix} \rightarrow \text{matrix multiplication} \rightarrow \text{dot product} \rightarrow \text{similarity} \rightarrow qk^\top } next: \boxed{ qk^\top \rightarrow \text{scaled scores} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{attention probabilities} } later: \boxed{ \text{attention probabilities} \rightarrow av \rightarrow \text{context vector} } and eventually: \boxed{ \text{context} \rightarrow \text{transformer block} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{probability} \rightarrow \text{decoding} } sources used for this step primary mathematical/llm grounding build a large language model (from scratch) — vector/matrix operations, learned weight matrices, q/k/v projections, attention scores. independent depth scoring pending. step 0.2 — probability → log-probability → softmax plan node: i0 · chat order #3 now we move from the linear-algebra primitives we just learned into the probability machinery that turns transformer outputs into meaningful distributions. this step is extremely important because the same mathematical ideas will later reappear in: attention → language-model training → decoding → distillation → kl divergence → rl/ppo/grpo. the master cheatsheet explicitly places these formulas at the mathematical foundation of the transformer and language-model objective. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.1 first: what problem are we trying to solve? suppose the transformer has processed: the cat is and now must predict the next token. the model does not directly output: "sleeping" instead, the final layer produces a vector of arbitrary real numbers called logits : z = \begin{bmatrix} 2.1\\ 0.3\\ 4.2\\ 1.0\\ ... \end{bmatrix} there is one logit for every vocabulary token. for example: token logit the 2.1 dog 0.3 sleeping 4.2 ran 1.0 ... ... but these numbers are not probabilities . they can be: negative positive larger than 1 smaller than 0 so we need a transformation: \boxed{\text{logits} \rightarrow \text{probabilities}} that transformation is softmax . 0.2.2 what is a probability distribution? suppose we have five possible next tokens. a probability distribution could be: p=[0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] a valid discrete probability distribution must satisfy two conditions: p_i\ge 0 and \sum_i p_i=1 so: 0.05+0.10+0.60+0.05+0.20=1 this means: all possible outcomes share 100% of the probability mass. this is exactly the kind of distribution a language model needs when choosing its next token. the supplied minillm material gives a concrete example where the next-token distribution is: [0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] for {the, cat, sat, dog, ran} . (source: minillm-slides) 0.2.3 why does a language model need probabilities? because language generation is inherently uncertain. take: the sky is possible continuations might be: p(\text{blue})=0.60 p(\text{cloudy})=0.15 p(\text{clear})=0.10 p(\text{dark})=0.05 etc. the model is effectively saying: given the context, how likely is each possible next token? mathematically: \boxed{p(x_t\mid x_{<t})} where: x_t = current/next token x_{<t} = all previous tokens this conditional probability is the heart of autoregressive language modeling. the nlp with transformers book describes gpt-style language modeling exactly this way: the model estimates the probability of a token sequence through conditional next-token probabilities. (source: natural language processing with transformers _ building) 0.2.4 autoregressive probability suppose the sentence is: i love cats let the tokens be: x_1=i,\quad x_2=love,\quad x_3=cats we want the probability of the whole sequence : p(i,love,cats) using the chain rule of probability: \boxed{ p(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } so: p(i,love,cats) = p(i)\, p(love\mid i)\, p(cats\mid i,love) this is called autoregressive factorization . it is in your cheatsheet as the language-model objective. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.5 why factorization matters calculating the probability of every possible full sentence directly would be impossible. instead, the model breaks the problem into manageable pieces: \text{whole sequence} becomes \text{next-token prediction at position 1} \text{next-token prediction at position 2} \text{next-token prediction at position 3} etc. so a transformer doesn't need to directly model: p(\text{"the cat sat on the mat"}) as one giant indivisible object. it models: p(\text{the}) then p(\text{cat}\mid\text{the}) then p(\text{sat}\mid\text{the cat}) and so on. this is the foundation of both training and generation . 0.2.6 the problem with multiplying probabilities consider: 0.8\times0.7\times0.9\times0.6\times0.5 =0.1512 now imagine a sequence of 1,000 tokens. you might multiply hundreds or thousands of numbers like: 0.001\times0.02\times0.4\times0.003\times\cdots the result becomes extremely tiny. this creates numerical problems. so we use logarithms . 0.2.7 log-probability take: p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_t p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) apply \log : \log p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \log \left( \prod_t p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) \right) using: \log(ab)=\log a+\log b we obtain: \boxed{ \log p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_t \log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } so multiplication becomes addition. that is enormously more convenient computationally. example suppose: p_1=0.8 p_2=0.7 p_3=0.9 then: p_{\text{sequence}} = 0.8(0.7)(0.9) = 0.504 log form: \log(0.504) which is equivalent to: \log(0.8)+\log(0.7)+\log(0.9) so instead of multiplying many tiny values, we add log-probabilities. 0.2.8 why are log-probabilities negative? because for probabilities: 0<p\le1 and therefore: \log p\le0 for example: \log(1)=0 \log(0.5)\approx-0.693 \log(0.1)\approx-2.303 \log(0.001)\approx-6.908 so: higher probability → log probability closer to 0. lower probability → more negative log probability. this gives us a very useful way to measure how well the model predicted the correct token. 0.2.9 negative log-probability because log probabilities are negative, training usually minimizes: \boxed{ -\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } this is the negative log-likelihood loss for one token . look at what happens: model predicts correct token with probability 0.9 -\log(0.9)\approx0.105 very small loss. model predicts it with probability 0.5 -\log(0.5)\approx0.693 larger loss. model predicts it with probability 0.01 -\log(0.01)\approx4.605 huge loss. therefore: \boxed{\text{better probability for the correct token} \rightarrow \text{smaller loss}} the cheatsheet expresses the per-position loss as: l_t=-\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}) and sequence-average loss as the mean over positions. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.10 now we reach softmax we have logits: z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_v where v is vocabulary size. we need to convert them into: p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_v such that: p_i\ge0 and: \sum_i p_i=1 softmax does exactly this. \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}} {\sum_j e^{z_j}} } this formula appears directly in the mathematical cheatsheet. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.11 understand softmax from the inside out suppose: z=[1,2,3] step 1: exponentiate e^1\approx2.718 e^2\approx7.389 e^3\approx20.086 so: [e^1,e^2,e^3] \approx [2.718,7.389,20.086] step 2: calculate the sum 2.718+7.389+20.086 = 30.193 step 3: divide each by the total p_1=\frac{2.718}{30.193}\approx0.090 p_2=\frac{7.389}{30.193}\approx0.245 p_3=\frac{20.086}{30.193}\approx0.665 therefore: \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}([1,2,3]) \approx [0.090,0.245,0.665] } check: 0.090+0.245+0.665\approx1 0.2.12 why the exponential? this is an important why , not a memorization detail. softmax uses: e^{z_i} for several useful reasons. 1. it guarantees positivity exponentials are always positive: e^z>0 so the resulting probabilities cannot be negative. 2. it preserves ordering if: z_3>z_2 then: e^{z_3}>e^{z_2} so larger logits still produce larger probabilities. 3. it amplifies differences compare: z=[1,2] difference = 1. exponentials: [e^1,e^2]=[2.718,7.389] now the larger value dominates much more strongly. this gives softmax a useful competitive behavior. 4. it normalizes dividing by: \sum_j e^{z_j} forces the results to sum to 1. so softmax is essentially: \boxed{ \text{positive transformation + normalization} } 0.2.13 logits are not probabilities this distinction is essential. suppose: z=[2,1,-1] these are logits. you cannot say: "token 1 has probability 2." that is impossible. after softmax: \operatorname{softmax}(z) produces valid probabilities. so: \boxed{ \text{logit} \neq \text{probability} } pipeline: \boxed{ \text{transformer hidden state} \rightarrow \text{linear projection} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{probabilities} } 0.2.14 a very important transformer connection remember our earlier attention equation: s=qk^t these are also just scores . they are not probabilities. then: a=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{qk^t}{\sqrt{d_k}}+m\right) produces attention weights. the attention handbook describes the process as: project → compare → scale → constrain → normalize → aggregate. in particular, row-wise softmax turns the compatibility scores into nonnegative weights that sum to one across allowed keys. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) so softmax appears in two extremely important places: attention \boxed{\text{scores}\rightarrow\text{attention weights}} output layer \boxed{\text{logits}\rightarrow\text{token probabilities}} same mathematical operation. different semantic purpose. 0.2.15 attention softmax vs language-model softmax this distinction is worth memorizing. suppose a sequence has n=4 tokens. attention scores for token 3 might be: [1.2,\;2.0,\;0.4,\;-\infty] after causal masking and softmax: [0.31,\;0.69,\;0.00,\;0.00] these tell us how the query distributes its attention over allowable positions. but at the output layer we might have: z=[2.1,0.7,4.3,-1.2,\ldots] softmax turns these into probabilities over the vocabulary . thus: softmax location distribution is over attention positions/tokens being attended to output layer vocabulary tokens this distinction will become very important later when we study decoding . 0.2.16 causal masking + softmax suppose we have: s= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5\\ 3 & 2 & 4\\ 1 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} for a causal language model: token 1 cannot look at future tokens 2 and 3. token 2 cannot look at future token 3. so we use a mask: m= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\infty & -\infty\\ 0 & 0 & -\infty\\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} therefore: s+m = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -\infty & -\infty\\ 3 & 2 & -\infty\\ 1 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} now apply softmax row-by-row. for row 1: \operatorname{softmax}[2,-\infty,-\infty] = [1,0,0] for row 2: \operatorname{softmax}[3,2,-\infty] gives approximately: [0.731,0.269,0] the -\infty effectively produces zero probability. so the causal mask works because: e^{-\infty}\rightarrow0 this is the mathematical mechanism behind preventing future-token information leakage. 0.2.17 softmax has a beautiful property: shift invariance suppose: z=[1,2,3] now add 10 to every number: z'=[11,12,13] softmax gives exactly the same result: \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}(z+c) = \operatorname{softmax}(z) } why? because: \frac{e^{z_i+c}} {\sum_j e^{z_j+c}} can be rewritten as: \frac{e^c e^{z_i}} {e^c\sum_j e^{z_j}} and e^c cancels. this gives us a very useful computational trick. 0.2.18 numerically stable softmax instead of calculating: \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} we usually compute: \boxed{ \operatorname{softmax}(z) = \operatorname{softmax}(z-\max(z)) } example: z=[1000,1001,1002] directly computing e^{1000} can overflow numerically. instead subtract 1002: [-2,-1,0] then: \operatorname{softmax}([1000,1001,1002]) = \operatorname{softmax}([-2,-1,0]) same probabilities, much safer numerically. 0.2.19 temperature now introduce another concept that will become central in decoding . temperature modifies softmax: \boxed{ p_i= \frac{e^{z_i/t}} {\sum_j e^{z_j/t}} } where: t>0 case 1: t=1 normal softmax. case 2: t<1 the distribution becomes sharper . example: t=0.5 logits become effectively: [2z_1,2z_2,\ldots] differences get amplified. the highest-probability token tends to dominate. case 3: t>1 the distribution becomes flatter . differences between logits matter less. more probability spreads to lower-ranked alternatives. intuition think of temperature as a control over certainty: \boxed{ t\downarrow \rightarrow \text{sharper} } \boxed{ t\uparrow \rightarrow \text{flatter} } this will later become a major text-decoding mechanism. 0.2.20 one-hot targets now connect probability to training. suppose vocabulary: [\text{the},\text{cat},\text{sat},\text{dog},\text{ran}] the correct next token is: sat represent the target as a one-hot vector: y=[0,0,1,0,0] suppose the model predicts: q=[0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] so: q_{\text{sat}}=0.60 the loss is: \boxed{ l=-\log(0.60) } l\approx0.5108 this exact worked example appears in the supplied minillm material. (source: minillm-slides) notice something interesting: the model predicted probabilities for all five tokens, but for a one-hot target the loss ultimately depends on the probability assigned to the correct token . 0.2.21 why negative log probability is such a good loss suppose the correct answer is sat . prediction a p(\text{sat})=0.9 loss: -\log(0.9)=0.105 prediction b p(\text{sat})=0.5 loss: -\log(0.5)=0.693 prediction c p(\text{sat})=0.01 loss: -\log(0.01)=4.605 this means the loss heavily punishes confidently wrong predictions . that's exactly what we want. a model saying: "i am 99% sure the answer is wrong" should be punished much more strongly than a model saying: "i am only somewhat uncertain." 0.2.22 from one token to the entire sentence for n tokens: l_t=-\log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}) average: \boxed{ l = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}) } this is the standard next-token training objective shown in your cheatsheet. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) therefore the complete training chain is: \boxed{ \text{tokens} \rightarrow \text{transformer} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{probabilities} \rightarrow -\log p(\text{correct token}) \rightarrow \text{loss} } that chain is one of the most important chains in the entire course. 0.2.23 connection to attention now connect today's lesson to yesterday's linear algebra. yesterday: q=xw_q k=xw_k v=xw_v then: s=qk^t today we add: a=\operatorname{softmax}(s/\sqrt{d_k}+m) and: o=av so we have: \boxed{ x \rightarrow q,k,v \rightarrow qk^t \rightarrow \text{scaled scores} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow a \rightarrow av } the attention handbook explicitly emphasizes that the attention weights are intermediate coefficients and that the actual output is av . (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) this is why yesterday's dot product was not the end of the story. 0.2.24 extremely important distinction there are now three different kinds of numbers you must not mix up: 1. learned parameters for example: w_q these are model parameters learned during training. 2. scores / logits examples: qk^t or final vocabulary logits: z these are raw compatibility/evidence scores. 3. normalized weights/probabilities examples: a=\operatorname{softmax}(qk^t) or: p=\operatorname{softmax}(z) these are normalized values. raschka explicitly distinguishes learned weight parameters from dynamic attention weights. (source: build a large language model (from scratch)) 0.2.25 the entire mathematical picture so far we can now build the first major chain: token ↓ embedding vector ↓ matrix transformations ↓ q, k, v ↓ dot product ↓ raw attention scores ↓ scale by √d_k ↓ causal mask ↓ softmax ↓ attention weights ↓ weighted sum of v ↓ contextual representation ↓ transformer layers ↓ final hidden state ↓ linear projection ↓ vocabulary logits ↓ softmax ↓ next-token probability distribution ↓ -log(probability of correct token) ↓ training loss once this chain is solid, a huge portion of transformer mathematics becomes much easier. 0.2.26 tensor-shape grounding let's make this precise. suppose: x\in\mathbb r^{n\times d} then: q=xw_q with: w_q\in\mathbb r^{d\times d_k} so: q\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k} likewise: k\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_k} therefore: qk^t has shape: (n\times d_k)(d_k\times n) giving: \boxed{n\times n} then: a\in\mathbb r^{n\times n} and if: v\in\mathbb r^{n\times d_v} then: av = (n\times n)(n\times d_v) giving: \boxed{n\times d_v} these exact shape relationships are summarized in your transformer cheatsheet. (source: step1_transformers_mathematical_cheatsheet) 0.2.27 a tiny complete numerical example let's make the entire softmax calculation concrete. suppose the model produces three logits: z=[2,1,0] exponentials: [e^2,e^1,e^0] \approx[7.389,2.718,1] sum: 7.389+2.718+1=11.107 therefore: p_1=\frac{7.389}{11.107}\approx0.665 p_2=\frac{2.718}{11.107}\approx0.245 p_3=\frac{1}{11.107}\approx0.090 so: \boxed{ p\approx[0.665,0.245,0.090] } suppose the correct token is token 2. then: l=-\log(0.245) \boxed{l\approx1.407} so the model receives a substantially larger penalty than it would if the correct token had probability 0.9. 0.2.28 pytorch implementation this is the computation you should be able to recognize immediately in code. import torch import torch.nn.functional as f # raw logits from a model logits = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # convert logits to probabilities probs = f.softmax(logits, dim=-1) print("logits:", logits) print("probabilities:", probs) print("sum:", probs.sum()) # suppose token 2 is the correct answer target = torch.tensor(1) # negative log probability loss = -torch.log(probs[target]) print("probability of correct token:", probs[target]) print("loss:", loss) conceptually: logits ↓ softmax ↓ probabilities ↓ select correct-token probability ↓ -log(...) ↓ loss 0.2.29 a safer practical version in real pytorch training, you usually don't manually do: softmax() -log() for the language-model loss. instead, functions such as cross-entropy loss are designed to operate directly on logits in a numerically stable way. that is one reason the next lesson— entropy, cross-entropy, and kl divergence —is so important. 0.2.30 what you should understand, not memorize at this point you should be able to explain: why probability? because the model needs to represent uncertainty over possible next tokens. why logits? because the neural network naturally produces unconstrained real-valued scores. why softmax? because we need to transform those scores into nonnegative normalized values. why log? because sequence probabilities are products, and logarithms convert products into sums while improving numerical behavior. why negative log probability? because we want high probability on the correct answer to correspond to low loss. why does softmax appear in attention? because raw compatibility scores need to become normalized coefficients before we aggregate value vectors. 0.2.31 one subtle point: attention weights are not automatically "probabilities" in the ordinary semantic sense mathematically, a row of attention weights has the properties: a_i\ge0 and \sum_i a_i=1 so it behaves like a distribution over positions. but we should be careful with interpretation. it does not automatically mean: "the model believes there is a 70% probability that this token is the reason for the prediction." the attention handbook specifically warns against automatically treating attention weights as faithful explanations of model decisions. (source: understanding_attention_handbook_01) this distinction will matter later when you study transformer interpretability. 0.2.32 master connection you can now see why our first two mathematical lessons were ordered this way. we started: \boxed{\text{vectors}} because embeddings, queries, keys, and values are vectors. then: \boxed{\text{matrices}} because projections and batched transformations are matrix operations. then: \boxed{\text{dot product}} because it creates compatibility scores. now: \boxed{\text{probability}} because scores must often become normalized distributions. then: \boxed{\text{log probability}} because language-model sequence probabilities are products. then: \boxed{\text{softmax}} because it converts raw scores into normalized weights/probabilities. next we need to understand: \boxed{ \text{entropy} \rightarrow \text{cross-entropy} \rightarrow \text{kl divergence} } because those concepts are the mathematical bridge from ordinary language-model training to: knowledge distillation → rlhf → rlvr → ppo → grpo → deepseek-r1. master check — 0.2 try these without looking back. q1 why can't a vector like: [2.3,-1.7,5.2] be directly interpreted as probabilities? independent depth scoring pending. step 0.3 — entropy → cross-entropy → kl divergence plan node: i0 · chat order #4 this is one of the most important mathematical steps in the entire course. you already understand: \text{logits}\rightarrow\text{softmax}\rightarrow\text{probabilities} now we need to answer: how do we measure whether one probability distribution is good, uncertain, or different from another? that gives us: \boxed{\text{entropy}} \boxed{\text{cross-entropy}} \boxed{\text{kl divergence}} and these are not isolated formulas. they form a chain that later becomes: \text{lm training} \rightarrow \text{knowledge distillation} \rightarrow \text{rlhf/rlvr} \rightarrow \text{ppo/grpo} your master cheatsheet explicitly places entropy, cross-entropy, and kl in the probability/information-theory foundation, and later uses kl directly in distillation and rl. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs) 0.3.1 first question: what is entropy trying to measure? suppose a model has two possible outcomes. distribution a p=[1,0] the model is completely certain. distribution b p=[0.5,0.5] the model has no preference. intuitively: \boxed{\text{distribution b is more uncertain than distribution a}} entropy gives us a mathematical way to quantify that uncertainty. 0.3.2 entropy for a discrete distribution: \boxed{ h(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i } where: p = probability distribution p_i = probability of outcome i h(p) = entropy this formula is part of the mathematical foundation in your master cheatsheet. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs) 0.3.3 why the minus sign? we already learned: 0<p_i\le1 therefore: \log p_i\le0 so: p_i\log p_i\le0 without the minus sign, entropy would generally be negative. we want uncertainty to be represented as a nonnegative quantity, so: -\sum p_i\log p_i is used. 0.3.4 perfect certainty take: p=[1,0] then: h(p) = -[1\log1+0\log0] since: \log1=0 the first term is zero. the 0\log0 term is interpreted through its limiting value as zero. therefore: \boxed{h(p)=0} so: a completely certain distribution has zero entropy. 0.3.5 maximum uncertainty for two outcomes now: p=[0.5,0.5] then: h(p) = -[0.5\log0.5+0.5\log0.5] since: \log(0.5)\approx-0.6931 we get: h(p)\approx0.6931 thus: \boxed{ h([0.5,0.5])\approx0.693 } which is larger than zero. therefore: \boxed{ \text{more spread-out distribution} \rightarrow \text{higher entropy} } 0.3.6 three outcomes consider: p=[1/3,1/3,1/3] entropy: h(p) = -3\left(\frac13\log\frac13\right) = -\log(1/3) =\log3 using natural logarithms: \boxed{h(p)\approx1.099} so the maximum entropy increases as more possible outcomes become equally likely. for v equally likely outcomes: \boxed{h_{\max}=\log v} when using natural logarithms. 0.3.7 the intuition behind entropy think of entropy as: how spread out is the probability mass? very concentrated: [0.99,0.01] → low entropy. very spread out: [0.5,0.5] → high entropy. for a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens, a model assigning almost all probability to one token has relatively low entropy, while a model spreading probability broadly across thousands of alternatives has higher entropy. 0.3.8 another interpretation: surprise there is another extremely useful interpretation. the surprise of observing event i is: \boxed{ i(i)=-\log p_i } why? because: highly likely event → small surprise unlikely event → large surprise for example: p=0.9 gives: -\log(0.9)\approx0.105 while: p=0.01 gives: -\log(0.01)\approx4.605 entropy is the expected surprise : \boxed{ h(p)=e_{x\sim p}[-\log p(x)] } expanding the expectation gives: h(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x) so entropy means: if outcomes are actually generated according to p , how much surprise do we expect on average? 0.3.9 now the crucial question: what is cross-entropy? entropy talks about: the distribution itself. cross-entropy asks: what happens when the true distribution is p , but i use another distribution q to assign probabilities? the formula is: \boxed{ h(p,q) = -\sum_i p_i\log q_i } your supplied hands-on machine learning text gives this exact definition and explains that cross-entropy is larger than the entropy of the true distribution when the assumed distribution is imperfect. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron) 0.3.10 why are there two distributions? this is the key conceptual difference. entropy: h(p) = -\sum_i p_i\log p_i uses: p\rightarrow p cross-entropy: h(p,q) = -\sum_i p_i\log q_i uses: p\rightarrow q so: quantity meaning h(p) uncertainty inherent in p h(p,q) how costly it is to encode outcomes from p using q 0.3.11 numerical example let's use: p=[0.7,0.2,0.1] and suppose our model uses: q=[0.6,0.3,0.1] first calculate entropy of p : h(p) = -[0.7\log0.7+0.2\log0.2+0.1\log0.1] numerically: \boxed{h(p)\approx0.802} now cross-entropy: h(p,q) = -[0.7\log0.6+0.2\log0.3+0.1\log0.1] giving: \boxed{h(p,q)\approx0.829} notice: 0.829>0.802 why? because q isn't exactly p . 0.3.12 the beautiful relationship cross-entropy can be decomposed into: \boxed{ h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) } this identity is explicitly used in the supplied minillm material to explain knowledge distillation. (source: minillm-slides) this equation is tremendously important. let's understand it rather than memorize it. 0.3.13 what is kl divergence? kl divergence measures how different q is from p , in an information-theoretic sense: \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i \log \frac{p_i}{q_i} } your supplied active-learning material describes kl divergence as measuring the difference between a true distribution p and an approximating distribution q , and notes that it is zero when the two distributions match. 0.3.14 derive the cross-entropy identity start with kl: d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i \log\frac{p_i}{q_i} use: \log\frac{a}{b} = \log a-\log b therefore: d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i\log p_i - \sum_i p_i\log q_i now recall: h(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i and: h(p,q)=-\sum_i p_i\log q_i so: d_{kl}(p\|q) = -h(p)+h(p,q) rearrange: \boxed{ h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) } there is the identity. 0.3.15 what does this identity actually mean? it says: \boxed{ \text{cross-entropy} = \text{intrinsic uncertainty} + \text{mismatch penalty} } specifically: h(p) is unavoidable uncertainty in the original distribution. and: d_{kl}(p\|q) is the additional cost caused by using the wrong distribution q . this is a fantastic mental model. 0.3.16 what happens when p=q ? suppose: q=p then: d_{kl}(p\|p) = \sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{p_i} = \sum_i p_i\log1 =0 therefore: h(p,p) = h(p) so: \boxed{ \text{perfect match} \rightarrow kl=0 \rightarrow ce=entropy } this exact idea is demonstrated in the supplied minillm slides: when the student exactly matches the teacher, kl is zero but the distillation cross-entropy remains equal to the teacher's entropy. (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.17 let's verify our numerical example we had: h(p)\approx0.8018 and: h(p,q)\approx0.8286 therefore: d_{kl}(p\|q) = h(p,q)-h(p) \approx0.8286-0.8018 \boxed{d_{kl}(p\|q)\approx0.0268} so: 0.8286 = 0.8018+0.0268 exactly. 0.3.18 important property: kl is nonnegative for valid distributions: \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q)\ge0 } and: d_{kl}(p\|q)=0 only when: p=q under the usual conditions. therefore: h(p,q)\ge h(p) this means: using the wrong distribution cannot give you lower cross-entropy than the true distribution's own entropy. 0.3.19 but kl is not a distance this is a common interview/exam trap. people often casually call kl a "distance," but technically it is a divergence , not a metric. why? a metric generally requires symmetry: d(p,q)=d(q,p) but kl generally does not satisfy this. usually: \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q)\neq d_{kl}(q\|p) } this asymmetry becomes extremely important later in knowledge distillation . 0.3.20 forward kl vs reverse kl there are two directions. forward kl \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q) } reverse kl \boxed{ d_{kl}(q\|p) } they are not interchangeable. your minillm materials explicitly distinguish these two and discuss their different behavior. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) 0.3.21 why direction matters consider p as the teacher and q as the student. forward kl: d_{kl}(p\|q) = \sum_xp(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} the teacher's probabilities p(x) are used as weights. so if the teacher assigns meaningful probability to something and the student gives it almost zero, the student gets heavily penalized. this tends toward covering teacher-supported modes . your supplied minillm material describes forward kl as strongly penalizing missing teacher-supported modes. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) reverse kl: d_{kl}(q\|p) = \sum_xq(x)\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} now the student's distribution determines which regions are emphasized. it strongly penalizes putting probability mass where the teacher says probability is very low. this is associated with mode-seeking behavior in the supplied minillm explanation. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) we will return to this in depth when we reach minillm . 0.3.22 cross-entropy in language-model training now connect today's mathematics directly to transformers. suppose vocabulary: v=\{\text{the, cat, sat, dog, ran}\} correct token: y=\text{sat} one-hot target: p=[0,0,1,0,0] model distribution: q=[0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] cross-entropy: h(p,q) = -\sum_ip_i\log q_i because all p_i are zero except the correct token: = -\log0.60 \boxed{ h(p,q)=0.5108 } this exact example is in the supplied minillm slides. (source: minillm-slides) so ordinary next-token training is just cross-entropy with a one-hot target. 0.3.23 why does one-hot cross-entropy collapse to -\log q_y ? suppose: y=[0,0,1,0] and: q=[0.1,0.2,0.6,0.1] then: -\sum_i y_i\log q_i becomes: - [ 0\log0.1+ 0\log0.2+ 1\log0.6+ 0\log0.1 ] everything disappears except: \boxed{-\log0.6} this is why the ordinary lm loss focuses on the probability assigned to the observed token. 0.3.24 now the big connection: distillation imagine we replace the hard one-hot target: [0,0,1,0,0] with the teacher's output: p_{\text{teacher}} = [0.02,0.05,0.70,0.03,0.20] now the student might predict: q_{\text{student}} = [0.05,0.10,0.60,0.05,0.20] the loss becomes: \boxed{ h(p_{\text{teacher}},q_{\text{student}}) = -\sum_v p_{\text{teacher}}(v) \log q_{\text{student}}(v) } now every vocabulary item contributes . this is the mathematical reason knowledge distillation carries more information than one-hot supervision. the supplied minillm example explicitly shows that the teacher's entire probability shape—not just the true token—is used. (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.25 why call this "dark knowledge"? suppose the teacher says: p= [0.01,0.02,0.70,0.05,0.22] a one-hot label only says: sat is correct. it loses the teacher's relative judgments among wrong answers. but the teacher distribution tells us: p(\text{sat})=0.70 p(\text{ran})=0.22 p(\text{dog})=0.05 etc. so the student learns: sat is preferred, but ran is also somewhat plausible. that extra structure is what the distillation material refers to as dark knowledge . (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.26 why temperature enters distillation a teacher may produce: [0.999,0.0005,0.0003,\ldots] that distribution is too sharp to reveal much information about secondary choices. temperature modifies logits before softmax: \boxed{ p_i^{(t)} = \frac{e^{z_i/t}} {\sum_j e^{z_j/t}} } with: t>1 the distribution becomes softer. for example: [0.999,0.0005,0.0003] might become something more informative such as: [0.70,0.20,0.10] the exact numbers depend on the logits, but the conceptual point is: \boxed{ t>1 \rightarrow \text{more information in the relative alternatives} } the supplied minillm slides explicitly use temperature to soften teacher outputs and expose relative confidence among alternatives. (source: minillm-slides) this will become a whole topic later. 0.3.27 the same kl appears later in rl this is where today's lesson becomes much more powerful. in reinforcement learning for language models, we often don't want the updated policy to move arbitrarily far from a reference policy. so kl divergence appears as a constraint or penalty. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{reward improvement} - \text{penalty for moving too far} } one common structure is: j(\theta) = e[r] - \beta d_{kl}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) the exact objective varies by method, but the mathematical idea is the same: \boxed{ kl=\text{distribution mismatch} } your master cheatsheet explicitly places kl in both knowledge distillation and rl sections. (source: master_mathematical_cheatsheet_all_lecture_pdfs_v2) so understanding kl now will make later rl mathematics much easier. 0.3.28 a unifying view we now have: entropy \boxed{ h(p)=e_{x\sim p}[-\log p(x)] } interpretation: how uncertain/spread out is p ? cross-entropy \boxed{ h(p,q)=e_{x\sim p}[-\log q(x)] } interpretation: how much surprise do i incur when data comes from p , but i use q to predict it? kl divergence \boxed{ d_{kl}(p\|q) = e_{x\sim p} \left[ \log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \right] } interpretation: how much extra information cost/mismatch arises from using q instead of p ? and: \boxed{ h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) } 0.3.29 the complete conceptual graph probability distribution │ ├───────────────┐ ↓ ↓ entropy cross-entropy │ │ │ │ │ ↓ │ kl divergence │ │ └───────┬───────┘ ↓ distribution mismatch │ ┌───────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ knowledge rl distillation ppo / grpo and ordinary language-model training sits underneath: logits ↓ softmax ↓ probability distribution q ↓ cross-entropy with target ↓ loss 0.3.30 one subtle but very important distinction do not confuse these: h(p) with: h(p,q) with: d_{kl}(p\|q) their roles are different. formula what it measures h(p) uncertainty of p itself h(p,q) prediction/encoding cost when true distribution is p , model uses q d_{kl}(p\vert q) mismatch between p and q and: \boxed{ ce = entropy + kl } not: ce=kl however, when optimizing q_\theta with p fixed: h(p) doesn't depend on \theta . therefore: \boxed{ \arg\min_\theta h(p,q_\theta) = \arg\min_\theta d_{kl}(p\|q_\theta) } this is why a distillation cross-entropy objective can be described as equivalent to minimizing forward kl with respect to the student's parameters. the supplied minillm material makes exactly this point. (source: minillm-slides) 0.3.31 why this matters for the entire course you've now built a mathematical bridge: \boxed{ \text{softmax} \rightarrow \text{probability distribution} \rightarrow \text{log probability} \rightarrow \text{entropy} \rightarrow \text{cross-entropy} \rightarrow \text{kl} } later: \boxed{ kl \rightarrow \text{distillation} } and: \boxed{ kl \rightarrow \text{rlhf/rlvr} \rightarrow ppo \rightarrow grpo } and later still: \boxed{ grpo \rightarrow deepseekmath \rightarrow deepseek-r1 } so this is not a side chapter of information theory. it is part of the mathematical spine of the whole curriculum. 0.3.32 master numerical example given: p=[0.7,0.2,0.1] q=[0.6,0.3,0.1] we found: \boxed{h(p)\approx0.8018} \boxed{h(p,q)\approx0.8286} \boxed{d_{kl}(p\|q)\approx0.0268} and verify: \boxed{ 0.8286\approx0.8018+0.0268 } this one example contains the entire relationship. 0.3.33 code it import torch p = torch.tensor([0.7, 0.2, 0.1]) q = torch.tensor([0.6, 0.3, 0.1]) # entropy h(p) entropy = -(p * torch.log(p)).sum() # cross-entropy h(p, q) cross_entropy = -(p * torch.log(q)).sum() # kl divergence d_kl(p || q) kl_divergence = (p * torch.log(p / q)).sum() print("entropy:", entropy.item()) print("cross-entropy:", cross_entropy.item()) print("kl divergence:", kl_divergence.item()) print("entropy + kl:", (entropy + kl_divergence).item()) you should observe approximately: entropy: 0.8018 cross-entropy: 0.8286 kl divergence: 0.0268 entropy + kl: 0.8286 0.3.34 one more connection to gradients you already learned in the previous lesson that we minimize negative log probability. cross-entropy gives us the same training objective: l = -\sum_i y_i\log q_i where y is the target distribution. for a one-hot target: l=-\log q_y and with softmax outputs, the gradient with respect to a class logit has the particularly elegant form: \boxed{ \frac{\partial l}{\partial z_i}=q_i-y_i } this is one of the reasons softmax + cross-entropy is so convenient for training neural networks. the supplied hands-on machine learning text derives the corresponding softmax-regression gradient in terms of predicted probabilities minus target indicators. (source: hands-on machine learning with scikit-lear - aurelien geron) we will derive this carefully in the calculus/optimization foundation step , rather than skipping the derivation. 0.3.35 your mental model should now be when you see: -\log p think: surprise / penalty for predicting probability p when you see: h(p) think: uncertainty of a distribution when you see: h(p,q) think: how well q predicts outcomes from p when you see: d_{kl}(p\|q) think: how much q differs from p , measured from p 's perspective when you see: h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) think: prediction cost = irreducible uncertainty + mismatch master check — step 0.3 do these before we move forward. q1 which distribution is more uncertain? p_1=[1,0] or: p_2=[0.5,0.5] and why? q2 calculate: h([0.5,0.5]) using natural logarithms. q3 what is the conceptual difference between: h(p) and: h(p,q)? q4 given: p=[0.5,0.5] q=[0.8,0.2] which quantity tells us that q does not perfectly match p ? q5 what happens to: d_{kl}(p\|q) when: p=q? q6 is: d_{kl}(p\|q) = d_{kl}(q\|p) generally true? q7 derive: h(p,q)=h(p)+d_{kl}(p\|q) in two or three mathematical steps. q8 why does ordinary lm cross-entropy with a one-hot target reduce to: -\log q_y? q9 why can we optimize cross-entropy and forward kl interchangeably when the teacher distribution p is fixed? q10 — the big one explain this entire chain in your own words: \boxed{ \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{softmax} \rightarrow p \rightarrow \text{cross-entropy} \rightarrow \text{kl} }
