(source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.21 numerical entropy example suppose a vocabulary has only two possible tokens: p=[0.9,0.1]. then: h = -(0.9\ln0.9+0.1\ln0.1). using: \ln0.9\approx-0.1053 and: \ln0.1\approx-2.3026, we get: h\approx0.325. so the model is relatively confident. 5.8.22 uniform distribution for two tokens: p=[0.5,0.5]. then: h = -(0.5\ln0.5+0.5\ln0.5) =\ln2 \approx0.693. thus: \boxed{\text{more uncertainty}\rightarrow\text{higher entropy}} 5.8.23 source's rough entropy interpretation the source gives rough rules of thumb: 0\text{–}0.5 → very low entropy, highly confident. 1\text{–}2 → moderate entropy. high entropy approaching: \log(|v|) means probabilities are spread across many tokens. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) for the source's toy vocabulary: |v|=7. maximum entropy: h_{\max}=\ln7\approx1.9459. 5.8.24 why entropy is useful in reasoning rl suppose: h: 1.8\rightarrow1.5\rightarrow1.2\rightarrow0.8. the model is becoming increasingly confident. that can be healthy. but suppose: 1.8\rightarrow1.3\rightarrow0.2 very rapidly. that may indicate: \boxed{\text{entropy collapse}} where the policy becomes too deterministic too quickly. the source explicitly identifies a sudden collapse to very low entropy as a warning sign of unstable training. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.25 important distinction: low entropy is not automatically bad a reasoning model eventually becoming more confident can be desirable. the source actually says: entropy should gradually decrease as the model becomes more confident. the problem is sudden collapse , not merely decreasing entropy. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) so: \boxed{ \text{gradual entropy decrease} \approx \text{potentially healthy} } whereas: \boxed{ \text{rapid entropy collapse} \approx \text{warning} } 5.8.26 put the advanced metrics together now imagine this training history: step reward eval acc resp. len entropy 0 0.20 30% 180 1.80 100 0.40 42% 240 1.55 200 0.60 51% 310 1.30 300 0.68 54% 360 1.10 400 0.70 45% 180 0.30 look carefully. at step 400: r\approx0.70 still looks good. but: \text{eval acc}:54\%\rightarrow45\% and: \text{length}:360\rightarrow180 and: h:1.10\rightarrow0.30. that is a much stronger warning than reward alone. 5.8.27 this is why metrics must be interpreted jointly never say: “reward increased, therefore training succeeded.” instead ask: \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\text{did reward improve?}\\ &\text{did evaluation accuracy improve?}\\ &\text{is response length sensible?}\\ &\text{are loss spikes controlled?}\\ &\text{are advantages providing useful variation?}\\ &\text{is entropy changing gradually?} \end{aligned} } that is the correct grpo-debugging mindset. 5.8.28 now the most interesting source experiment: format reward so far the reward was primarily: \boxed{\text{answer correctness}} for example: r_{\text{correct}}= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{correct}\\ 0 & \text{wrong} \end{cases} the source then adds an auxiliary signal: \boxed{\text{format reward}}. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.29 what is the format reward? the experiment wants the model to structure reasoning as: <think> reasoning... </think> \boxed{answer} the source defines: r_{\text{format}}= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{<think> appears before </think>}\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.30 total reward with format the source uses: \boxed{ r= r_{\text{rlvr}} + w_fr_{\text{format}} } where: w_f=\text{format\_reward\_weight}. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) suppose: r_{\text{correct}}=1 and: r_{\text{format}}=1 with: w_f=1. then: r=1+1=2. 5.8.31 why was this experiment done? because the researchers/book want to make the output structure explicit: \boxed{ \text{reasoning} \rightarrow \text{final answer} } the <think> markers separate those parts. but now we have created a new problem: what happens if the model learns to optimize format rather than correct reasoning ? and this is exactly what the source investigates. 5.8.32 the surprising result in the source's format-reward run: the model improves initially; later evaluation accuracy becomes worse; average reward stays approximately constant; shorter response lengths correlate with the later accuracy decline. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) this is a beautiful rl example of: \boxed{\text{reward design matters}} 5.8.33 why can this happen? suppose: r_{\text{correct}}\in\{0,1\} and: r_{\text{format}}\in\{0,1\}. with: w_f=1, consider these two responses: response a correct + correct format: r=1+1=2. response b wrong + correct format: r=0+1=1. therefore even a wrong answer gets positive reward. the model receives reinforcement for: \boxed{\text{format adherence}} without necessarily receiving reinforcement for: \boxed{\text{correctness}}. the source gives this as one possible explanation for the observed degradation. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.34 this is a reward-hacking-like phenomenon conceptually: what we want: correct reasoning + correct answer + proper format but our reward says: correctness reward + format reward the model can discover that format is an easier source of guaranteed reward. therefore: \boxed{ \text{easy reward component} \rightarrow \text{can dominate harder reward component} } this is one of the most important lessons from this experiment. 5.8.35 proposed solution 1 — reduce format weight the source suggests reducing: w_f: 1.0\rightarrow0.1. then: correct + correctly formatted r=1+0.1=1.1. wrong + correctly formatted r=0+0.1=0.1. the correctness signal now dominates much more strongly. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.36 proposed solution 2 — conditional format reward instead of always granting the format reward, use: \boxed{ r_{\text{format,new}} = r_{\text{format}} \cdot r_{\text{correct}} } therefore: correct + correct format 1\times1=1. wrong + correct format 1\times0=0. so: \boxed{\text{wrong answers receive no format bonus}} the source gives precisely this conditional implementation. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.37 this creates a cleaner reward structure without conditioning: r= r_c+w_fr_f. with conditioning: \boxed{ r= r_c+w_fr_fr_c } or equivalently: r= r_c(1+w_fr_f). this means: r_c=0 \rightarrow r=0. thus the auxiliary reward cannot rescue an incorrect answer. 5.8.38 numerical comparison take: w_f=1. case 1: correct + formatted r_c=1,\quad r_f=1. unconditional: r=2. conditional: r=1+(1)(1)(1)=2. no difference. case 2: wrong + formatted r_c=0,\quad r_f=1. unconditional: r=1. conditional: r=0. huge difference. that is the entire motivation for the conditional reward. 5.8.39 important tokenizer issue there is another subtle implementation point. the base model initially does not have <think> as one token in the source experiment. the tokenizer encodes: <think> into several subword tokens. the reasoning tokenizer instead has dedicated ids: \boxed{151667} for <think> and: \boxed{151668} for </think> . (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) the source says that simply training the base model with these new tokens would perform poorly because the base model has not previously encountered them in this form. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.40 why this matters conceptually a reward function can only reinforce behavior that the model can meaningfully represent. if your tokenizer/model setup has no learned familiarity with a new special token, merely writing: r_{\text{format}}=1 does not magically give the model a pretrained concept of that token. so: \boxed{ \text{reward design} + \text{tokenization/model support} } must be considered together. 5.8.41 the full diagnostic mental model you should now think of grpo training as a control system: reward │ ▼ learning │ ▼ policy │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ reward accuracy length │ ▼ entropy │ ▼ stability the model isn't judged by one scalar. you monitor the whole system . 5.8.42 exam numerical — reward design given: r_c=0,\quad r_f=1,\quad w_f=0.5. unconditional r=0+0.5(1) =\boxed{0.5}. conditional r=0.5(1)(0)=\boxed{0}. this is a very likely conceptual numerical. 5.8.43 exam numerical — evaluation accuracy suppose math-500 evaluation gives: 420 correct answers. then: \text{accuracy} = \frac{420}{500} = 0.84. therefore: \boxed{84\%}. 5.8.44 exam numerical — entropy for: p=[0.8,0.2], calculate: h=-(0.8\ln0.8+0.2\ln0.2). h\approx0.500. thus: \boxed{h\approx0.50}. this is near the source's “very low to low” entropy boundary. 5.8.45 exam numerical — advantage collapse given: r=[1,1,1,1]. mean: \mu=1. therefore: r_i-\mu=0. thus: \boxed{a_i=0\;\forall i}. consequently: \boxed{l_{\text{pg}}=0}. no relative update occurs for that group. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.46 exam numerical — diagnose the run suppose: \text{reward}:0.3\rightarrow0.7 \text{eval accuracy}:45\%\rightarrow35\% \text{response length}:500\rightarrow150 \text{entropy}:1.2\rightarrow0.2. what should you conclude? not: “reward improved, so training succeeded.” the stronger diagnosis is: \boxed{ \text{possible instability / collapse} } because reward improved while external accuracy dropped, response length sharply shortened, and entropy collapsed. this interpretation is consistent with the source's observed failure patterns. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.8.47 the deepest idea from this step there are three levels of success : level 1 — the optimizer is numerically running gradients exist and parameters change. level 2 — the reward improves the verifier likes the sampled behavior more. level 3 — actual reasoning ability improves external evaluation improves. the real objective is: \boxed{ \text{level 3} } not merely level 2. 5.8.48 step 5.8 master summary remember this diagnostic sequence: \boxed{ \text{reward} \rightarrow \text{accuracy} \rightarrow \text{length} \rightarrow \text{advantage stats} \rightarrow \text{entropy} \rightarrow \text{stability} } and for reward engineering: \boxed{ r=r_{\text{correct}}+w_fr_{\text{format}} } can be problematic when the auxiliary reward is too strong. a safer source-proposed variant is: \boxed{ r = r_{\text{correct}} + w_fr_{\text{format}}r_{\text{correct}} } so that format cannot compensate for incorrectness. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.1 first: what problem was deepseekmath trying to solve? the target was not merely: “make a language model bigger.” the goal was to make an open 7b model very strong at mathematical reasoning . the supplied slides state that deepseekmath-rl 7b reached: \boxed{51.7\%} top-1 accuracy on the competition-level math benchmark, without tools or majority voting. (source: deepseekmath-slides) that result came from two ingredients: \boxed{ \text{better math data} + \text{better rl algorithm} } specifically: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath corpus} + \text{grpo} } (source: deepseekmath-slides) this is the first major lesson: reasoning performance is not only a model-architecture problem. data construction and post-training matter enormously. 5.9.2 contribution 1 — the deepseekmath corpus before rl can improve mathematical reasoning, the starting model needs sufficient mathematical knowledge. that means the first question is: where do we get enough high-quality mathematical text? the slides state that deepseek built: \boxed{\text{120b math tokens}} from common crawl using an iterative classifier-based mining pipeline. (source: deepseekmath-slides) this is much larger than the earlier public math corpora discussed in the deck. the slide explicitly gives: \text{openwebmath}\approx13.6b versus: \text{deepseekmath corpus}\approx120.2b. (source: deepseekmath-slides) so the approximate ratio is: \frac{120.2}{13.6} \approx 8.84. thus the deepseekmath corpus is about: \boxed{8.8\times} the size of openwebmath by token count. 5.9.3 why not simply search the web for “math”? because mathematical content is distributed across the web. a naive keyword filter would miss: pages where equations dominate but the word “math” is absent, mathematical discussions written in unusual styles, educational pages, forums, multilingual mathematical material. the deepseekmath approach therefore uses a classifier . the core idea is: \boxed{\text{teach a classifier what math pages look like}} and then use that classifier to search the enormous common crawl corpus. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.4 the iterative mining pipeline this is one of the most important diagrams from the deck. the pipeline is: \boxed{ \text{seed corpus} \rightarrow \text{train fasttext classifier} \rightarrow \text{recall math-like pages} \rightarrow \text{find high-recall domains} \rightarrow \text{human url-path annotation} \rightarrow \text{expand seed} \rightarrow \text{repeat} } (source: deepseekmath-slides) let's unpack every stage. stage a — start with a seed corpus they begin with a relatively small set of known mathematical text. the deck uses openwebmath as the starting seed. conceptually: d_0=\{\text{known math pages}\}. this is not enough to cover the web. stage b — train a fasttext classifier the seed corpus gives examples of: y=1:\text{math} and presumably: y=0:\text{not math}. the classifier learns: f(x)\rightarrow p(\text{math}\mid x). the deck specifically describes a fasttext classifier . (source: deepseekmath-slides) stage c — search common crawl now run the classifier against a massive collection of web pages. for each page: x_i \rightarrow f(x_i) \rightarrow \text{math score}. high-scoring pages are candidates for inclusion. so instead of humans reading billions of pages: \boxed{\text{classifier does the first large-scale filtering}} 5.9.5 why classify domains instead of every page? this is a particularly clever part. suppose a domain has many pages. for example, imagine: 100,000 pages from one website. suppose more than 10% of the pages already recalled by the classifier are mathematical. that is evidence that the domain itself has a strong mathematical region. instead of asking humans to inspect: 10,000 individual pages, they identify the useful url paths. for example: mathoverflow.net/questions/ could be marked as a valuable path. the slide explicitly describes this domain-level annotation strategy as a way of converting huge numbers of page-level judgments into a manageable number of url-pattern judgments. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.6 why is this better? suppose there are: 40b candidate pages. manual page-by-page annotation is obviously infeasible. but perhaps only a relatively small number of domains have obvious mathematical sections. so the process changes from: \boxed{\text{annotate billions of pages}} to approximately: \boxed{\text{identify useful domains/url patterns}} this is a classic scalable-data-engineering idea: find structure at a higher level of abstraction. 5.9.7 stage d — human annotation improves the classifier's blind spots this creates the bootstrapping loop. initially: d_0=\text{small seed}. train: c_0. use it to discover new mathematical regions: d_1. then train: c_1. and repeat: d_0 \rightarrow c_0 \rightarrow d_1 \rightarrow c_1 \rightarrow d_2 \rightarrow \cdots the supplied slides describe this as effectively allowing the classifier's own blind spots to guide the next search round. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.8 why does this work? imagine the initial classifier has learned mostly: \text{“textbook-like mathematics”}. then it may fail on: forum discussions, competition solutions, specialized technical pages, different writing styles, different languages. the newly discovered high-quality domains provide examples of these previously unseen patterns. so the next classifier becomes broader. this is essentially: \boxed{\text{iterative data discovery}} rather than one-shot filtering. 5.9.9 the process converged the deck says that after four iterations they reached roughly: \boxed{35.5m\text{ web pages}} and: \boxed{120b\text{ tokens}}. iteration 4 was stopped because about: \boxed{98\%} of its pages had already been found in iteration 3. that suggests the seed/data-discovery process had largely converged. (source: deepseekmath-slides) conceptually: \text{new iteration} \rightarrow \text{very little new information}. so continuing the mining loop gives diminishing returns. 5.9.10 exam numerical — corpus growth given: 13.6b tokens initially and: 120.2b tokens after iterative mining. compute the increase: 120.2-13.6 = 106.6b. so: \boxed{106.6b} additional tokens were obtained relative to openwebmath. the multiplicative growth is: \frac{120.2}{13.6}\approx8.84. so: \boxed{\approx8.8\times} 5.9.11 why does corpus size matter for training? suppose the model is trained for: 150b tokens. consider a small dataset: d=15b. then the model must see the same data repeatedly: \frac{150}{15}=10 times. but with a: 120b token corpus: \frac{150}{120}=1.25 corpus-equivalent passes. so the model can encounter substantially more fresh text before repetition dominates. the slides explicitly make this point: smaller datasets plateau earlier because the model repeatedly sees the same data, whereas the much larger deepseekmath corpus sustains continued improvement later in training. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.12 the controlled experiment the deck gives an especially important experimental design: keep the model and training-token budget the same; change only the corpus. it describes: \boxed{\text{same 1.3b model}} \boxed{\text{same 150b training tokens}} and vary the corpus. the deepseekmath corpus wins across the listed benchmarks. (source: deepseekmath-slides) this is good experimental methodology because we are trying to isolate: \text{effect of corpus quality/scale}. 5.9.13 a very important lesson about scaling we normally hear: \text{more parameters}\rightarrow\text{better model}. deepseekmath emphasizes another axis: \boxed{\text{better data}\rightarrow\text{better model}}. the deck states that deepseekmath-base 7b outperformed the listed open baselines across all eight benchmarks and even outperformed minerva 540b on those comparisons. (source: deepseekmath-slides) therefore: \boxed{ \text{parameter count is not the only scaling lever} } data quality and domain specialization can move the curve significantly. 5.9.14 the model initialization matters deepseekmath-base 7b did not start from a generic general-purpose 7b model. the supplied deck explicitly says it starts from: \boxed{\text{deepseek-coder-base-v1.5}} rather than a general llm. (source: deepseekmath-slides) this is strategically important. why would a code-specialized base help math? because mathematical reasoning and code reasoning both benefit from representations involving: symbolic structures, precise syntax, algorithmic reasoning, structured sequences. the slides state the initialization choice , but they do not in the cited passage provide a complete causal proof that this is why it worked. so that explanatory connection should be treated as interpretation, not as a direct claim from the source. 5.9.15 deepseekmath is therefore already specialized before rl think of the sequence: common crawl │ ▼ iterative math mining │ ▼ deepseekmath corpus │ ▼ deepseek-coder-base-v1.5 │ ▼ deepseekmath-base │ ▼ instruction tuning │ ▼ deepseekmath-instruct │ ▼ grpo + verifiable rewards │ ▼ deepseekmath-rl the last three model names are reflected in the supplied materials, and the rl stage explicitly starts from deepseekmath-instruct. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.16 what does sft do here? at a high level, sft gives the model examples of: (\text{problem},\text{desired reasoning/answer}). it teaches the model to produce useful solution trajectories. then rl does something different. rl asks: among the behaviors the model can generate, which ones should become more probable? this distinction is crucial. \boxed{ \text{sft teaches behavior from demonstrations} } while: \boxed{ \text{rl optimizes behavior according to reward} } this will become very important when we compare sft, rft, dpo, ppo and grpo. 5.9.17 deepseekmath-instruct → deepseekmath-rl the supplied slides give a clean controlled rl experiment. they apply grpo to: \boxed{\text{deepseekmath-instruct}} using only the chain-of-thought instruction-tuning data for: \boxed{\text{gsm8k and math}} and no new rl training dataset. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.18 the performance change gsm8k before rl: 82.9\% after rl: 88.2\%. so: 88.2-82.9 = \boxed{5.3\text{ percentage points}}. math before: 46.8\% after: 51.7\%. increase: 51.7-46.8 = \boxed{4.9\text{ percentage points}}. cmath before: 84.6\% after: 88.8\%. increase: 88.8-84.6 = \boxed{4.2\text{ percentage points}}. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.19 why is cmath especially interesting? the rl data came from: \text{gsm8k + math}. but the improvement also appears on: \text{cmath}. the slides explicitly point out that cmath is out-of-domain for the rl data and use this to argue that the improvement generalizes beyond exactly the data trained on. (source: deepseekmath-slides) this is much more convincing than merely saying: “the training reward went up.” we are seeing: \boxed{ \text{rl training} \rightarrow \text{better external performance} } even on a related benchmark not used as the exact rl training source. 5.9.20 why grpo instead of ppo? now the reason should be completely clear from our previous lessons. ppo typically needs: \boxed{\text{policy}} + \boxed{\text{value model}} grpo removes the learned value-model path and obtains the learning signal through group-relative comparisons. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) thus: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} \rightarrow \text{grpo} \rightarrow \text{later deepseek-r1} } the book explicitly identifies grpo as the algorithm introduced in deepseekmath and later used for deepseek-r1. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.9.21 the key insight: group-relative comparison suppose one math prompt produces: 4 responses: r=[1,1,0,0]. mean: \mu=0.5. so the model doesn't merely learn: “response 1 is correct.” it learns: “responses 1 and 2 performed better than the other sampled responses for this same problem.” thus: a_{1},a_{2}>0 and: a_{3},a_{4}<0. this produces both: \boxed{\text{reinforcement}} and: \boxed{\text{suppression}}. the supplied deepseekmath slides later make this comparison against online rft explicit: grpo's continuous advantage gives stronger reinforcement to above-average responses and actively penalizes below-average ones. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.22 why online rft is weaker than grpo this is a beautiful exam/interview concept. suppose we use: r\in\{0,1\}. online rft effectively treats: r=1 as: \text{reinforce}. but all correct responses get roughly the same binary signal. grpo instead computes: a_i= \frac{r_i-\mu}{\sigma+\epsilon}. now the coefficient is relative to the group . the deck describes grpo's richer gradient coefficient as the reason it beats online rft on both gsm8k and math in the displayed comparison. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.23 an important conceptual decomposition the deepseekmath deck offers a useful unifying perspective: \boxed{ \text{sft, rft, dpo, ppo, grpo} } can be viewed through two major questions: 1. where does the training data come from? for example: \text{offline} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{online}. 2. how strongly should each token be pushed? that is the gradient coefficient / learning signal. the supplied deck explicitly frames these methods as differing along these axes. this perspective becomes extremely useful because it prevents you from treating: \text{sft},\text{rft},\text{dpo},\text{ppo},\text{grpo} as five completely unrelated algorithms. 5.9.24 online vs offline — critical distinction offline generate responses once from a fixed model: \pi_0 \rightarrow \text{dataset} \rightarrow \text{train}. rft and dpo in the deck are categorized this way. online keep generating from the current policy : \pi_t \rightarrow \text{new responses} \rightarrow \text{reward} \rightarrow \pi_{t+1}. online rft and grpo are described this way. (source: deepseekmath-slides) as training progresses: \pi_t\neq\pi_0. therefore online methods continually receive data from the model they are currently training. 5.9.25 why does this become increasingly important? early in training: \pi_t\approx\pi_0. so the distinction between frozen-data generation and fresh sampling is smaller. later: \pi_t may be substantially different. then a fixed dataset describes the old policy's behavior, whereas online sampling reveals the current policy's behavior. the slides explicitly state that online methods pull ahead as the current policy diverges from the original sft model, with online rft outperforming offline rft in the cited comparison. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.26 numerical checkpoint suppose an online rl system generates: g=8 responses per prompt, and: 3 are correct. then: r=[1,1,1,0,0,0,0,0]. mean: \mu_r = \frac{3}{8} = 0.375. the correct responses have: r_i-\mu_r = 1-0.375 = 0.625. the incorrect responses have: 0-0.375 = -0.375. before standardization, you can already see the direction: \boxed{+0.625\text{ for correct}} \boxed{-0.375\text{ for incorrect}}. after dividing by the group standard deviation, these become normalized advantages. 5.9.27 very important: why multiple samples are necessary suppose we generate only: g=1 response. then: \mu=r_1. hence: r_1-\mu=0. there is no meaningful group-relative comparison. so grpo inherently needs: \boxed{g>1} for a meaningful group baseline. this is exactly why grpo's sampling structure differs from a one-response-per-prompt ppo-style setup. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.9.28 deepseekmath's central design philosophy the whole process can now be viewed as: \boxed{ \text{start with strong domain data} } then: \boxed{ \text{teach the model to solve problems} } then: \boxed{ \text{sample multiple attempts} } then: \boxed{ \text{verify correctness} } then: \boxed{ \text{compare attempts within each problem} } then: \boxed{ \text{increase probability of stronger reasoning trajectories} } that is the conceptual heart of deepseekmath. 5.9.29 exam question: why does better data matter even with the same compute? suppose: \text{model}=1.3b and: \text{training tokens}=150b. experiment a uses corpus a. experiment b uses corpus b. everything else is held constant. if: \text{performance}_b> \text{performance}_a, then the improvement is evidence that: \boxed{\text{data composition/quality matters}} rather than the improvement being explained simply by: \text{model size} or: \text{training-token budget}. that is the logic behind the controlled corpus comparison in the slides. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.30 exam numerical: rl gain math accuracy goes: 46.8\%\rightarrow51.7\%. absolute improvement: \boxed{4.9\text{ percentage points}}. relative percentage improvement: \frac{51.7-46.8}{46.8}\times100 = \frac{4.9}{46.8}\times100 \approx10.47\%. so the distinction is: \boxed{4.9\text{ percentage points}} versus approximately: \boxed{10.5\%\text{ relative improvement}}. do not confuse those two in an exam. 5.9.31 one more numerical: corpus repetition suppose: d=20b training tokens are available and we train on: 100b tokens. approximate corpus-equivalent exposure: \frac{100}{20}=5. so the model sees the equivalent of: \boxed{5\text{ corpus passes}}. if instead: d=120b and: t=100b, then: \frac{100}{120}=0.833. so the model does not even need one full corpus-equivalent pass. this is the intuition behind why a large corpus can avoid rapid repetition. the slides make this exact qualitative point. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.9.32 the deepseekmath → deepseek-r1 connection this is worth memorizing: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath introduced grpo} } and later: \boxed{ \text{deepseek-r1 used the same family of ideas} } the book explicitly presents grpo as originally introduced in deepseekmath and later used for deepseek-r1. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) so when you study deepseek-r1, do not think: “grpo suddenly appeared in r1.” it did not. the lineage is: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} \rightarrow \text{grpo} \rightarrow \text{deepseek-r1} } 5.9.33 the most important mental model from step 5.9 deepseekmath is not simply: \boxed{\text{7b model + rl}} it is: \boxed{ \begin{array}{c} \text{specialized high-quality math corpus}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{domain-specialized pretrained model}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{instruction tuning}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{online rollouts}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{verifiable rewards}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{group-relative advantages}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{grpo optimization}\\ \downarrow\\ \text{deepseekmath-rl} \end{array} } and this gives us a clean division of labor: \boxed{ \text{pretraining} \rightarrow \text{knowledge} } \boxed{ \text{sft} \rightarrow \text{demonstrated behavior} } \boxed{ \text{grpo/rl} \rightarrow \text{optimize successful behavior} } step 5.9 numerical bank you should now be able to solve: n1. deepseekmath has 120.2b tokens and openwebmath has 13.6b. compute the ratio. n2. a classifier iteration finds 35.5m pages. iteration 4 contains 98% pages already found in iteration 3. conceptually, why stop? n3. math goes 46.8% → 51.7%. compute both absolute and relative improvements. n4. a grpo group has rewards [1,1,0,0] . compute mean reward and the unnormalized reward deviations. n5. a corpus has 25b tokens and training uses 150b tokens. approximately how many corpus-equivalent passes occur? n6. why is g=1 insufficient for a meaningful group-relative grpo baseline? n7. explain why cmath improving from 84.6% to 88.8% is more interesting than simply observing that the training reward increased. one-line memory anchor memorize this: \boxed{ \textbf{deepseekmath = better math data + online verifiable rl + grpo} }

core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.9 — deepseekmath: where grpo came from this lesson: step 5.10 — the actual deepseekmath grpo objective source references: build a deepseek model (from scratch) ; build a reasoning model (from scratch) ; deepseekmath-slides ; deepseek-r1-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.10 — the actual deepseekmath grpo objective plan node: i7 · chat order #51 now we go one level deeper. in the previous steps, we used a simplified sequence-level grpo implementation to understand the mechanics. that was useful for learning, but it is important not to confuse it with the original deepseekmath formulation. the supplied deepseekmath slides make this distinction explicit: \boxed{\text{deepseekmath: token-level clipping}} whereas the later deepseek-r1 formulation shown in the supplied r1 slides uses: \boxed{\text{one sequence-level ratio for the whole response}} (source: deepseekmath-slides; deepseek-r1-slides) this distinction is extremely important for exams and for understanding later grpo variants. 5.10.1 start from the big picture for one prompt q : q the old/current policy generates g responses: o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_g. each response contains tokens: o_i=(o_{i,1},o_{i,2},\ldots,o_{i,|o_i|}). then: \boxed{ \text{prompt} \rightarrow \text{multiple responses} \rightarrow \text{reward} \rightarrow \text{advantages} \rightarrow \text{policy update} } the original deepseekmath objective then performs the policy update at the token level . (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.10.2 the full objective the supplied slide gives the deepseekmath objective in the following structure: \boxed{ j_{\mathrm{grpo}}(\theta) = \mathbb e \left[ \frac1g \sum_{i=1}^{g} \frac1{|o_i|} \sum_{t=1}^{|o_i|} \min \left( r_{i,t}(\theta)a_{i,t}, \operatorname{clip} \left(r_{i,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right) a_{i,t} \right) - \beta d_{\mathrm{kl}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) \right] } where \boxed{ r_{i,t}(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t}) }{ \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t}) } } and the advantage is derived from the rewards of the group. this is the key equation for this step. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.10.3 now we decode the formula piece by piece do not try to memorize the entire equation at once. we will construct it. part 1 — g g is the number of sampled responses for one prompt. example: g=4. then: o_1,o_2,o_3,o_4. the group comparison is what makes this group relative policy optimization. 5.10.4 part 2 — o_i for response i : o_i=(o_{i,1},o_{i,2},\ldots,o_{i,t_i}) where: t_i=|o_i| is its number of generated tokens. example: response 1 = [token1, token2, token3, token4] then: |o_1|=4. 5.10.5 part 3 — why divide by g ? the objective averages across sampled responses: \frac1g\sum_{i=1}^{g}. without this normalization, increasing group size would automatically increase the magnitude of the objective. so: \boxed{ \frac1g } makes the contribution an average over the group. 5.10.6 part 4 — why divide by |o_i| ? inside each response: \frac1{|o_i|} \sum_{t=1}^{|o_i|}. this means the token-level contributions are averaged over the response length. that matters because otherwise a longer response contains more terms in the sum and can contribute disproportionately. for example, imagine: |o_1|=10 and: |o_2|=100. without length normalization, the second response has ten times as many token-level terms. the original formulation explicitly includes: \boxed{\frac1{|o_i|}} to average the token contributions within each response. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.10.7 part 5 — the token probability ratio now we reach the most important quantity: \boxed{ r_{i,t}(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t}) }{ \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t}) } } read this in english: how much more or less likely is the current policy to generate this particular token compared with the policy that generated the rollout? 5.10.8 example suppose the old policy assigned: p_{\text{old}}=0.20 to the sampled token. after updating the model, the current policy assigns: p_{\text{new}}=0.30. then: r= \frac{0.30}{0.20} = 1.5. therefore: \boxed{r=1.5} means the current model considers that sampled token: \boxed{50\%\text{ more likely}} than the old model did. 5.10.9 three interpretations of the ratio r=1 p_{\text{new}}=p_{\text{old}} no probability change. r>1 p_{\text{new}}>p_{\text{old}} the current policy is increasing the probability. r<1 p_{\text{new}}<p_{\text{old}} the current policy is decreasing the probability. thus: \boxed{ r\text{ measures policy movement} } 5.10.10 part 6 — the advantage the ratio alone doesn't say whether we want the probability to increase or decrease. that comes from: \boxed{a_{i,t}}. the advantage answers: was this sampled behavior better or worse relative to the other responses? for outcome-based reward, the same group-level reward signal can conceptually be applied across the generated tokens of a response. suppose: r=[1,1,0,0]. then: \mu_r=0.5. the correct responses have: r_i-\mu_r>0 and wrong responses have: r_i-\mu_r<0. after normalization: a>0 for stronger responses and: a<0 for weaker responses. the supplied grpo material defines this group-relative signal from the within-group rewards. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.10.11 why the product ra ? this is the key rl intuition. we have: r\times a. suppose: a>0. this means: we want to reinforce this action. so increasing its probability is desirable. if: r>1, then: ra gets larger. that is good. now suppose: a<0. this means: we want to suppress this action. if: r<1, the policy is reducing its probability. that is desirable. so the sign of a tells the optimizer: \boxed{\text{up or down}} while r tells it: \boxed{\text{how much the probability moved}} 5.10.12 a numerical example suppose: a=0.8. and: r=1.2. then: ra = 1.2(0.8) = 0.96. a positive contribution. now suppose: a=-0.8 and: r=0.8. then: ra = 0.8(-0.8) = -0.64. the update is moving the probability downward for a negatively advantaged action. 5.10.13 why can't we just use ra ? because the model could move too aggressively. suppose: a=1 and: r=10. then: ra=10. the model has dramatically increased the probability of this sampled behavior in one update. repeated aggressive changes can destabilize policy optimization. this is where clipping enters. 5.10.14 part 7 — clipping the clipped ratio is: \boxed{ \operatorname{clip}(r,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) } suppose: \epsilon=0.2. then: 1-\epsilon=0.8 and: 1+\epsilon=1.2. therefore: r<0.8 \rightarrow 0.8 and: r>1.2 \rightarrow 1.2. so the allowed effective ratio range is: \boxed{[0.8,1.2]}. 5.10.15 numerical example suppose the ratios are: [1.1,1.3,0.7,1.0]. with: \epsilon=0.2 the clipped ratios become: [1.1,1.2,0.8,1.0]. so: \boxed{ [1.1,1.3,0.7,1.0] \rightarrow [1.1,1.2,0.8,1.0] } 5.10.16 why use \min ? the objective has: \min \left( ra,\, \operatorname{clip}(r,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)a \right). this is inherited from the ppo-style clipped objective. the idea is: don't allow the optimizer to obtain an arbitrarily large benefit from moving the policy too far in one update. 5.10.17 positive-advantage case suppose: a=+1. and: r=1.5. then: ra=1.5. clipped: 1.2\times1=1.2. therefore: \min(1.5,1.2)=1.2. so the objective does not give the model the full benefit of pushing that probability from 1.0 to 1.5. 5.10.18 negative-advantage case suppose: a=-1 and: r=0.5. then: ra=-0.5. clipped: 0.8(-1)=-0.8. therefore: \min(-0.5,-0.8) = -0.8. this case is subtle. because the objective is being maximized , the clipped surrogate prevents exploiting an overly large probability reduction as an arbitrarily favorable update. when implementing it as a pytorch minimization loss, the whole objective is negated. 5.10.19 the three-policy distinction you should now permanently separate these three models. current policy \boxed{\pi_\theta} this is the model being trained. it changes after optimizer steps. old policy \boxed{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}} this is the policy that generated the sampled responses. it provides the denominator: \frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}}. its purpose is: \boxed{\text{control the size of the current update}} reference policy \boxed{\pi_{\text{ref}}} this is used for kl regularization. its purpose is: \boxed{\text{prevent excessive long-term drift}} the supplied deepseekmath slide explicitly identifies the current policy, pre-update/old policy, and fixed reference policy as separate roles. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.10.20 old vs reference — an interview favorite think: old policy │ │ ratio ▼ "how far did i move from the policy that generated these samples?" while: reference policy │ │ kl ▼ "how far have i drifted from my long-term anchor?" so: \boxed{ \text{old}=\text{short-term comparison} } \boxed{ \text{reference}=\text{long-term anchor} } 5.10.21 part 8 — kl regularization the objective subtracts: \boxed{ \beta d_{\mathrm{kl}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) } from the reward-maximizing objective. the intuition is: \text{maximize task performance} - \text{penalty for excessive drift}. thus: \boxed{\beta} controls the strength of this constraint. 5.10.22 what happens when \beta changes? small \beta the model is allowed to move further from the reference. potential benefit: \text{more freedom} potential risk: \text{policy drift / instability}. large \beta the model is strongly constrained. potential benefit: \text{stability} potential risk: \text{learning can become too weak}. the supplied material discusses exactly this tradeoff. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.10.23 now the most important distinction: token-level vs sequence-level this is where the earlier lessons become connected. deepseekmath for each token: \boxed{ r_{i,t} = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}) }{ \pi_{\text{old}}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}) } } so: r_{i,1},r_{i,2},r_{i,3},\ldots can all be different. the clipping happens independently at the token level. (source: deepseekmath-slides) deepseek-r1 formulation shown in the supplied slides the r1 slide instead uses: \boxed{ r_i = \frac{\pi_\theta(o_i|q)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i|q)} } one ratio for the entire response. the slide explicitly calls this a change from deepseekmath's token-level formula to a sequence-level ratio . (source: deepseek-r1-slides) 5.10.24 where does the sequence probability come from? an autoregressive model factorizes a response probability as: \boxed{ \pi(o_i|q) = \prod_{t=1}^{|o_i|} \pi(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}) } therefore the sequence ratio becomes: \frac{\pi_\theta(o_i|q)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i|q)} = \frac{ \prod_t \pi_\theta(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}) }{ \prod_t \pi_{\text{old}}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}) } which is: \boxed{ r_i = \prod_{t=1}^{|o_i|} r_{i,t} } this relation is mathematically extremely important. 5.10.25 why log probabilities are used in practice products of many probabilities can become extremely tiny. instead use: \log \pi(o_i|q) = \sum_t \log\pi(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}). therefore: \log r_i = \log\pi_\theta(o_i|q) - \log\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i|q). then: \boxed{ r_i = \exp( \log\pi_\theta(o_i|q) - \log\pi_{\text{old}}(o_i|q) ) } this connects directly to the log-probability implementation we already built. 5.10.26 numerical demonstration: token-level vs sequence-level suppose one response contains 3 tokens and the token ratios are: r_1=1.1, \quad r_2=1.3, \quad r_3=0.7. the sequence ratio is: r_{\text{seq}} = 1.1\times1.3\times0.7. calculate: 1.1\times1.3=1.43 then: 1.43\times0.7=1.001. so: \boxed{r_{\text{seq}}\approx1.001} even though the individual token ratios include: 1.3 and: 0.7. this is a fundamental difference. 5.10.27 why this matters more for long responses suppose every token moves by only: 1.01. for 100 tokens: r_{\text{seq}} = 1.01^{100}. using the approximation: 1.01^{100}\approx2.705. so tiny per-token movements can compound into a large sequence-level ratio. likewise, if: r_t=0.99 for 100 tokens: 0.99^{100}\approx0.366. thus sequence-level ratios are highly sensitive to accumulated token-level changes. this is one reason the distinction between sequence-level and token-level optimization matters enormously for long reasoning traces. 5.10.28 exam numerical — ratio old probability: 0.25. current probability: 0.30. then: r=\frac{0.30}{0.25}=1.2. answer: \boxed{1.2} 5.10.29 exam numerical — clipping given: r=1.5,\qquad \epsilon=0.2. the clipping range is: [0.8,1.2]. therefore: \boxed{\operatorname{clip}(1.5,0.8,1.2)=1.2}. 5.10.30 exam numerical — sequence ratio suppose: r_1=1.2,\quad r_2=0.9,\quad r_3=1.1. then: r_{\text{seq}} = 1.2(0.9)(1.1). =1.188. therefore: \boxed{r_{\text{seq}}=1.188}. 5.10.31 exam numerical — log-ratio suppose: \log p_{\text{new}}=-5 and: \log p_{\text{old}}=-5.4. then: \log r = -5-(-5.4) = 0.4. therefore: r=e^{0.4} \approx1.492. so the current policy assigns approximately: \boxed{49.2\%} more probability to the sampled event. 5.10.32 tensor shapes suppose: batch size b=2 , group size g=4 , response length t=128 . then token log-probabilities can be represented as: \boxed{ [b,g,t]=[2,4,128]. } so: \text{logp}_{\text{new}} \in \mathbb r^{2\times4\times128}. similarly: \text{old\_logp}, \text{ref\_logp} \in \mathbb r^{2\times4\times128}. the ratio: r=\exp(\text{new\_logp}-\text{old\_logp}) therefore also has: \boxed{[2,4,128]} shape. for outcome-level reward, advantages might initially have: [b,g]=[2,4] and be expanded across the token dimension to: [2,4,128]. this matches the structure of the token-level objective. 5.10.33 one complete toy example let: g=4 with rewards: r=[1,1,0,0]. suppose normalized advantages are approximately: a=[+0.866,+0.866,-0.866,-0.866]. now consider the first response with three token ratios: r=[1.1,1.3,0.9]. take: \epsilon=0.2. thus: r_{\text{clip}} = [1.1,1.2,0.9]. for: a=0.866, the unclipped terms are: [1.1(0.866),1.3(0.866),0.9(0.866)] \approx [0.953,1.126,0.779]. clipped terms: [1.1(0.866),1.2(0.866),0.9(0.866)] \approx [0.953,1.039,0.779]. take the minimum token by token: \boxed{ [0.953,1.039,0.779] } then average over the three response tokens: \frac{0.953+1.039+0.779}{3} \approx0.924. that is the token-level surrogate contribution for this response before averaging over the group and applying the kl component. 5.10.34 what exactly changed between our earlier simplified code and this? earlier we used essentially: l = -\frac1n \sum_i a_i\log p_i and later: \text{ratio}=\exp(\text{new logp}-\text{old logp}) with clipping and kl. that was intentionally educational. the full deepseekmath-style expression adds: \boxed{ \text{token-level ratio} } and: \boxed{ \frac1{|o_i|} \sum_t } inside each response. so the progression is: \boxed{ \text{simple policy gradient} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{group-relative advantage} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{clipped importance ratio} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{kl reference constraint} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{full token-level grpo} } 5.10.35 why did we learn the simplified version first? because the full equation hides the idea under notation. the conceptual dependency is: \boxed{ a \rightarrow r \rightarrow \text{clip} \rightarrow \text{kl} } once you understand those four pieces independently, the full objective becomes straightforward. that is exactly the conceptual bridge between the chapter's introductory implementation and the original algorithm. the source itself notes that its simpler earlier implementation omitted parts of the full objective for pedagogical reasons. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) 5.10.36 another important connection: grpo vs online rft the supplied deepseekmath slides make a powerful observation. online rft and grpo both: \boxed{\text{sample from the current policy}} but their learning coefficients differ. online rft essentially uses a binary correctness signal. grpo uses the group-relative advantage: \boxed{ a_i= \frac{r_i-\mu_r}{\sigma_r+\epsilon} } so above-average responses receive stronger positive reinforcement and below-average responses receive negative reinforcement. (source: deepseekmath-slides) therefore: \boxed{ \text{same online data source} \neq \text{same learning rule} } 5.10.37 deepseekmath vs deepseek-r1 — memorize this table property deepseekmath deepseek-r1 formulation shown in supplied slides group sampling yes yes group-relative advantage yes yes old-policy ratio yes yes clipping yes yes reference kl yes in original objective yes ratio granularity token-level sequence-level ratio r_{i,t} r_i response probability token conditional probability whole-response probability the supplied slides explicitly identify the token-level/sequence-level difference. (source: deepseekmath-slides; deepseek-r1-slides) 5.10.38 and this explains later grpo variants the chapter 7 material lists later modifications such as: \boxed{\text{dapo}} with token-level loss, \boxed{\text{gspo}} with sequence-level importance sampling/clipping, and: \boxed{\text{cispo}} which clips importance weights directly. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) so when you later see these names, don't treat them as random new algorithms. they are modifications of specific pieces of the grpo machinery: grpo │ ├── advantage normalization ├── importance ratio ├── clipping ├── kl └── response/token aggregation │ ├── dapo ├── dr. grpo ├── gspo └── cispo 5.10.39 the complete reasoning chain now you should be able to narrate the algorithm without looking at the formula: for each question, sample several responses from the old policy. verify each response and obtain rewards. compare those rewards within the group to produce relative advantages. for every generated token, compare the current policy probability with the old policy probability using an importance ratio. clip that ratio so one update cannot move the policy too aggressively. average the token contributions within each response and the responses within the group. finally, use a kl penalty to discourage excessive drift from the reference policy. that is the deepseekmath grpo objective in words. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.10.40 master formula map keep this hierarchy in your notes: \boxed{ a_i = \frac{r_i-\mu_r}{\sigma_r+\epsilon} } then: \boxed{ r_{i,t} = \frac{\pi_\theta(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})} } then: \boxed{ \tilde r_{i,t} = \operatorname{clip}(r_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) } then: \boxed{ \min(r_{i,t}a_{i,t},\tilde r_{i,t}a_{i,t}) } then: \boxed{ \frac1{|o_i|} \sum_t(\cdot) } then: \boxed{ \frac1g\sum_i(\cdot) } then: \boxed{ -\beta d_{\mathrm{kl}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}) } and finally: \boxed{ j_{\mathrm{grpo}} = \text{clipped policy improvement} - \text{reference-policy drift penalty} } 5.10.41 exam numerical bank n1 — ratio p_{\text{old}}=0.4,\quad p_{\text{new}}=0.5 r=\boxed{1.25}. n2 — clipping r=1.5,\quad\epsilon=0.2 \boxed{r_{\text{clip}}=1.2}. n3 — sequence ratio r_1=1.1,\quad r_2=1.2,\quad r_3=0.8 r_{\text{seq}} = 1.1(1.2)(0.8) = \boxed{1.056}. n4 — length-normalized surrogate three token contributions: [0.6,0.9,1.2]. then: \frac{0.6+0.9+1.2}{3} = \boxed{0.9}. n5 — advantage direction a=-0.7,\quad r=0.6. interpretation: \boxed{\text{the response/token is being downweighted}} because it has negative advantage and the current probability is below the old probability. n6 — token vs sequence ratio given: r_1=1.1,\;r_2=1.1,\;r_3=1.1. sequence-level ratio: 1.1^3=1.331. thus: \boxed{r_{\text{seq}}=1.331}. n7 — long sequence compounding if every token ratio is: 1.01 for 100 tokens: 1.01^{100}\approx\boxed{2.705}. this demonstrates why sequence-level ratios can compound strongly. the one distinction you absolutely must remember \boxed{ \textbf{deepseekmath grpo: token-level ratio} } \boxed{ \textbf{deepseek-r1 formulation shown here: sequence-level ratio} } that single distinction will make the later discussion of dapo, dr. grpo, gspo, cispo, and deepseek-r1 much easier. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.1 first reconstruct the deepseekmath pipeline the whole experiment should be viewed as: \boxed{ \text{deepseek-coder-base-v1.5} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{math-focused pretraining} } using the large deepseekmath corpus: \boxed{120b\text{ math tokens}} \downarrow \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath-base 7b} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{instruction tuning} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath-instruct} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{grpo + verifiable rewards} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath-rl} } the supplied slides describe deepseekmath-base 7b as starting from deepseek-coder-base-v1.5, and the rl stage as applying grpo to deepseekmath-instruct. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.2 what reward is available? for many mathematical problems, we know the correct answer. so after the model generates: o_i we can verify it. for a simplified binary reward: r_i= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{correct}\\ 0 & \text{incorrect} \end{cases} this is: \boxed{\text{outcome supervision}} because the reward concerns the final outcome . the key advantage is that we do not need a human to manually score every generated reasoning trace. 5.11.3 why can math use rlvr? because the answer can often be checked mechanically. suppose the model answers: 2x+3=11 with: x=4. a verifier can simply calculate: 2(4)+3=11. therefore: r=1. for: x=3, we get: 2(3)+3=9\neq11 so: r=0. thus: \boxed{\text{problem}+\text{verifier}\rightarrow\text{scalable reward}} this is the basis of rl with verifiable rewards. 5.11.4 the key experimental question suppose the pretrained/instruction-tuned model already has a chance of solving a problem. example: model samples 8 answers: correct wrong wrong correct wrong wrong wrong wrong the model already knew how to produce a correct solution sometimes . grpo can increase the probability of the successful trajectories. that motivates the question: \boxed{ \text{does rl create new capability, or sharpen existing capability?} } 5.11.5 pass@k define: \boxed{\text{pass@k}} as: is there at least one correct answer among k sampled responses? for example, with: k=5 suppose: [w,w,c,w,w]. there is one correct answer. therefore: \boxed{\text{pass@5}=1}. if: [w,w,w,w,w], then: \boxed{\text{pass@5}=0}. 5.11.6 why is pass@k important? pass@k measures something close to: \boxed{ \text{can the model produce a correct solution at all?} } suppose the model has: \text{pass@8}=80\%. that means that across eight attempts, a correct answer appears for many problems. but that does not mean the first/default answer will be correct. the correct response might be buried among several wrong ones. 5.11.7 majority@k / maj@k now consider: \boxed{\text{maj@k}} the question becomes: among the k sampled answers, is the most common answer correct? example: [83,83,38,83,38]. the majority answer is: 83. if the correct answer is 83: \boxed{\text{maj@5}=1}. 5.11.8 compare the two consider: samples: 83 83 38 41 17 assume 83 is correct. then: \text{pass@5}=1 because at least one response is correct. and: \text{maj@5}=1 because the correct answer is also the majority. now consider: 83 38 38 41 17 again 83 is correct. then: \text{pass@5}=1 but: \text{maj@5}=0 because 38 is the majority. this distinction is crucial. 5.11.9 what happens after rl? the supplied deepseekmath slides report an important observation: \boxed{\text{maj@k improves}} while: \boxed{\text{pass@k changes little}} under the discussed rl analysis. (source: deepseekmath-slides) that means the model may already have been capable of producing correct solutions. rl makes the correct solution more dominant in the output distribution. 5.11.10 visualize the distribution before rl: correct solution 20% wrong strategy a 25% wrong strategy b 20% wrong strategy c 20% other 15% there is a correct solution, but it isn't dominant. after rl: correct solution 55% wrong strategy a 15% wrong strategy b 12% wrong strategy c 10% other 8% the model's probability mass has been reshaped. so: \boxed{ \text{capability already present} \rightarrow \text{probability mass shifted toward successful behavior} } this is the interpretation emphasized by the supplied deck. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.11 this is the paper's interpretation, not a universal theorem the slides phrase this as the paper's own interpretation: rl is sharpening the probability distribution so that correct answers become more likely to dominate top-of-distribution decoding. (source: deepseekmath-slides) so we should be careful. this does not prove: \boxed{\text{rl can never create new reasoning capabilities}} it means that, for this particular deepseekmath analysis, the pass@k/maj@k behavior suggests that a significant part of the gain can be explained as making successful existing behaviors more likely . that distinction is important. 5.11.12 why does this make intuitive sense? suppose the model already generates: a=\text{correct solution} with probability: p(a)=0.2. there are many competing incorrect solutions. rl rewards sampled trajectories that succeed. repeatedly reinforcing successful trajectories pushes: p(a) upward. for example: 0.2 \rightarrow 0.35 \rightarrow 0.50 \rightarrow 0.65. eventually the correct solution becomes dominant. thus greedy or ordinary top-of-distribution decoding becomes much more likely to return the correct answer. 5.11.13 a simple probability numerical suppose: p(\text{correct})=0.2. assuming independent samples, the probability of getting at least one correct response in k samples is: \boxed{ \text{pass@k} = 1-(1-p)^k } for this simplified setting. for: k=5, we get: 1-(0.8)^5. 0.8^5=0.32768. therefore: \text{pass@5} = 1-0.32768 = \boxed{0.67232}. so: \boxed{67.2\%}. this formula is a useful mathematical interpretation of pass@k, though the supplied slide's primary point is the empirical pass@k vs maj@k behavior rather than a derivation of this formula. 5.11.14 suppose rl increases p now suppose rl changes: p=0.2 \rightarrow p=0.6. then: \text{pass@5} = 1-(1-0.6)^5 =1-0.4^5 =1-0.01024 =\boxed{98.976\%}. so increasing the probability of successful reasoning dramatically increases the chance of seeing at least one correct answer. but in the slide's interpretation, the particularly important gain is that correct answers become more likely to be the dominant/selected answer , not merely somewhere in the sample set. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.15 now connect this directly to grpo remember: a_i= \frac{r_i-\mu_r}{\sigma_r+\epsilon}. suppose: r=[1,0,0,0]. then the one successful response receives: a>0. the incorrect responses receive: a<0. therefore the policy update approximately says: \boxed{ \text{increase probability of successful trajectory} } and: \boxed{ \text{decrease probability of unsuccessful trajectories} } repeated across many problems, that reshapes the distribution. that is exactly the bridge: \boxed{ \text{grpo mathematics} \rightarrow \text{distribution sharpening} } 5.11.16 why grpo beats online rft now compare two approaches. online rft correct: r=1 wrong: r=0. the correct rollouts receive a binary reinforcement signal. grpo use: a_i= \frac{r_i-\mu}{\sigma+\epsilon}. so the signal is relative. the supplied deck says that online rft and grpo use the same online data source; their key difference is the gradient coefficient . grpo provides a richer continuous signal that reinforces above-average responses more strongly and penalizes below-average ones. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.17 numerical comparison suppose: r=[1,1,0,0]. mean: \mu=0.5. unnormalized deviations: [+0.5,+0.5,-0.5,-0.5]. online rft essentially gives: [1,1,0,0]. grpo instead gives positive/negative relative signals. therefore: \boxed{ \text{grpo has directional suppression as well as reinforcement} } rather than merely: \boxed{ \text{rewarded = reinforce} } 5.11.18 why actively penalizing bad responses matters imagine all four responses: r=[1,1,0,0]. you want to increase: p(o_1),p(o_2) and decrease: p(o_3),p(o_4). grpo naturally supplies: a_{1},a_{2}>0 and: a_{3},a_{4}<0. this gives the policy a much richer update direction. that richer gradient coefficient is exactly what the supplied deck highlights. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.19 outcome supervision vs process supervision now we reach another important experiment. outcome supervision reward only the final result. for example: \boxed{ r= 1\quad\text{if final answer is correct} } 0\quad\text{otherwise}. this is: \boxed{\text{grpo+os}} in the supplied slide terminology. 5.11.20 process supervision instead of only evaluating the final answer, provide reward signals at intermediate reasoning steps. for example: step 1 → correct setup +1 step 2 → correct algebra +1 step 3 → correct substitution +1 step 4 → correct answer +1 the slide describes process supervision as giving one reward per reasoning step , rather than only a final-answer reward. (source: deepseekmath-slides) this produces: \boxed{\text{grpo+ps}}. 5.11.21 why should process supervision help? consider this reasoning chain: s_1\rightarrow s_2\rightarrow s_3\rightarrow s_4 where only the final answer is checked. suppose the final answer is wrong. with outcome supervision: r=0. but maybe: s_1 and: s_2 were perfectly correct, and the mistake happened at: s_3. outcome supervision doesn't tell us exactly where the reasoning went wrong. this creates a credit-assignment problem . 5.11.22 process supervision provides finer credit assignment instead of: [0] we might have: [1,1,0,0]. now the learning system receives more localized information. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{final reward} \rightarrow \text{coarse credit} } while: \boxed{ \text{step rewards} \rightarrow \text{fine-grained credit} } the supplied slides report that: \boxed{\text{grpo+ps}} edges out: \boxed{\text{grpo+os}} in the cited comparison, suggesting the finer credit assignment is useful. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.23 why doesn't deepseekmath simply use process supervision everywhere? because it is more expensive and difficult. for outcome supervision: \text{one final verification}. for process supervision: \text{verify many intermediate steps}. that raises the requirements for: step-level correctness checking, reward-model or verifier quality, data construction, computational cost. the supplied material identifies the empirical benefit but does not provide a complete cost analysis in the cited slide, so we should not attach a specific cost number here. 5.11.24 iterative rl — another important idea the deck also introduces iterative grpo . suppose we have a reward model trained using behavior from: \pi_0. after substantial rl: \pi_t may generate responses that look very different. the old reward model may now be operating out of distribution. therefore its judgments can become less trustworthy. the supplied slides describe iterative grpo as periodically: retraining the reward model on fresh rollouts, retaining 10% older data as replay, resetting the reference policy, continuing training. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.25 why does this make sense? we have a moving policy: \pi_0 \rightarrow \pi_1 \rightarrow \pi_2 \rightarrow \pi_3. if the reward model was trained on: \pi_0\text{'s outputs}, then eventually: \pi_3 may produce very different outputs. thus: \boxed{ \text{policy distribution shifts} \rightarrow \text{reward model distribution shift} } this is another form of instability in rl training. 5.11.26 why keep old data? the supplied slide says the iterative procedure retains about: \boxed{10\%} older data as replay. conceptually, this prevents the new reward model from completely forgetting the earlier distribution while adapting to the current one. (source: deepseekmath-slides) so: \boxed{ \text{fresh data} + \text{some historical data} } helps maintain continuity. 5.11.27 put all deepseekmath experiments into one hierarchy we can now see the evolution: \boxed{\text{sft}} teaches the model from demonstrations. then: \boxed{\text{offline rft}} uses fixed sampled responses. then: \boxed{\text{online rft}} continually samples from the updated policy. then: \boxed{\text{grpo}} adds richer group-relative gradient coefficients. then: \boxed{\text{grpo+ps}} adds finer-grained process supervision. then: \boxed{\text{iterative grpo}} refreshes reward modeling as the policy changes. this is the experimental progression presented across the supplied deepseekmath slides. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.28 the most important conceptual axis the slide's unifying lens is: \boxed{ \text{what data do we train on?} } and: \boxed{ \text{what gradient coefficient do we apply?} } so: training method │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ │ │ data source gradient signal │ │ offline / online binary / relative / token / process ... this makes the algorithms much easier to compare. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.29 deepseekmath result — the headline number after applying grpo to deepseekmath-instruct: \text{math} : 46.8\%\rightarrow51.7\%. therefore: \boxed{+4.9\text{ percentage points}}. gsm8k: 82.9\%\rightarrow88.2\% \boxed{+5.3\text{ points}}. cmath: 84.6\%\rightarrow88.8\% \boxed{+4.2\text{ points}}. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.30 why the cmath result matters the rl training data came from: \boxed{\text{gsm8k + math}} yet cmath also improved. so the result is not simply: \text{memorize training benchmark}. it suggests some transfer of the improved reasoning behavior to a related out-of-domain benchmark. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.31 one subtle but important conclusion deepseekmath teaches us that rl can be extremely effective without necessarily requiring the model to learn an entirely new algorithmic capability from scratch . the evidence in the deck suggests: \boxed{ \text{successful behaviors already present} } can be: \boxed{ \text{amplified and made more likely} } through reinforcement. this is why: \text{pass@k}\approx\text{stable} while: \text{maj@k}\uparrow is so informative. (source: deepseekmath-slides) 5.11.32 numerical — pass@k a model has: p=0.3 chance of producing a correct answer in any individual sample. for: k=4, under the simplified independent-sampling assumption: \text{pass@4} = 1-(1-0.3)^4 = 1-(0.7)^4 = 1-0.2401 = \boxed{0.7599}. so: \boxed{75.99\%}. 5.11.33 numerical — probability sharpening suppose before rl: p(\text{correct})=0.25. after rl: p(\text{correct})=0.55. probability increase: 0.55-0.25 = \boxed{0.30}. so the correct behavior gained: \boxed{30\text{ percentage points}} of probability mass in this toy example. this illustrates the deck's “sharpening” interpretation. 5.11.34 numerical — outcome vs process supervision suppose four reasoning steps receive: [1,1,0,1]. under process supervision, total step reward might be: 1+1+0+1 = \boxed{3} depending on the reward design. under binary outcome supervision, if the final answer is wrong: \boxed{r_{\text{outcome}}=0}. the process signal therefore contains substantially more information about where the successful/unsuccessful trajectory differed , although the exact aggregation depends on the particular training setup. 5.11.35 interview question question: why does grpo need multiple responses for the same prompt?
