core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.3 — why grpo instead of ppo? , step 5.7 — the full grpo training algorithm this lesson: step 5.20 — retool: reinforcement learning for strategic tool use source references: retool-slides ; build an ai agent (from scratch) original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.20 — retool: reinforcement learning for strategic tool use plan node: i9 · chat order #61 we now move to the next major topic in your supplied material: \boxed{\text{retool — reinforcement learning for strategic tool use in llms}} this is a very natural continuation of the deepseek-r1 story. we just studied: \boxed{ \text{text-only reasoning} } with deepseek-r1. retool asks a more advanced question: what happens when the model is allowed to leave the text stream, execute real code, read the result, and then continue reasoning? the supplied retool slides frame this as the transition from reasoning in text to reasoning with external computational feedback . (source: retool-slides) 5.20.1 first understand the problem retool is solving deepseek-r1 can reason for a long time using text: let me calculate... 3 × 17 = 51 51 + 29 = 80 ... this can work well. but consider a problem requiring: \boxed{ \text{exact arithmetic over 1000 cases} } or: \boxed{ \text{solving a complicated system of equations} } or: \boxed{ \text{geometric computation} } or: \boxed{ \text{searching many candidate values} }. the model has to perform all of this through token generation. the slides point out the key weakness: \boxed{ \text{one arithmetic mistake can contaminate everything afterward} } because the model is effectively performing computation through its own token stream. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.2 the fundamental distinction text reasoning: \boxed{ \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{write answer} } retool reasoning: \boxed{ \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{call tool} \rightarrow \text{observe real result} \rightarrow \text{continue reasoning} } this is the key conceptual jump. 5.20.3 why a code interpreter helps suppose the model needs: 1234567\times891011. a text-only model might internally generate: 1234567 × 891011 = ... and potentially make a bookkeeping error. with a code interpreter: 1234567 * 891011 the external environment computes the result. then the model receives: 109950... and continues reasoning. so the computation has moved from: \boxed{\text{llm token prediction}} to: \boxed{\text{deterministic external execution}}. 5.20.4 but retool is not simply “give the model a calculator” this distinction is extremely important. the goal is not: always call the calculator. the goal is: learn when using a tool is worth it. the slides explicitly state that nothing tells the model when to use code; the timing itself is something rl must teach. (source: retool-slides) therefore the target behavior is: \boxed{ \text{sometimes use code} } and: \boxed{ \text{sometimes do not use code} }. 5.20.5 tool use becomes a decision problem imagine two questions. question a what is the capital of south korea? the model already knows: \boxed{\text{seoul}} no computation is necessary. question b what is 1234\times5678 ? the model can invoke: \boxed{\text{calculator/code}} because exact computation is useful. the related agent/tool-use material shows exactly this kind of selective tool choice: answer directly when the model has the needed information, call a tool when external computation is beneficial. (source: build an ai agent (from scratch)) retool takes that idea and trains the decision itself through rl . 5.20.6 the most important change: what is a rollout? this is where retool becomes mathematically interesting. earlier, in text-only grpo/rl, a rollout was approximately: \boxed{ o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_t } all produced by the language model. now the rollout becomes an interleaved trajectory . for example: \boxed{ t_1 \oplus c_1 \oplus f_1 \oplus t_2 \oplus c_2 \oplus f_2 \oplus o } where: t_i = model-generated reasoning text, c_i = model-generated code, f_i = interpreter feedback, o = final answer. the slides explicitly describe the rollout this way. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.7 let's make that concrete suppose the task is: find a number satisfying some complicated condition. the model might generate: i should search the candidate space. for x in range(1,10000): ... generation pauses. the sandbox executes the code and returns: candidate = 699 then the model continues: the computation gives 699. i should verify the condition... then perhaps: ... followed by another interpreter result. finally: \boxed{699} the entire thing is treated as one trajectory. that is the core retool idea. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.8 three kinds of content now exist inside the trajectory this is an exam-important distinction. type 1 — model reasoning \boxed{\text{generated by policy}} type 2 — model code \boxed{\text{generated by policy}} type 3 — interpreter feedback \boxed{\text{generated by environment}} so unlike ordinary text-only rl: \boxed{ \text{not every token in the trajectory is generated by the policy} } that fact drives several important engineering decisions later. 5.20.9 why does generation have to pause? suppose the model generates: print(2+2) the model cannot generate the output itself, because that output is supposed to come from the external interpreter. so when: \boxed{\texttt{}} is detected: \boxed{ \text{generation pauses} } and the code is sent to the sandbox. the returned result is then inserted into the context, and generation resumes. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.10 this produces a turn-by-turn rollout think of it like: \boxed{ \text{llm turn} \rightarrow \text{environment turn} \rightarrow \text{llm turn} \rightarrow \text{environment turn} \rightarrow\cdots } this is already very close to the structure of an agent-environment interaction . that is why the slides connect retool to the broader concept of agentic rl . (source: retool-slides) 5.20.11 retool vs deepseek-r1 this is one of the most important comparisons in the course. deepseek-r1 trajectory: \boxed{ \text{long text reasoning} } external environment: \boxed{ \text{none during the reasoning trace} } reward: \boxed{ \text{final correctness} } optimization: \boxed{ \text{grpo} } retool trajectory: \boxed{ \text{text} + \text{code} + \text{interpreter feedback} } external environment: \boxed{ \text{real code sandbox} } reward: \boxed{ \text{final correctness} } optimization: \boxed{ \text{ppo} } the retool slides explicitly emphasize that retool uses plain ppo rather than grpo . (source: retool-slides) 5.20.12 why is retool using ppo rather than grpo? recall from our grpo lessons: grpo avoids a learned value model by estimating a baseline from multiple sampled responses. ppo normally uses: \boxed{ v_\phi(s_t) } a learned value function. the retool slides explicitly say: \boxed{\text{not grpo}} and state that retool uses standard ppo with a learned value function. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.13 ppo review for a policy: \pi_\theta the probability ratio is: \boxed{ r_t(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_t\mid q,o_{... followed by: ... and then continued reasoning. the slides say rl works by exploring variations of behavior the model already has, so the base model first needs the ability to use the protocol at all. (source: retool-slides) therefore: \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft} \rightarrow \text{rl} } 5.20.18 what does cold-start sft teach? very important: \boxed{ \text{protocol mechanics} } not necessarily: \boxed{ \text{optimal tool-use strategy} }. the slides explicitly distinguish these. the cold-start stage teaches things like: where code goes, when interpreter output appears, how to continue after feedback, how the formatting protocol works. then rl learns: \boxed{ \text{when using the tool is actually useful} }. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.19 where does the cold-start data come from? the slides describe: step a collect verified text-only reasoning traces: d_{\text{init}}. these can be filtered by human review and by deepseek-r1. step b automatically transform those traces by replacing appropriate manual calculations with executable code and its real output. this produces: \boxed{ d_{\text{ci}} } the code-augmented dataset. step c keep traces passing: \boxed{ \text{format check} \land \text{answer correctness} }. step d sft the base model on this data. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.20 a crucial idea: failed tool attempts can remain the slides specifically state that the transformation can leave surrounding reasoning, including failed attempts , untouched. this matters because the eventual rl policy can learn what happens after failure. for example: greedy(...) then: nameerror then: oops, i need to define the function. then corrected code. this sets up exactly the kind of environment interaction that later rl can exploit. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.21 retool's reward is surprisingly simple you might expect: r= r_{\text{correct}} + r_{\text{code}} + r_{\text{format}} + r_{\text{efficiency}}. but the slides say the reward is deliberately much simpler. for final answer \hat a and ground truth a : \boxed{ r(a,\hat a) = \begin{cases} +1,&\text{if correct}\\ -1,&\text{otherwise} \end{cases} } the correctness check is rule-based. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.22 why isn't successful code execution rewarded? suppose the reward gave: +0.2 whenever code successfully executed. the model could exploit this. it could generate useless code like: print("hello") which executes successfully. then: r_{\text{code}}=+0.2 without helping solve the problem. that creates a reward-hacking opportunity. the slides therefore deliberately omit a separate “successful execution” reward. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.23 the principle behind this reward design the rule is: \boxed{ \text{don't reward tool use for its own sake.} } instead: \boxed{ \text{tool use only receives indirect credit if it helps produce a correct answer.} } so the model must learn: \boxed{ \text{useful tool calls} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{many tool calls}. } 5.20.24 this is very similar to our earlier format-reward lesson previously, we studied why adding: r_{\text{format}} can create undesirable optimization pressure. here the same principle appears in another form. if we reward: \text{code execution} directly, the model may optimize for: \text{code execution} rather than: \text{problem solving}. therefore: \boxed{ \text{reward should measure the desired outcome, not an easy-to-game proxy} }. 5.20.25 numerical example: reward hacking suppose: r_{\text{correct}}= \begin{cases} +1\\ -1 \end{cases} and someone adds: r_{\text{code}}=+0.2 for executable code. then a wrong answer with successful code receives: -1+0.2 = \boxed{-0.8}. a model can improve average reward by learning to generate executable code even when it does not solve the problem. that is precisely why retool avoids this additional reward. 5.20.26 the rollout now becomes a hybrid trajectory let's write one formally. suppose: \tau= [t_1,t_2,c_1,f_1,t_3,c_2,f_2,o]. the policy generates: t_1,t_2,c_1,t_3,c_2,o while the environment produces: f_1,f_2. so: \boxed{ \tau = \tau_{\text{policy}} \oplus \tau_{\text{environment}} } conceptually. this is different from ordinary language-model rl, where essentially the whole token trajectory comes from the policy. 5.20.27 exam numerical: trajectory length suppose the model generates: 1200 reasoning/code tokens. the interpreter produces: 300 feedback tokens. the final answer contributes: 20 model-generated tokens. then total context/trajectory tokens: 1200+300+20 = \boxed{1520}. the important insight is that: \boxed{300} tokens are environment-generated. 5.20.28 this creates a major training problem should the model be trained to predict the interpreter's output? no. why? because: \boxed{ \text{the model did not generate it} } the interpreter generated it. this leads to one of retool's most important engineering details: \boxed{ \text{mask interpreter tokens from the loss} } the slides explicitly state this. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.29 why must interpreter tokens be masked? suppose the sandbox outputs: 42 the student/policy did not choose: 42. the environment did. if the loss forced the model to predict that token, the model would be penalized or rewarded for something it did not actually control. that corrupts the policy-learning signal. so: \boxed{ \text{loss applies to policy-generated tokens} } and not: \boxed{ \text{environment-generated tokens} }. 5.20.30 this is a very important exam question question: why are interpreter tokens masked in retool? answer: because those tokens come from the external sandbox rather than from the policy. including them in the policy loss would train the model to predict environment-generated text and would interfere with the learning signal for the model's own actions. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.31 second engineering trick: kv-cache reuse we already studied kv caching. normally, when the model continues generation, it can reuse: k,v for previous tokens. retool exploits this. when the code executes: \boxed{ \text{everything generated so far is already cached} } then the interpreter returns new feedback. only the new feedback tokens need new kv computation before generation resumes. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.32 why is this especially important in retool? because otherwise every tool call would potentially force: \boxed{ \text{recompute the entire prefix} } which would be very expensive. with kv reuse: \boxed{ \text{old prefix cache} + \text{new feedback cache} } allows generation to continue efficiently. 5.20.33 numerical kv-cache intuition suppose before the code call the context has: 10,000 tokens. interpreter returns: 200 new tokens. without cache reuse, you might conceptually recompute attention-related states for roughly: 10,200 context tokens. with reuse: \boxed{ \text{reuse existing 10,000} } and only process: \boxed{200} new tokens for the cache extension. this is a conceptual efficiency illustration; actual implementation cost also depends on attention kernels and architecture. 5.20.34 there is a third engineering component: asynchronous sandbox execution the interpreter may take time. suppose one model rollout executes: 300\text{ ms} worth of code while another takes: 5\text{ s}. if all rollouts share one synchronous execution path, the fast rollouts may sit idle waiting for the slow one. the slides therefore describe an asynchronous sandbox pool so that slow executions do not stall the rest of training. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.35 why is this a distributed-systems problem? because retool has at least two computational systems: \boxed{\text{policy inference}} and: \boxed{\text{code-execution environment}}. they interact asynchronously. you therefore care about: scheduling, queueing, isolation, failures, timeout handling, result routing, cache state. the source specifically mentions the asynchronous sandbox pool as a scale-enabling component. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.36 the full retool architecture put everything together: training prompt │ ▼ policy llm │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ │ │ text reasoning │ │ │ ▼ │ code sandbox pool │ │ │ ▼ │ interpreter output │ │ └─────────────┬───────────┘ ▼ context updated │ ▼ policy continues │ ▼ final answer │ ▼ rule-based verifier │ ▼ +1 / -1 │ ▼ ppo update this is the architecture described across the retool slides. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.37 retool has changed the meaning of “reasoning” before: \boxed{ \text{reasoning} = \text{generating useful text} } after retool: \boxed{ \text{reasoning} = \text{generating text + choosing actions + interpreting feedback} } this is the beginning of tool-augmented reasoning . 5.20.38 the deeper rl interpretation we can write: \boxed{ s_t = \text{current problem + reasoning history + tool feedback} } the action a_t can be: \boxed{ \text{text token} } or part of: \boxed{ \text{code/tool invocation} }. the environment then returns: \boxed{ f_{t+1} = \text{interpreter feedback} }. so: \boxed{ (s_t,a_t) \rightarrow s_{t+1} } now includes external computation. this is much closer to classical environment-interaction rl than ordinary text-only generation. 5.20.39 the key difference from ordinary tool calling ordinary tool calling often works like: \text{llm} \rightarrow \text{tool} \rightarrow \text{answer}. retool allows: \boxed{ \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{tool} \rightarrow \text{observe} \rightarrow \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{tool} \rightarrow \text{observe} \rightarrow \text{answer} } and crucially: \boxed{ \text{rl decides whether and when to call the tool}. } that timing is the learned skill. 5.20.40 the “aha moment” we will study later one of the supplied slides gives a very important example. the model first generates code that calls: greedy() although that function has not been defined. the sandbox returns: \boxed{\text{nameerror}} the model then reads the traceback and says, essentially: the function needs to be defined and produces corrected code. the important point is: \boxed{ \text{no explicit training example taught this exact repair} } according to the slide. it emerged from optimizing correctness while interacting with the tool environment. (source: retool-slides) we will derive this emergence carefully in the next retool steps. 5.20.41 retool vs grpo vs deepseek-r1 this table is worth memorizing: property deepseekmath deepseek-r1 retool rl algorithm grpo grpo ppo trajectory reasoning/output long reasoning chain reasoning + code + tool feedback external environment no no yes reward verifier verifier verifier value model no no yes group sampling baseline yes yes no tool selection learned? no no yes environment feedback no no yes the supplied slides explicitly frame these methods as a progression toward richer trajectories and more agentic rl. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.42 the progression you should understand this is probably the most important conceptual slide in the entire retool deck. stage 1 \boxed{ \text{single answer} } deepseekmath-style rl. stage 2 \boxed{ \text{long reasoning chain} } deepseek-r1. stage 3 \boxed{ \text{reasoning chain + actions + environment feedback} } retool. so: \boxed{ \text{answer} \rightarrow \text{reasoning} \rightarrow \text{acting} } this is exactly the progression the final retool slide calls the course's rl arc and identifies with the broader idea of agentic rl . (source: retool-slides) 5.20.43 numerical bank — retool level 1 — reward correct answer: \boxed{r=+1} incorrect: \boxed{r=-1}. level 2 — hybrid trajectory model tokens: 1200. interpreter tokens: 300. final answer: 20. total: \boxed{1520}. environment fraction: \frac{300}{1520}\times100 \approx \boxed{19.7\%}. level 3 — ppo ratio suppose: \pi_{\theta}(o_t|s_t)=0.12 and: \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t|s_t)=0.10. then: r_t = \frac{0.12}{0.10} = \boxed{1.2}. if: \epsilon=0.2, clipping interval: [0.8,1.2]. therefore: \boxed{r_t^{clip}=1.2}. level 4 — reward-hacking numerical suppose incorrect response: r_{\text{correct}}=-1 but executable-code bonus: +0.2. total: \boxed{-0.8}. this illustrates why a separate execution bonus can create incentives for useless tool use. level 5 — credit assignment a trajectory contains: 500\text{ text tokens} + 100\text{ code tokens} + 50\text{ interpreter tokens} + 10\text{ final tokens}. total: 660. but only policy-generated tokens are: 500+100+10 = \boxed{610}. interpreter tokens: \boxed{50} should not be treated as policy-generated loss targets. 5.20.44 exam conceptual bank q1. what is novel about retool? it makes the rollout a hybrid trajectory containing model-generated reasoning/code plus real external tool feedback, and uses rl to learn when and how to use the tool . (source: retool-slides) q2. why not reward successful code execution directly? because the model could generate arbitrary code that runs successfully without helping solve the task, creating reward hacking. (source: retool-slides) q3. why mask interpreter tokens? because the interpreter generated them, not the policy. training the policy to predict them would corrupt the policy-learning signal. (source: retool-slides) q4. why does retool use ppo rather than grpo? the supplied deck explicitly specifies ppo with a learned value function rather than grpo's group-relative baseline. (source: retool-slides) q5. why is cold-start sft needed? the model first needs to learn the mechanics of the code/interpreter protocol so that rl can explore the strategic question of when tool use is useful. (source: retool-slides) 5.20.45 the deepest takeaway deepseek-r1 taught us: \boxed{ \text{spend more computation inside the model's reasoning process} } retool adds: \boxed{ \text{spend computation outside the model when that is advantageous} } so the model learns a new decision: \boxed{ \text{should i continue reasoning in tokens, or should i invoke a computational tool?} } that creates the transition: \boxed{ \text{llm reasoning} \rightarrow \text{tool-augmented reasoning} \rightarrow \text{agentic rl} } and that is why retool is an important next step after deepseekmath and deepseek-r1. (source: retool-slides) retool mental model remember just this for now: \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft} \rightarrow \text{learn protocol} } \boxed{ \text{ppo} \rightarrow \text{learn strategy} } \boxed{ \text{correctness reward} \rightarrow \text{learn whether tool use actually helps} } \boxed{ \text{kv-cache + masked interpreter tokens + async sandbox} \rightarrow \text{make it scalable} }

core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.20 — retool: reinforcement learning for strategic tool use this lesson: step 5.21 — retool ppo objective, step by step source references: build a deepseek model (from scratch) ; build a reasoning model (from scratch) ; retool-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.21 — retool ppo objective, step by step plan node: i9 · chat order #62 now we go one level deeper. in step 5.20, we established: \boxed{\text{retool = ppo + real code execution + correctness reward}} the key novelty was the hybrid rollout . now we need to understand exactly how ppo operates on that rollout. the retool slides explicitly state that the training objective is plain ppo , not grpo, and that the advantage comes from a learned value function. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.1 start from ordinary language-model rl an llm can be viewed as a policy: \boxed{\pi_\theta} where: \theta = model parameters s_t = state/context at step t o_t = token/action generated at step t the model gives: \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t) which means: probability that the current policy assigns to token o_t , given the current context s_t . for a language model, the state is essentially the current context. so: s_t= (q,o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_{t-1}) where q is the original question. 5.21.2 what does the state look like in retool? this is where retool differs. the context can contain: \boxed{ \text{question} + \text{reasoning} + \text{code} + \text{interpreter output} } for example: question: solve the problem. reasoning: i should search candidate values. code: ... interpreter: 699 reasoning: the candidate appears to be 699... therefore: \boxed{ s_t=(q,o_{}\mid s_t)=0.25 p(\texttt{answer}\mid s_t)=0.05. the model samples one action/token. the important point is: \boxed{ \text{tool invocation itself is generated through the policy} } the model decides to emit code. 5.21.4 then the environment may intervene suppose the model emits: x = 17 * 41 print(x) the sandbox executes it. the result: 697 gets inserted into the context. so the next state becomes: \boxed{ s_{t+1} = \text{previous state} + \text{interpreter feedback} } this is why retool's trajectory is different from ordinary text-only rl. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.5 now ask: how do we update the policy? suppose a rollout eventually gets: r=+1. we want the model to become more likely to repeat useful behavior that led to that successful trajectory. but we do not want: \text{one successful rollout} \rightarrow \text{massive policy change}. this is exactly the problem ppo addresses. 5.21.6 why ppo uses the old policy during rollout collection, we have: \pi_{\text{old}}. after collecting the rollout, we construct a new policy: \pi_\theta. for a sampled token o_t , compare: \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t) against: \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t\mid s_t). define the ratio: \boxed{ r_t(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t) }{ \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t\mid s_t) } } this is the central quantity in ppo. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.7 intuition behind the ratio suppose old policy: p_{\text{old}}(o_t)=0.10 and new policy: p_{\text{new}}(o_t)=0.12. then: r_t = \frac{0.12}{0.10} = \boxed{1.2}. so the new policy increased the probability by: 20\%. if: r_t=1, nothing changed. if: r_t<1, the new policy decreased the probability. 5.21.8 but probability ratio alone isn't enough we also need to know: was this action good or bad? that information is represented by the advantage : \boxed{\hat a_t} this is the crucial quantity in ppo. 5.21.9 what does advantage mean? conceptually: \boxed{ a(s_t,o_t) = \text{how good this action was} - \text{how good we expected the state to be} } for a positive advantage: \hat a_t>0 the action was better than expected. for a negative advantage: \hat a_t<0 the action was worse than expected. therefore: \boxed{ \text{positive advantage} \rightarrow \text{increase probability} } and: \boxed{ \text{negative advantage} \rightarrow \text{decrease probability}. } 5.21.10 where does ppo get advantage from? this is the exact difference from grpo. ppo uses a learned value function: \boxed{ v_\phi(s_t) } where \phi are the parameters of the value model/value head. the supplied reasoning source explicitly explains: ppo's value function estimates expected future outcome quality, while grpo removes this learned value model and gets its relative signal from a sampled group. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.21.11 return vs value suppose the eventual rollout produces reward: r=+1. the value model might predict: v_\phi(s_t)=0.4. then a simple advantage estimate is: \hat a_t = r-v_\phi(s_t). so: \hat a_t = 1-0.4 = \boxed{0.6}. interpretation: the outcome was considerably better than the value model expected. 5.21.12 negative example suppose: r=-1 and: v_\phi(s_t)=-0.2. then: \hat a_t = -1-(-0.2) = \boxed{-0.8}. so: \boxed{ \text{strongly negative advantage} } and ppo pushes the probability of the sampled action downward. 5.21.13 why not simply use reward? this question is extremely important. suppose every token in a 1,000-token trajectory gets the same reward: r=+1. that doesn't tell us what the model expected from each state. the value function provides a baseline: v_\phi(s_t). thus: \boxed{ a_t = \text{actual outcome} - \text{expected outcome} } gives a more informative learning signal. this is the role of the value model in ppo. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.21.14 ppo objective before clipping ignoring clipping for a moment: \boxed{ j(\theta) = \mathbb e \left[ r_t(\theta)\hat a_t \right] } where: r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(o_t|s_t)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_t|s_t)}. so: \boxed{ \text{policy change} \times \text{quality of action} } determines the learning signal. 5.21.15 example with positive advantage suppose: r_t=1.15 and: \hat a_t=0.8. then: r_t\hat a_t = 1.15\times0.8 = \boxed{0.92}. the action was good, and the new policy increased its probability. that is desirable. 5.21.16 example with negative advantage suppose: r_t=0.85 and: \hat a_t=-0.8. then: r_ta_t = 0.85(-0.8) = \boxed{-0.68}. the action was bad and the new policy reduced its probability. that is also desirable. 5.21.17 why clipping is necessary imagine the model suddenly changes: 0.10\rightarrow0.50. then: r_t= \frac{0.50}{0.10} = 5. a fivefold increase is enormous. a single rollout could therefore cause an unstable update. ppo prevents excessive policy movement through clipping. 5.21.18 ppo clipping define: \boxed{ \operatorname{clip}(r_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) } suppose: \epsilon=0.2. then: 1-\epsilon=0.8 and: 1+\epsilon=1.2. therefore: r_t is restricted to: \boxed{[0.8,1.2]}. 5.21.19 full clipped ppo objective the retool slide gives the standard ppo form: \boxed{ j_{\text{ppo}}(\theta) = \mathbb e_t \left[ \min \left( r_t(\theta)\hat a_t,\, \operatorname{clip} (r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat a_t \right) \right] } this is the core retool training objective. (source: retool-slides) now we will understand exactly why the min is there. 5.21.20 case a: positive advantage suppose: a_t=+2 and: r_t=1.5. raw objective: r_ta_t = 1.5\times2 = 3. clipped ratio: \operatorname{clip}(1.5,0.8,1.2) = 1.2. therefore: 1.2\times2 = 2.4. take minimum: \boxed{ \min(3,2.4)=2.4 } so ppo refuses to give the full benefit of the 50% probability increase. 5.21.21 case b: negative advantage now: a_t=-2 and: r_t=0.5. raw: 0.5(-2) = -1. clipped: \operatorname{clip}(0.5,0.8,1.2) = 0.8. then: 0.8(-2) = -1.6. take minimum: \boxed{ \min(-1,-1.6)=-1.6 } this makes excessive policy movement toward a bad action unattractive. 5.21.22 the geometric intuition think of ppo as saying: \boxed{ \text{"improve the policy, but don't move too far in one update."} } so: \text{good action} \rightarrow \text{increase probability} but only moderately. and: \text{bad action} \rightarrow \text{decrease probability} but again with controlled updates. 5.21.23 now bring retool back into the equation here is where everything becomes interesting. the action might be a normal reasoning token: i should search... or: or: for x in range(...) the model may therefore receive credit for a sequence like: \boxed{ \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{call tool} \rightarrow \text{observe} \rightarrow \text{correct} \rightarrow \text{answer} } the probability ratio is calculated for model-generated tokens within that hybrid trajectory. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.24 important subtlety: interpreter output isn't the policy action suppose: print(5*9) produces: 45 the model generated: \boxed{\texttt{print(5*9)}} but the environment generated: \boxed{\texttt{45}} therefore the policy ratio is conceptually associated with model-generated decisions, not with the external environment's generated text. this connects directly to the earlier engineering rule: \boxed{ \text{mask interpreter tokens} } from the retool deck. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.25 full miniature trajectory consider: question: find the valid value of x. model: i should search the candidate space. model: for x in range(1,1000): ... environment: 699 model: the interpreter found 699. model: \boxed{699} policy-generated sequence: \boxed{ \text{reasoning} + \text{code} + \text{final answer} } environment-generated sequence: \boxed{ \text{699} } final reward: r=+1. now ppo computes advantages over the relevant model-generated positions and updates the policy so useful behavior becomes more likely. 5.21.26 full mathematical pipeline here is the entire calculation: step 1 — sample trajectory \tau\sim\pi_{\text{old}} step 2 — execute tool calls \text{code} \rightarrow \text{sandbox} \rightarrow \text{feedback} step 3 — obtain final reward r(\tau)\in\{-1,+1\} step 4 — value prediction v_\phi(s_t) step 5 — advantage conceptually: \hat a_t \approx \text{return}-v_\phi(s_t) step 6 — policy ratio r_t= \frac{\pi_\theta(o_t|s_t)} {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_t|s_t)} step 7 — clipping \tilde r_t = \operatorname{clip} (r_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon) step 8 — ppo objective \boxed{ \min(r_ta_t,\tilde r_ta_t) } step 9 — gradient update \theta \leftarrow \theta+\eta\nabla_\theta j_{\text{ppo}} that is the complete policy-update pipeline at the conceptual level. (source: retool-slides; build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.21.27 why retool does not use grpo here now compare the advantage calculation. ppo \boxed{ \hat a_t \approx r_t-v_\phi(s_t) } requires: \boxed{ \text{learned value function} } grpo uses a group of responses: r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_g and constructs group-relative advantages. for example: a_i= \frac{r_i-\mu_r}{\sigma_r}. no value model is required. the supplied sources make exactly this distinction: grpo replaces the learned value-model path with group-relative normalization. 5.21.28 why this distinction matters computationally ppo: \boxed{ \text{policy model} + \text{value model} } grpo: \boxed{ \text{policy model} + \text{multiple sampled responses} } the value model can be expensive for large llm systems. grpo was attractive in deepseekmath and deepseek-r1 partly because it eliminates that separate learned value model. (source: build a reasoning model (from scratch)) retool nevertheless uses ppo according to the supplied deck. 5.21.29 full numerical ppo example now let's perform one complete calculation. suppose at one model-generated token: \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t|s_t)=0.20 and after the update candidate: \pi_{\theta}(o_t|s_t)=0.24. then: r_t= \frac{0.24}{0.20} = \boxed{1.2}. suppose: v_\phi(s_t)=0.3 and final reward: r=1. then simple advantage estimate: a_t=1-0.3 = \boxed{0.7}. set: \epsilon=0.2. then: \operatorname{clip}(1.2,0.8,1.2)=1.2. raw: 1.2(0.7)=0.84. clipped: 1.2(0.7)=0.84. therefore: \boxed{ j_t=0.84 } no clipping penalty occurs because the ratio is exactly at the upper boundary. 5.21.30 now push beyond the boundary suppose instead: \pi_\theta=0.30. then: r_t=\frac{0.30}{0.20}=1.5. advantage: a_t=0.7. raw: 1.5(0.7)=1.05. clipped: 1.2(0.7)=0.84. ppo chooses: \boxed{ \min(1.05,0.84)=0.84 } so increasing the probability from 0.20 all the way to 0.30 does not receive unlimited optimization credit. 5.21.31 one very important interpretation ppo clipping does not literally force: r_t\in[0.8,1.2]. the new policy can have a ratio outside the interval. instead, the objective stops rewarding the excessive movement in the favorable direction . this is a subtle but highly important exam/interview point. 5.21.32 why this is valuable for retool imagine that one successful trajectory contained: call code → get result → use result → answer correctly without clipping, ppo might aggressively increase the probability of all those actions. with clipping: \boxed{ \text{successful strategy} \rightarrow \text{reinforced gradually} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{successful rollout} \rightarrow \text{huge policy jump} }. 5.21.33 the complete retool learning loop now put all previous steps together: question │ ▼ old policy πold │ ▼ generate reasoning/code │ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ │ normal text │ ▼ sandbox │ ▼ interpreter result │ └──────► context │ ▼ continue generation │ ▼ final answer │ ▼ correctness checker │ ▼ r = ±1 │ ▼ value function vφ │ ▼ advantage ât │ ▼ ppo ratio rt(θ) │ ▼ clipping │ ▼ policy gradient │ ▼ new policy this is the architecture you should have in your head before moving to implementation. the retool deck's central ppo and hybrid-trajectory description supports this structure. (source: retool-slides) 5.21.34 numerical bank — level 5 exam question consider: \pi_{\text{old}}=0.08 \pi_\theta=0.16 v_\phi(s_t)=0.25 r=1 \epsilon=0.2. calculate the clipped ppo term. step 1 r_t=\frac{0.16}{0.08}=2. step 2 a_t=1-0.25=0.75. step 3 clip: \operatorname{clip}(2,0.8,1.2)=1.2. step 4 raw: 2(0.75)=1.5. clipped: 1.2(0.75)=0.9. step 5 \boxed{ \min(1.5,0.9)=0.9 } so the ppo objective contribution is: \boxed{0.9}. 5.21.35 one more exam question: negative advantage suppose: \pi_{\text{old}}=0.20, \pi_\theta=0.10, a_t=-1. then: r_t=0.5. for: \epsilon=0.2, we get: \operatorname{clip}(0.5,0.8,1.2)=0.8. raw: 0.5(-1)=-0.5. clipped: 0.8(-1)=-0.8. therefore: \boxed{ \min(-0.5,-0.8)=-0.8 } this demonstrates how ppo treats large probability movement associated with a negative advantage. 5.21.36 the five things you must remember \boxed{1.\quad r_t= \frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{old}}}} measures how much the new policy changed the probability of the sampled action. \boxed{2.\quad a_t} measures whether the action/outcome was better or worse than expected. \boxed{3.\quad v_\phi(s_t)} provides ppo's learned baseline for estimating advantage. \boxed{4.\quad \operatorname{clip}} prevents one update from receiving excessive incentive for moving too far. \boxed{5.\quad \text{retool's special part}} the state/trajectory contains: \boxed{ \text{reasoning + code + real interpreter feedback} } rather than text alone. (source: retool-slides) the conceptual bridge you should now see the complete progression: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} \rightarrow \text{grpo} \rightarrow \text{deepseek-r1} \rightarrow \text{long reasoning} \rightarrow \text{retool} \rightarrow \text{tool-interacting reasoning} } and mathematically: \boxed{ \text{reward} \rightarrow \text{advantage} \rightarrow \text{probability ratio} \rightarrow \text{clipping} \rightarrow \text{policy update} }

(source: retool-slides) 5.23.1 start with one question suppose the training question is: \boxed{q=\text{“solve this computationally difficult problem.”}} and the ground-truth answer is: \boxed{a=699}. the model starts generating from q . at this moment, the policy is: \boxed{\pi_{\text{old}}} because this is the policy used to collect the rl rollout. 5.23.2 token 1 onward: ordinary generation the model begins: i need to find the valid candidate. then perhaps: a direct manual search would be tedious. these are ordinary policy-generated tokens. formally: o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_t \sim \pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid s_t). nothing special has happened yet. 5.23.3 the model reaches a tool decision eventually it generates: this is a critical event. the model has effectively taken the action: \boxed{ a_t=\text{invoke computational tool} } the retool prompt gives the model the ability to use executable python, but does not hard-code when to use it. that timing is meant to be learned through rl. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.4 the model now generates code for example: for x in range(1, 1000): ... the model continues until it reaches: at that moment: \boxed{ \text{generation pauses} } the slide explicitly states that code is sent to the real sandbox when is detected. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.5 important: the model does not generate the next observation the model generated: \boxed{\text{code}} but the next result comes from: \boxed{\text{environment}}. so the system executes: \text{code} \longrightarrow \text{sandbox} \longrightarrow \text{output / error}. this is the point where the llm temporarily gives control to an external environment. 5.23.6 the sandbox returns real feedback suppose the code returns: 699 the system inserts something conceptually like: 699 into the rollout. the model now sees: \boxed{ \text{its previous reasoning} + \text{its code} + \text{actual computation result} } and generation resumes. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.7 the rollout is still one trajectory this point is easy to misunderstand. we do not create separate trajectories: \tau_1=\text{reasoning} \tau_2=\text{code} \tau_3=\text{interpreter} instead, retool treats everything as one trajectory: \boxed{ \tau= t_1 \oplus c_1 \oplus f_1 \oplus t_2 \oplus c_2 \oplus f_2 \oplus o } the slide explicitly describes this concatenation into a single token sequence. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.8 why this matters because the eventual reward belongs to the whole strategy . suppose: \tau= \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{feedback} \rightarrow \text{correction} \rightarrow \text{final answer}. the reward doesn't separately say: r_{\text{reason}}=... r_{\text{code}}=... r_{\text{feedback}}=... instead: \boxed{ r(\tau)=+1 } if the final answer is correct. thus ppo must determine how to assign learning signal across the model's own decisions throughout the trajectory. 5.23.9 second tool call now imagine the first result is not enough. the model reasons: the candidate is 699, but i should verify the condition. then it generates another: ... the sandbox executes again. suppose it returns: valid now the trajectory is: \boxed{ t_1 \oplus c_1 \oplus f_1 \oplus t_2 \oplus c_2 \oplus f_2 } and generation resumes again. this can repeat until the model chooses to produce its final answer. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.10 the final answer eventually: \boxed{699} is produced. the system extracts the answer from the \boxed{} expression. so: \hat a=699. ground truth: a=699. 5.23.11 the verifier computes the reward retool uses a rule-based correctness checker. therefore: r(a,\hat a)= \begin{cases} +1,&\text{equivalent}\\ -1,&\text{otherwise} \end{cases} so here: \boxed{ r=+1 } the retool deck explicitly says this is the entire reward and deliberately does not add a separate reward merely for successfully executing code. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.12 why does the reward arrive only at the end? consider two trajectories. trajectory a reason → code → useful result → correct answer reward: +1. trajectory b reason → useless code → useless result → wrong answer reward: -1. the model therefore has to discover that tool use is valuable when it improves eventual task success. that is why the deck says that correctness-only reward forces each code call to “earn its keep” through its contribution to the final result. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.13 now the ppo stage begins the rollout is now complete. we have: \boxed{\tau} and: \boxed{r(\tau)}. we now need to turn that into learning signals. for each policy-generated token o_t , ppo evaluates: \boxed{ r_t(\theta) = \frac{ \pi_\theta(o_t\mid s_t;ci) }{ \pi_{\text{old}}(o_t\mid s_t;ci) } } as given in the retool objective. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.14 what exactly is s_t here? this is extremely important. in ordinary text-only rl: s_t= [q,\text{previous generated tokens}]. in retool: \boxed{ s_t= [q,\text{reasoning},\text{code},\text{interpreter feedback},\ldots] } so after the sandbox says: 699 the next policy decision is conditioned on that new observation. this is where the environment actually changes the model's future behavior. 5.23.15 example: before and after tool feedback before execution: p(\text{“699”}\mid s_t) = \text{some probability}. after the interpreter returns: 699, the context changes: s_t\rightarrow s_{t+1}. the model may now assign: p(\text{“the answer is”}\mid s_{t+1}) a much larger probability. therefore the external tool isn't merely attached to the end of the system. it changes the future token distribution of the policy. 5.23.16 now the most important engineering detail: interpreter masking suppose the trajectory is: token 1: i token 2: will token 3: calculate token 4: token 5: print ... token 20: token 21: token 22: 699 token 23: token 24: therefore token 25: ... tokens 21–23 came from the environment. so: \boxed{ \text{do not train the policy to predict them} } the retool slide explicitly says interpreter-generated tokens are excluded from the loss. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.17 why exactly? suppose the sandbox returns: 17\times41=697. the model did not choose: 697. the environment did. therefore giving the policy a token-level prediction loss for 697 would amount to saying: “model, you should have predicted this environment output.” but the model had no control over that output. so: \boxed{ \text{credit only decisions made by the policy} } is the correct learning principle. 5.23.18 visualize the loss mask imagine: tokens: [ reasoning reasoning code code code int int int reasoning reasoning final ] mask: [ 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 1 1 1 ] where: 1=\text{policy token} 0=\text{interpreter token}. thus the policy loss only sees: \boxed{ \text{model-generated tokens} } and ignores: \boxed{ \text{environment-generated tokens} }. 5.23.19 another important point: the feedback is still in the context masking does not mean removing interpreter output. this distinction is critical. the interpreter output is: \boxed{ \text{visible to the model} } but: \boxed{ \text{not treated as a policy prediction target} }. so the model can read: 699 and use 699 in later reasoning. but the loss does not ask the model to generate 699 . 5.23.20 second engineering optimization: kv-cache reuse now suppose the model has already generated: n=5000 tokens before making its code call. all of those tokens already have cached keys and values. when the interpreter returns: m=50 new tokens, retool does not need to recompute the entire previous prefix. instead: \boxed{ k,v_{\text{old prefix}} \text{ are reused} } and only the new feedback is appended. the slide explicitly identifies this as one of the engineering details making multi-turn tool use affordable at rl scale. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.21 why this is such a big deal without cache reuse: \text{tool call} \rightarrow \text{reprocess entire prefix}. with reuse: \text{tool call} \rightarrow \text{reuse prefix cache} + \text{process new observation}. so repeated tool calls become much more manageable. 5.23.22 numerical kv-cache question suppose: l_{\text{old}}=8000 cached tokens. interpreter adds: l_{\text{new}}=100. with kv reuse, the new feedback extends the cache by: \boxed{100\text{ tokens}} rather than requiring the whole 8100-token history to be treated as new input for cache construction. again, this is the conceptual cache-efficiency calculation; the deck's claim is specifically that the old prefix can be reused and only new interpreter-feedback tokens need cache computation/appending. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.23 why asynchronous execution is needed now imagine a batch of 1000 rollouts. one rollout's code: 20\text{ ms} another: 100\text{ ms} another: 2\text{ s} another: 8\text{ s}. if all code execution were strictly synchronous, slow executions could cause the entire generation pipeline to wait. retool therefore uses an asynchronous sandbox pool so slow executions do not stall the rest of rl training. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.24 distributed-systems interpretation you can view the system as: \boxed{ \text{inference workers} } communicating with: \boxed{ \text{sandbox worker pool} } through asynchronous requests/results. conceptually: llm worker │ │ code request ▼ queue │ ├──► sandbox 1 ├──► sandbox 2 ├──► sandbox 3 └──► sandbox n │ ▼ execution result │ ▼ llm worker that architecture follows the slide's description of an asynchronous sandbox pool; details such as the exact queue technology are not specified by the supplied slides. 5.23.25 what happens if the code crashes? this is one of retool's most interesting properties. suppose the model produces: greedy() but greedy is undefined. the environment returns: \boxed{\text{nameerror}} the model sees that real feedback. it can then reason: the function has not been defined. and produce corrected code. the supplied slide presents this as an emergent self-correction behavior that appeared through rl rather than being explicitly demonstrated in a training example. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.26 this is the birth of tool-mediated self-correction text-only self-correction: \text{model} \rightarrow \text{its own critique} \rightarrow \text{its own revision} retool can do: \boxed{ \text{model} \rightarrow \text{real execution} \rightarrow \text{real error} \rightarrow \text{revision} } that is much more grounded because the correction is based on an externally generated observation. 5.23.27 why is an error useful for rl? suppose: \text{code}_1 \rightarrow \text{nameerror} \rightarrow \text{code}_2 \rightarrow \text{correct answer}. the overall trajectory receives: r=+1. thus the successful trajectory contains: \boxed{ \text{failure} + \text{recovery} } the rl optimizer can reinforce the policy behavior surrounding that successful recovery. this is why useful behavior can emerge even without an sft example showing exactly that same error correction. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.28 important distinction: the environment isn't being trained the policy is trained. the sandbox is an environment that provides feedback. so: \boxed{ \theta_{\text{llm}} \rightarrow \text{updated} } while the code interpreter remains the external execution mechanism. this is conceptually the standard agent-environment separation. 5.23.29 full rollout in mathematical notation let's define: \tau= (o_1,o_2,\ldots,o_t) with some positions corresponding to interpreter outputs. the model generates certain positions according to: o_t\sim\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid s_t). when a code boundary is reached: c_i \rightarrow e(c_i) = f_i where e is the sandbox execution function. then: s_{t+1} = s_t\oplus c_i\oplus f_i. eventually: \hat a=\operatorname{extract}(\tau). then: r(\tau) = \begin{cases} +1,&\operatorname{equivalent}(a,\hat a)\\ -1,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} that scalar reward then drives ppo. 5.23.30 the complete lifecycle now the entire retool rollout can be written as: \boxed{ q } \downarrow \boxed{ \pi_{\text{old}}\text{ generates reasoning} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{model chooses code} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{sandbox execution} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{real output/error} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{output inserted into context} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{model resumes} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{repeat if necessary} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{final }\boxed{a} } \downarrow \boxed{ r\in\{-1,+1\} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{ppo advantage + ratio + clipping} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{update policy} } 5.23.31 full numerical example let's make one trajectory. model-generated tokens: t_m=900. interpreter tokens: t_i=100. total trajectory: t=1000. the model makes two tool calls. first call code tokens: 150. interpreter: 30. second call code tokens: 200. interpreter: 70. the remaining model-generated tokens are: 900-(150+200)=550 which can include reasoning and final answer. check: 550+150+200+30+70 = \boxed{1000}. thus the interpreter contributes: \frac{100}{1000} = \boxed{10\%} of trajectory tokens. but those 100 tokens are masked from the policy loss while remaining visible in the context. 5.23.32 ppo numerical example on one generated token suppose a model-generated token has: \pi_{\text{old}}=0.10 and candidate new policy: \pi_\theta=0.13. so: r_t=1.3. suppose: \hat a_t=0.6 and: \epsilon=0.2. then: \operatorname{clip}(1.3,0.8,1.2)=1.2. raw: 1.3(0.6)=0.78. clipped: 1.2(0.6)=0.72. therefore: \boxed{ j_t=\min(0.78,0.72)=0.72. } the model still benefits from making that useful action more likely, but ppo limits the optimization incentive for a movement beyond the clipping region. 5.23.33 what exactly is being learned? not simply: \boxed{\text{“use python.”}} the model is learning something much richer: \boxed{ \text{given the current state, what action sequence maximizes eventual correctness?} } the action sequence can contain: \text{text} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{interpretation} \rightarrow \text{text} \rightarrow \text{code} \rightarrow \text{final answer}. that is why retool is better understood as strategic tool-use learning , not merely tool calling. 5.23.34 why the result is interesting the supplied results show a dramatic difference between: \text{sft only} \text{text-only rl} and: \boxed{\text{rl + real code interpreter}} on aime2024 for the specified qwen2.5-32b-instruct setup: 26.7\% \rightarrow 40.9\% \rightarrow 40.0\% \rightarrow 67.0\%. the supplied slide attributes the large jump specifically to combining rl with the ability to call a real code interpreter, rather than to sft or text-only rl alone. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.35 training efficiency result the supplied deck also reports that retool's accuracy curve rises much faster and reaches its plateau around step 400, while the text-only baseline continues improving beyond step 1000. it reports retool reaching its higher accuracy using approximately: \boxed{37\%} of the training steps used by that text-only rl baseline. (source: retool-slides) this supports a deeper interpretation: \boxed{ \text{tools don't merely increase capability; they can simplify exploration} } because certain computations no longer have to be discovered entirely through token-level reasoning. 5.23.36 one subtle but powerful conclusion earlier we said: \text{rl} = \text{discover/strengthen behavior}. retool reveals what kind of behavior can be discovered: \boxed{ \text{interaction strategy} } not just verbal reasoning. the model can discover: \text{“i should calculate now.”} \text{“that output looks suspicious.”} \text{“the interpreter gave me an error.”} \text{“i should fix the code.”} \text{“now i have enough evidence to answer.”} that is a qualitatively richer policy than: \boxed{ \text{keep generating text until answer} }. 5.23.37 exam checkpoint you should now be able to explain all six of these without memorizing the deck: 1. what is the retool rollout? \boxed{ \text{single hybrid trajectory of reasoning + code + interpreter feedback + answer} } 2. who generates interpreter tokens? \boxed{\text{the external sandbox}} 3. are interpreter tokens trained with the policy loss? \boxed{\text{no, they are masked.}} 4. why reuse kv cache? \boxed{ \text{to avoid recomputing the entire prefix after tool execution} } 5. why asynchronous sandbox execution? \boxed{ \text{to prevent slow code executions from stalling rl generation} } 6. what does ppo actually learn? \boxed{ \text{which model-generated actions, including tool-use decisions, lead to successful outcomes} } these points are directly grounded in the retool rollout and engineering slides. (source: retool-slides) 5.23.38 master picture for steps 5.20–5.23 we can now compress everything into one equation chain: \boxed{ \underbrace{ d_{\text{init}} \rightarrow d_{\text{ci}} \rightarrow \text{sft} }_{\text{learn protocol}} } then: \boxed{ \underbrace{ \text{policy rollout} \rightarrow \text{code execution} \rightarrow \text{environment feedback} \rightarrow \text{final answer} }_{\text{generate hybrid trajectory}} } then: \boxed{ \underbrace{ r=\pm1 \rightarrow \hat a_t \rightarrow r_t \rightarrow \operatorname{clip} \rightarrow \nabla_\theta }_{\text{ppo learns strategy}} } so the overall retool idea is: \boxed{ \textbf{sft teaches the model how to talk to the tool;} \quad \textbf{rl teaches the model when and why to use it.} }
