(source: retool-slides) 5.24.1 first understand what is being measured at every saved rl checkpoint, retool evaluates the model's own generated responses. the six metrics are: \boxed{ \text{response length} } \boxed{ \text{code ratio} } \boxed{ \text{code lines} } \boxed{ \text{correct code count} } \boxed{ \text{code pass rate} } \boxed{ \text{code invocation timing} } the important point is: \boxed{ \text{none of these were separately optimized as explicit rewards} } according to the slide. the only reward was: \boxed{ r= \begin{cases} +1 & \text{correct}\\ -1 & \text{incorrect} \end{cases} } yet the six behaviors changed systematically. (source: retool-slides) that is the first major lesson. 5.24.2 signal 1 — response length before rl, the model's responses were approximately: \boxed{10,000\text{ tokens}} on the reported measurement. after rl, they ended around: \boxed{6,000\text{ tokens}} which is roughly a: \frac{10000-6000}{10000}\times100 = \boxed{40\%} reduction. (source: retool-slides) but something more interesting happens during training. the curve does not simply decrease monotonically. the slide says response length: falls sharply at first, then rises again, and ultimately ends substantially shorter than before rl. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.3 why does response length initially fall? before rl, the model may perform computation manually in text: first calculate this... then calculate that... let's check another possibility... now substitute... let's recompute... after discovering useful code-based strategies, it can replace many textual arithmetic steps with: ... followed by: <interpreter> ... </interpreter> so: \boxed{ \text{manual textual computation} \rightarrow \text{compact executable computation} } this compresses the reasoning trajectory. the slide explicitly attributes the initial length reduction to code replacing laborious manual calculation. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.4 why does response length rise again? this is the subtle part. after learning basic code usage, the model starts discovering more elaborate computational strategies . so the trajectory becomes: \text{simple reasoning} \rightarrow \text{compact code} \rightarrow \text{more sophisticated code strategies}. the code itself can become larger and more powerful. therefore: \boxed{ \text{better tool use does not necessarily mean fewer tokens at every stage} } the final result is still about 40% shorter, but the path there involves more sophisticated behavior. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.5 signal 2 — code ratio now define the intuition behind code ratio . conceptually: \boxed{ \text{code ratio} = \frac{\text{responses containing code}} {\text{total responses}} } the reported trend is striking. initially: \boxed{\text{under }20\%} of responses used code. by the end: \boxed{\text{nearly }98\%} of responses used code. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.6 what does that mean? before rl: \text{most responses} \rightarrow \text{text-only}. after rl: \text{almost all responses} \rightarrow \text{tool-augmented}. so the policy has discovered: \boxed{ \text{code is broadly useful for this task distribution} } under the learned reward. this is extremely important because nobody directly said: “use python in 98% of your answers.” instead: \boxed{ \text{correctness reward} \rightarrow \text{policy discovers high-value code use} } according to the reported analysis. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.7 but doesn't this look like overuse? yes—and this is an important nuance. a code ratio of nearly 98% means the model learned to use code very frequently on the evaluated task distribution. that does not imply: \boxed{ \text{98\% is universally optimal} } the deck only reports the behavior that emerged in this training/evaluation setup. you should not generalize that number to arbitrary tasks. this is a source-derived observation, not a universal law. 5.24.8 signal 3 — number of code lines now we go deeper. the model isn't merely calling code more often. the code itself becomes more substantial. the slide reports that the number of code lines rises throughout training and becomes nearly: \boxed{5\times} longer by the end. (source: retool-slides) so we have: \boxed{ \text{code frequency}\uparrow } and simultaneously: \boxed{ \text{code complexity/size}\uparrow } at least as measured by line count. 5.24.9 why is that important? suppose early behavior is: print(a * b) that is raw arithmetic. later behavior might look more like: for candidate in candidates: if condition_1(candidate): if condition_2(candidate): ... now the model is using the tool not merely as a calculator. it's delegating a larger computational subproblem. therefore: \boxed{ \text{tool role expands} } from: \text{calculator} toward: \boxed{ \text{computational reasoning module} }. 5.24.10 signal 4 — correct code counts the slide reports that the number of correct code executions on the test set rises approximately: \boxed{5\times}. so we now have three simultaneous trends: \text{more responses use code} \text{code blocks become longer} \text{more of those code executions are correct}. this is evidence that the model is not merely generating random or increasingly verbose code. the useful computational behavior itself is improving. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.11 signal 5 — code pass rate this is arguably the most informative metric. the reported pattern is: \boxed{ \text{correct final-answer responses} \rightarrow \text{code pass rate near 100\%} } while: \boxed{ \text{incorrect final-answer responses} \rightarrow \text{lower code pass rate}. } the deck calls buggy code a leading indicator of a wrong final answer . (source: retool-slides) 5.24.12 why is this important? consider: successful trajectory \text{correct code} \rightarrow \text{useful result} \rightarrow \text{correct answer}. failed trajectory \text{buggy code} \rightarrow \text{bad/no result} \rightarrow \text{wrong answer}. so code correctness is strongly associated with final reasoning success in the reported experiment. this suggests that the external tool doesn't merely act as a computational accelerator: \boxed{ \text{the quality of the interaction itself becomes diagnostic} } for the final answer. 5.24.13 signal 6 — tool invocation timing this is especially important for understanding strategy . early in training, the model tends to: \boxed{ \text{reason in text first} \rightarrow \text{use code later} } the slide reports that tool invocation gradually shifts earlier in the response. (source: retool-slides) so the model learns: \boxed{ \text{reach for the tool sooner} } when it recognizes that computation will be useful. 5.24.14 why does earlier tool use help? imagine a problem that requires a long search. text-first strategy: 500\text{ reasoning tokens} \rightarrow \text{finally invoke code}. tool-early strategy: 50\text{ reasoning tokens} \rightarrow \text{invoke code}. the second strategy can obtain an objective computational result earlier, which can then influence all subsequent reasoning. so: \boxed{ \text{earlier external feedback} \rightarrow \text{earlier correction/grounding} } this is one reason tool integration can simplify the exploration problem. the source explicitly reports the timing shift but does not give a universal mathematical rule saying “earlier is always better.” that broader claim would be an inference. 5.24.15 put all six signals together now the six signals tell a coherent story. 1. response length \boxed{\downarrow} overall. 2. code ratio \boxed{\uparrow} from under 20% to nearly 98%. 3. code line count \boxed{\uparrow} nearly 5×. 4. correct code count \boxed{\uparrow} approximately 5×. 5. code pass rate \boxed{ \text{high for correct responses} } and lower for incorrect ones. 6. invocation timing \boxed{ \text{moves earlier} } the interesting combination is: \boxed{ \text{less textual labor} + \text{more sophisticated computation} } 5.24.16 this is a genuine strategy shift the phrase to remember is: \boxed{ \textbf{rl is changing how the model solves the problem} } rather than merely: \boxed{ \textbf{rl is changing the model's final answer probability} } the six metrics show evidence of a behavioral strategy transformation. 5.24.17 the “aha moment” now we reach the most interesting example from the deck. the model generates code containing: greedy() but greedy() has not been defined. the sandbox returns: \boxed{\text{nameerror}} the model reads the traceback and recognizes the problem. it then generates corrected code. the slide presents this as an emergent behavior: no training example explicitly demonstrated this exact “fix after error” behavior, yet it emerged through optimizing correctness reward. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.18 why is this an “aha moment”? because the model has effectively learned: \boxed{ \text{tool failure} \rightarrow \text{inspect feedback} \rightarrow \text{diagnose} \rightarrow \text{repair} \rightarrow \text{continue} } this is much more sophisticated than: \text{generate code} \rightarrow \text{hope it works}. it has acquired an interaction strategy. 5.24.19 where did the learning signal come from? the model did not receive a reward saying: +0.3 for fixing errors. it only received the final correctness reward: r= \begin{cases} +1\\ -1 \end{cases} therefore, the reasoning is: \boxed{ \text{successful recovery} \rightarrow \text{higher chance of final correctness} } and ppo reinforces trajectories containing such useful behavior. this is precisely why the deck calls it emergent. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.20 numerical reward illustration imagine two policies encountering the same code bug. policy a \text{error} \rightarrow \text{give up} \rightarrow r=-1. policy b \text{error} \rightarrow \text{inspect traceback} \rightarrow \text{fix} \rightarrow \text{correct answer} \rightarrow r=+1. then trajectories resembling policy b receive the better learning signal. over repeated rl updates: p(\text{error recovery behavior}) can increase. this is the mechanism by which a self-correction strategy can emerge without a dedicated error-repair reward. 5.24.21 another major discovery: code's role changes before rl, the slide says code is used predominantly for: \boxed{ 79.1\% } of code snippets for raw calculation . after rl: \boxed{ 51.4\% } of code snippets are for calculation. (source: retool-slides) that means: 79.1\%-51.4\% = \boxed{27.7\text{ percentage points}} of the distribution shifts away from raw calculation. 5.24.22 where does that usage go? the slide identifies new roles including: \boxed{\text{optimization}} \boxed{\text{geometric calculation}} \boxed{\text{solution search}} so code evolves from: \boxed{ \text{calculator} } toward: \boxed{ \text{general computational reasoning tool} }. this is an especially important result because it demonstrates that the model learned new uses for the tool , not merely more frequent use of the same calculator behavior. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.23 let's quantify that shift suppose, purely illustratively, there are: 1000 code snippets before rl. at 79.1% calculation: 791 are calculation-oriented. after rl, at 51.4%: 514 are calculation-oriented. thus: 791-514 = \boxed{277} fewer snippets fall into that category. the remaining: 486 snippets belong to other categories. these numbers are a direct arithmetic illustration of the percentages reported in the slide, not additional source statistics. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.24 why is this result so important? because it demonstrates: \boxed{ \text{tool use} \neq \text{calculator use} } a sufficiently capable model can learn to use code for: \text{search} \text{optimization} \text{geometry} and other computational subroutines. thus: \boxed{ \text{external computation becomes part of the reasoning strategy} } 5.24.25 same question, two reasoning styles the slide provides a particularly useful comparison. for the same four-digit-integer problem: text-only reasoning the model performs a long manual modular-arithmetic derivation and reaches: \boxed{629} which is wrong. a single arithmetic mistake propagates through later steps. code-interpreter reasoning the model delegates the arithmetic to two short code blocks and reaches: \boxed{699} which is confirmed by the interpreter. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.26 this illustrates the core advantage text-only: \boxed{ \text{many dependent manual operations} } a single error: \boxed{ e_1 \rightarrow e_2 \rightarrow e_3 \rightarrow \cdots } can corrupt the entire chain. tool-assisted: \boxed{ \text{delegate exact computation} } and receive: \boxed{ \text{externally verified intermediate result} }. the model can then reason from a more reliable computational observation. 5.24.27 tool use therefore changes the location of computation this is an excellent mental model. before: \boxed{ \text{llm} \rightarrow \text{does everything itself} } after retool: \boxed{ \text{llm} \leftrightarrow \text{external computation} } the intelligence is no longer just: \text{generate tokens}. it becomes: \boxed{ \text{decide what to compute internally} + \text{decide what to delegate externally} } 5.24.28 why this is “agentic rl” now the final slide's conclusion makes sense. the course's progression is: \boxed{ \text{single answer trajectory} } then: \boxed{ \text{long reasoning trajectory} } then: \boxed{ \text{reasoning + external actions + feedback} } that corresponds to: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} \rightarrow \text{deepseek-r1} \rightarrow \text{retool} } the supplied deck calls this progression toward a richer notion of trajectory and identifies it as the essence of agentic rl . (source: retool-slides) 5.24.29 the deep connection to our previous lessons recall our earlier distinction: rl \boxed{ \text{discover / strengthen behavior} } distillation \boxed{ \text{transfer / compress behavior} } retool adds: \boxed{ \text{discover / strengthen interaction strategy} } so now the overall evolution is: \text{reasoning behavior} \rightarrow \text{tool-use behavior} \rightarrow \text{agentic behavior}. 5.24.30 exam-style numerical bank numerical 1 — response reduction before rl: 10000 tokens. after rl: 6000. reduction: 4000. percentage: \frac{4000}{10000}\times100 = \boxed{40\%}. this matches the reported approximate reduction. (source: retool-slides) numerical 2 — code ratio suppose 5000 responses are evaluated and 98% contain code. 5000(0.98) = \boxed{4900} responses use code. remaining: 5000-4900 = \boxed{100}. the 98% figure comes from the supplied deck; the 5000-response example is illustrative. (source: retool-slides) numerical 3 — code-line growth suppose average code size before rl is: 12\text{ lines}. a nearly 5× increase gives: 12\times5 = \boxed{60\text{ lines}}. this illustrates the reported “nearly 5×” trend; 12 lines is hypothetical. (source: retool-slides) numerical 4 — calculation share suppose 2000 code snippets exist. before rl: 2000(0.791) = \boxed{1582} calculation snippets. after rl: 2000(0.514) = \boxed{1028}. decrease: 1582-1028 = \boxed{554}. so approximately 554 fewer snippets are classified as raw calculation-oriented. again, 2000 is illustrative; 79.1% and 51.4% come from the supplied slide. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.31 exam-style conceptual question question: why is the emergence of error correction especially strong evidence that retool is learning a strategy rather than merely memorizing tool-call syntax? because the supplied example shows: \text{invalid code} \rightarrow \text{real sandbox error} \rightarrow \text{interpretation of error} \rightarrow \text{code repair} \rightarrow \text{successful completion} without an explicit training example demonstrating that exact repair behavior. the reported explanation is that correctness-only rl makes successful recovery valuable because it increases the probability of eventually obtaining the correct answer. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.32 final retool behavioral model by the end of our retool sequence, you should mentally see: \boxed{ \text{before rl} } \text{text-heavy} + \text{rare code} + \text{mostly arithmetic use} and: \boxed{ \text{after rl} } \text{shorter overall responses} + \text{very frequent code} + \text{longer/more sophisticated code} + \text{more correct code} + \text{earlier tool invocation} + \text{error recovery} all of those behaviors emerge under the single correctness objective reported by the deck. (source: retool-slides) 5.24.33 the most important takeaway retool does not simply teach: \boxed{ \text{“llm + calculator”} } it teaches a policy of: \boxed{ \text{reason} \rightarrow \text{decide whether computation helps} \rightarrow \text{invoke tool} \rightarrow \text{read feedback} \rightarrow \text{adapt} \rightarrow \text{verify} \rightarrow \text{answer} } and the remarkable part is that the rl objective does not explicitly specify all those intermediate behaviors. instead: \boxed{ \text{correctness reward} \rightarrow \text{emergent strategy} } this is the central lesson of step 5.24. (source: retool-slides) course-level progression so far \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} \rightarrow \text{grpo} } \boxed{ \text{deepseek-r1} \rightarrow \text{long reasoning + rlvr} } \boxed{ \text{r1 distillation} \rightarrow \text{transfer reasoning to smaller models} } \boxed{ \text{retool} \rightarrow \text{reasoning + external computation + learned tool strategy} }

retool ablation deltas and their limits status: primary_table_checked; experiments_not_reproduced retool v1 table1 on aime2024 lists qwen2.5-32b-instruct26.7,coldstart40.9,textrl40.0 and retool67.0. differences versus base are14.2,13.3 and40.3 percentage points; versus textrl, retool gains27.0points. these are reported comparisons, not a reproduced experiment or proof that every use of tools causes a27-point gain. primary/official source · §3,table1; supplied retool slides10–11 remaining evidence: reproduce sampling, tool sandbox, training budget and evaluator before claiming experimental replication. the inherited statement remains below for traceability; use this version-specific qualification when interpreting it. core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.24 — what retool actually discovers during rl this lesson: step 5.25 — retool results and ablation logic source references: retool-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.25 — retool results and ablation logic plan node: i9 · chat order #66 now we will learn how to read the retool results scientifically . do not just memorize: 26.7\rightarrow40.9\rightarrow40.0\rightarrow67.0 the important question is: \boxed{\text{what does each comparison isolate?}} that is what an ablation study is doing. 5.25.1 first: what is an ablation? suppose a complete system has components: a+b+c. we want to know which component actually matters. so we remove components one at a time: a a+b a+b+c. then compare performance. this is an ablation. the key logic is: \boxed{ \text{change one important ingredient while keeping the rest comparable} } and observe what happens. 5.25.2 retool's four configurations the supplied slide gives this progression on aime2024 , using the specified qwen2.5-32b-instruct setup: (source: retool-slides) configuration aime2024 base model, no training 26.7% + cold-start sft, no rl 40.9% + rl, text-only, no code interpreter 40.0% + rl, with code interpreter — retool 67.0% let's not jump to the conclusion yet. we will derive every comparison. 5.25.3 comparison 1 — base model → cold-start sft we start with: 26.7\%. after cold-start sft: 40.9\%. absolute improvement: 40.9-26.7 = \boxed{14.2\text{ percentage points}}. this is exactly the \delta shown by the slide. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.4 what does this comparison prove? it shows that: \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft is useful} } for this setup. more specifically, the sft stage provides a substantial gain before rl begins. this is consistent with what we learned earlier: \boxed{ \text{sft teaches the model the code/interpreter protocol} } so the model can participate in the later rl environment. 5.25.5 what does it not prove? it does not prove: \boxed{ \text{sft is better than rl generally} } because that isn't the experiment being performed. it also does not prove that: \boxed{ \text{sft alone is sufficient} } because the full retool system later improves substantially beyond 40.9%. so our scientifically correct statement is: in this reported setup, cold-start sft produces a 14.2-point improvement over the untrained base model on aime2024. not: sft solves tool-use reasoning. 5.25.6 comparison 2 — cold-start sft vs text-only rl now compare: 40.9\% versus: 40.0\%. difference: 40.0-40.9 = \boxed{-0.9\text{ percentage points}}. so text-only rl is actually 0.9 points lower than cold-start sft in this reported comparison. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.7 this is the surprising result you might have expected: \text{sft}+rl > \text{sft}. but in the reported comparison, the text-only rl configuration reaches: 40.0\% while sft alone reaches: 40.9\%. so: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl adds almost nothing beyond sft here} } the slide explicitly emphasizes this interpretation. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.8 why is this important? because it isolates something very specific. it tells us that: \boxed{ \text{rl by itself is not the source of the giant improvement} } at least in this particular comparison. the big gain comes when rl has access to: \boxed{ \text{real code execution} } 5.25.9 comparison 3 — base → text-only rl the slide also shows: 26.7\%\rightarrow40.0\%. so the absolute improvement is: 40.0-26.7 = \boxed{13.3\text{ points}}. this is the slide's reported \delta . (source: retool-slides) so text-only rl does improve over the raw base model . but compare: 13.3 to sft's: 14.2. they are very similar. thus the important conclusion isn't: text-only rl does nothing. instead: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl helps relative to the raw base, but provides little additional gain over the cold-start sft baseline in this experiment} } that is a much more precise interpretation. 5.25.10 comparison 4 — text-only rl → retool now comes the major jump. text-only rl: 40.0\%. retool: 67.0\%. improvement: 67.0-40.0 = \boxed{27.0\text{ percentage points}}. this is the critical comparison. 5.25.11 comparison 5 — sft → retool cold-start sft: 40.9\%. retool: 67.0\%. improvement: 67.0-40.9 = \boxed{26.1\text{ percentage points}}. so almost the entire extraordinary jump occurs when the system moves from: \boxed{ \text{sft/text reasoning} } to: \boxed{ \text{rl + actual code execution} }. 5.25.12 comparison 6 — base → retool from: 26.7\% to: 67.0\%. absolute improvement: 67.0-26.7 = \boxed{40.3\text{ percentage points}}. that is the slide's reported overall gain. (source: retool-slides) so relative to the original base performance: \frac{67.0-26.7}{26.7}\times100 \approx \boxed{151.3\%} relative improvement. be careful: \boxed{40.3\text{ points}} and: \boxed{151.3\%\text{ relative improvement}} are different quantities. the slide reports the former; the latter is our arithmetic calculation. 5.25.13 now identify the actual experimental variable let's construct the progression: 26.7 \downarrow +14.2 40.9 \downarrow -0.9 40.0 \downarrow +27.0 67.0. what changes most dramatically in the last transition? \boxed{ \text{real code-interpreter interaction} } that is why the slide concludes that the gain is specifically associated with learning when and how to use the tool , rather than with rl or tools alone. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.14 why can't we just say “the tool caused everything”? because that would be too strong. retool contains multiple ingredients: \text{cold-start sft} + \text{rl} + \text{code interpreter}. the 67.0% result belongs to the combination . the ablation demonstrates that the combination performs dramatically better than the text-only variants. but a single ablation table cannot establish every possible causal decomposition under every alternative training setup. so the careful statement is: \boxed{ \text{in the reported experiment, the large additional gain appears when rl is combined with real tool interaction.} } that is exactly the interpretation supported by the deck. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.15 why is the “rl without tool” baseline necessary? this is a very important experimental-design principle. suppose the authors only reported: 40.9\%\rightarrow67.0\%. someone could argue: maybe rl itself creates the 26-point improvement. to test that hypothesis, they include: \boxed{ \text{rl without code interpreter} } and obtain: 40.0\%. that comparison weakens the explanation: \text{“rl alone caused the 27-point jump.”} because under this setup: \boxed{ 40.0\% \not\approx 67.0\% } 5.25.16 this is how you should read ablations when you see: a=40.9 b=40.0 c=67.0 ask: what changed between a and c? and: what changed between b and c? here: a vs c \text{sft} \rightarrow \text{sft + rl + tool interaction} b vs c \text{text-only rl} \rightarrow \text{tool-integrated rl}. the second comparison is especially informative because both involve rl, so it more directly isolates the contribution of adding the tool interaction to the rl setup described in the slide. 5.25.17 a simple causal diagram conceptually: base model │ ┌───────┴────────┐ │ │ sft text rl │ │ 40.9 40.0 │ │ └──────┬─────────┘ │ + real tool │ 67.0 the exact experimental paths are those shown in the deck; this diagram is just a visualization of the ablation logic. 5.25.18 retool versus external baselines the headline slide reports that on the specified setup: retool aime2024: \boxed{67.0\%} aime2025: \boxed{49.3\%}. it says this exceeds every listed baseline, including: openai o1-preview 44.6\% / 37.9\% and: qwen2.5-math-instruct-tir 72b 40.0\% on aime2024. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.19 but there is another important result the slide says replacing the backbone with: \boxed{\text{deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b}} raises performance further to: \boxed{ 72.5\%\text{ aime2024} } and: \boxed{ 54.3\%\text{ aime2025}. } (source: retool-slides) 5.25.20 what does this teach us? it reinforces an idea we already encountered during distillation: \boxed{ \text{base-model quality matters} } retool isn't independent of the backbone. same broad tool/rl idea: \text{different backbone} \rightarrow \text{different ceiling}. so: \boxed{ \text{tool use is an additional capability, not a replacement for model capability} } that broader wording is an inference from the reported comparison; the deck itself simply reports the stronger-backbone result. 5.25.21 let's compare the two backbones numerically qwen2.5-32b-instruct retool: 67.0\%. deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b backbone: 72.5\%. difference: 72.5-67.0 = \boxed{5.5\text{ points}}. for aime2025: 54.3-49.3 = \boxed{5.0\text{ points}}. these are arithmetic calculations from the slide's reported numbers. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.22 training efficiency: why fewer steps matter now consider the learning curves. the slide reports: \boxed{ \text{retool plateau }\approx\text{ step }400 } while: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl continues past step }1000 } and retool reaches its higher accuracy using approximately: \boxed{37\%} of the training steps of the text-only rl baseline. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.23 numerical interpretation suppose the text-only baseline requires: 1000 steps. then: 0.37\times1000 = \boxed{370} steps. the reported plateau around 400 steps is therefore broadly consistent with the approximate 37% statement. but notice the wording: \boxed{\text{about }37\%} and: \boxed{\text{around step }400}. these are approximate empirical observations, not an exact algebraic identity. 5.25.24 why could tool use make exploration easier? this is the deeper interpretation proposed by the slide. consider text-only rl. the model must discover: \text{how to reason} + \text{how to calculate} + \text{how to search} + \text{how to verify}. all inside generated text. with a computational tool: \boxed{ \text{computation is delegated to an external mechanism} } so the model can explore higher-level strategies such as: \text{what to calculate} rather than having to manually simulate every arithmetic step in language. thus the slide's interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{tools do not merely increase the final ceiling;} \text{they make the exploration problem easier.} } (source: retool-slides) 5.25.25 be careful about the word “easier” the slide says: tool use doesn't just raise the ceiling; it makes the exploration problem itself easier to solve. (source: retool-slides) this is an interpretation of the observed learning curve. it does not give a formal theorem that external tools mathematically reduce rl sample complexity in every setting. so in an exam: good: \boxed{ \text{the reported learning curve suggests improved exploration efficiency.} } too strong: \boxed{ \text{tools always reduce sample complexity.} } 5.25.26 another important numerical comparison compare: 67.0 with: 40.0. relative improvement from text-only rl: \frac{67.0-40.0}{40.0}\times100 = \boxed{67.5\%}. so retool's aime2024 accuracy is about 67.5% higher relative to the text-only rl baseline in this particular reported comparison. again: 27\text{ points} is the source-friendly quantity; 67.5\% is our derived relative-improvement calculation. 5.25.27 what exactly do the ablations support? let's formalize the conclusions. conclusion a \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft is useful.} } evidence: 26.7\rightarrow40.9. conclusion b \boxed{ \text{text-only rl does not provide a large additional gain over sft in this setup.} } evidence: 40.9\rightarrow40.0. conclusion c \boxed{ \text{adding real code interaction to rl produces the major gain.} } evidence: 40.0\rightarrow67.0. conclusion d \boxed{ \text{a stronger reasoning backbone can raise the retool result further.} } evidence: 67.0\rightarrow72.5. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.28 what the ablation does not prove this is equally important. the table does not establish that: \boxed{\text{retool is universally better than every rl method}} or: \boxed{\text{code interpreters are universally better than other tools}} or: \boxed{\text{67\% is a universal upper bound}} or: \boxed{\text{sft is unnecessary}} or: \boxed{\text{text-only rl never works}} those claims go beyond the supplied evidence. the experiment is about the reported setup and comparisons. 5.25.29 why this matters for research-paper reading a common mistake is: \boxed{ \text{correlation} \rightarrow \text{absolute causal claim} } the correct research mindset is: identify the controlled comparison. identify what changed. identify what stayed approximately constant. attribute the result only to what the experiment actually isolates. for retool, the most informative isolation is: \boxed{ \text{text-only rl} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{rl + real code interpreter} } because both are rl variants in the reported ablation. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.30 exam numerical set question 1 base: 26.7\%. retool: 67.0\%. find absolute improvement. \boxed{40.3\text{ points}} question 2 sft: 40.9\%. text-only rl: 40.0\%. difference: \boxed{-0.9\text{ points}} so text-only rl is 0.9 points below sft. question 3 text-only rl: 40.0\%. retool: 67.0\%. absolute gain: \boxed{27.0\text{ points}} relative gain: \frac{27}{40}\times100 = \boxed{67.5\%}. question 4 qwen2.5-32b retool: 67.0\%. distill-qwen-32b backbone: 72.5\%. gain: \boxed{5.5\text{ points}}. question 5 text-only rl uses 1000 steps. retool uses 37%. 1000(0.37) = \boxed{370\text{ steps}}. 5.25.31 exam-style reasoning question question: an experiment reports 26.7% for a base model, 40.9% after sft, 40.0% after text-only rl, and 67.0% after rl with a code interpreter. what is the strongest conclusion supported by the ablation? correct reasoning: 40.9\approx40.0 but: 67.0\gg40.0. therefore the reported results indicate that the major gain is associated with combining rl with real tool interaction , rather than with text-only rl alone. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.32 the entire result section in one picture \boxed{ \text{base} = 26.7 } \downarrow \quad +14.2 \boxed{ \text{cold-start sft} = 40.9 } \downarrow \quad -0.9 \boxed{ \text{text-only rl} = 40.0 } \downarrow \quad +27.0 \boxed{ \text{retool} = 67.0 } and with the stronger reported backbone: \boxed{ 72.5 } on aime2024. (source: retool-slides) 5.25.33 the key insight the most important result is not merely : 67\%. it is the decomposition: \boxed{ \text{sft helps} } \boxed{ \text{text-only rl adds little here} } \boxed{ \text{rl + real tool interaction adds a major gain} } this tells us that retool is not simply: \boxed{\text{“ppo applied to a math model.”}} the valuable learned capability is: \boxed{ \text{strategic interaction with an external computational environment} } which is exactly what the preceding six behavioral signals also suggested. (source: retool-slides) where retool now fits in the full course we can now see the complete conceptual ladder: \boxed{ \text{deepseekmath} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{grpo learns from relative outcome quality} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{deepseek-r1} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{rl strengthens long reasoning chains} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{r1 distillation} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{transfer reasoning into smaller models} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{retool} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{learn when/how to interact with an external computational tool} } that is the complete conceptual purpose of this topic.

core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.26 — indic language benchmarks: why indicxtreme exists this lesson: step 5.27 — indiccorp v2: building the indic pretraining corpus source references: indicxtreme-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.27 — indiccorp v2: building the indic pretraining corpus plan node: i10 · chat order #68 now we go through indiccorp v2 from raw web sources to the final 20.9b-token corpus , exactly in the order of the supplied deck. the central pipeline is: \boxed{ \text{discover sources} \rightarrow \text{human verify} \rightarrow \text{crawl} \rightarrow \text{language filter} \rightarrow \text{script filter} \rightarrow \text{punctuation/length filter} \rightarrow \text{offensive-content filter} \rightarrow \text{deduplicate} \rightarrow 20.9b\text{ tokens} } the important idea is that large-scale web collection is not treated as “just scrape everything.” the corpus uses a quality gate before crawling and multiple automatic cleaning stages afterward. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.1 first: what is indiccorp v2? indiccorp v2 is the pretraining corpus component of the overall indic work. the deck describes it as: \boxed{20.9\text{b tokens}} across: \boxed{24\text{ languages}} and: \boxed{4\text{ language families}}. its purpose is to provide substantially better indic-language monolingual pretraining data. (source: indicxtreme-slides) remember the separation: \boxed{ \text{indiccorp}=\text{training data} } \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme}=\text{evaluation benchmark} } \boxed{ \text{indicbert v2}=\text{model trained on indiccorp and evaluated on indicxtreme} } 5.27.2 step 1 — find good source websites the first question is: where should the text come from? the deck says the corpus prioritizes clean, diverse text , and therefore chooses news articles as the primary source . this is a deliberate departure from generic web corpora such as: \boxed{\text{cc-100}} and: \boxed{\text{mc4}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.3 why news? think about the alternatives. a generic commoncrawl-style dump may contain: \text{forums} + \text{blogs} + \text{spam} + \text{machine-generated pages} + \text{duplicated pages} + \text{navigation text} + \text{advertising} + \text{clean articles}. a news source is much more likely to provide structured natural-language prose. so the corpus construction process deliberately prioritizes: \boxed{ \text{high-quality source domains} } rather than simply maximizing raw token count. this is source-derived from the deck; the expanded list of typical web-noise categories is explanatory context. 5.27.4 step 2 — discover new sources the researchers did not rely only on existing indiccorp v1 sources. the deck says new sources were found using: \boxed{\text{news repositories}} and: \boxed{\text{automatic web search}}. the search queries are generated from frequent words in the target language . retrieved pages are then inspected to identify candidate source urls. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.5 why use frequent words as search queries? suppose the target language is hindi. a corpus builder can obtain frequent hindi words and use them as search queries. conceptually: w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_k are frequent words. then: w_i \rightarrow \text{search engine} \rightarrow \text{candidate pages} \rightarrow \text{candidate source domains}. this increases the chance of discovering websites that actually publish text in the target language. the deck emphasizes that this discovery stage is noisy. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.6 why is source discovery noisy? because a page retrieved using a language-specific word does not guarantee: \boxed{ \text{clean indic-language text} }. a retrieved url might contain: \text{offensive content} or: \text{machine-generated content}. so the researchers need another stage: \boxed{ \text{human verification} }. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.7 step 3 — human verification before crawling this is one of the most important design decisions. before crawling a candidate site: \boxed{ \text{a human checks the url} } the annotator visits the candidate url and verifies that it is: a genuine website, containing clean data, in the language of interest. only verified urls are then passed to the web-crawling system. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.8 why verify the url before crawling? because crawling is expensive. imagine discovering: 100,000 candidate websites. suppose many are: \text{spam} or: \text{wrong language} or: \text{machine-generated}. if you crawl everything first and clean it later, you waste: \boxed{\text{crawl bandwidth + storage + processing}} on obviously bad sources. so indiccorp inserts a quality gate early: \boxed{ \text{candidate url} \rightarrow \text{human verification} \rightarrow \text{crawl} } rather than: \text{candidate url} \rightarrow \text{crawl everything} \rightarrow \text{huge cleanup}. the deck explicitly identifies this as the distinction in the “verified source urls” row compared with cc-100 and mc4. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.9 how aggressive is this gate? across languages: \boxed{1\%-33\%} of candidate urls are discarded as noisy. so different languages have different source quality. that itself is informative. a language with: 1\% rejection is very different from one with: 33\% rejection. the exact language-by-language values are not given on this slide, only the overall range. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.10 numerical example — url verification suppose: 10,000 candidate urls are collected. if: 20\% are rejected, then: 10,000\times0.20 = \boxed{2,000} urls are rejected. accepted: 10,000-2,000 = \boxed{8,000}. this is an illustrative calculation; the actual slide gives a rejection range of 1–33%, not this specific 20% example. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.11 step 4 — crawl the verified sources once urls pass human review, they are handed to the: \boxed{\text{open-source webcorpus toolkit}} for crawling. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so the sequence is: \boxed{ \text{search} \rightarrow \text{candidate url} \rightarrow \text{human verification} \rightarrow \text{web crawl} } this separation is very important. 5.27.12 why not make the entire pipeline human? because the corpus is: \boxed{20.9\text{ billion tokens}} which is far too large for full manual inspection. so the design is hybrid: \boxed{ \text{human supervision at strategic quality gates} } plus: \boxed{ \text{automatic large-scale filtering} }. this pattern appears repeatedly throughout the indic work. 5.27.13 step 5 — language identification (lid) after crawling, the raw text needs to be checked for language. the deck says paragraph-level language filtering is performed using: \boxed{\text{cld3}} and: \boxed{\text{langdetect}} in parallel. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so conceptually: \text{paragraph} \rightarrow \begin{cases} \text{cld3}\\ \text{langdetect} \end{cases} \rightarrow \text{language decision}. 5.27.14 why use two language-id tools? the deck's reason is practical rather than theoretical: \boxed{ \text{one tool has language-specific limitations} } it notes that cld3 misses: \boxed{\text{assamese and oriya}} and that neither of the two tools supports: \boxed{\text{bodo and dogri}}. therefore lid filtering is skipped for bodo and dogri. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a very useful data-engineering lesson: \boxed{ \text{automation is only as good as its coverage on the target population} } 5.27.15 why is skipping lid for bodo and dogri not necessarily a contradiction? because a filter that cannot correctly recognize the language could be worse than not applying it. suppose the true language is: l. if the detector doesn't support l , then applying its output may cause systematic false rejection. so: \boxed{ \text{unsupported detector} \rightarrow \text{do not blindly trust detector output} } the deck specifically says lid filtering is skipped for bodo and dogri. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.16 step 6 — script-based cleaning language identification alone isn't enough. a page can still contain: \text{indic text} + \text{english phrases} + \text{latin transliteration}. therefore the next filter checks the proportion of characters written in the language's native script. the deck uses a threshold: \boxed{0.75}. a sentence is dropped if: \boxed{ \frac{\text{native-script characters}} {\text{total characters}} <0.75 } (source: indicxtreme-slides) this formula is a direct expression of the threshold described by the slide. 5.27.17 numerical example — script threshold suppose a sentence contains: 200 characters. of these: 150 are in the native script. then: \frac{150}{200} = 0.75. so it is: \boxed{\text{not dropped under the stated }<0.75\text{ rule}} because the fraction is exactly 0.75, not below 0.75. 5.27.18 another example suppose: 200 characters total and: 140 native-script characters. then: \frac{140}{200} = 0.70. because: 0.70<0.75, the sentence is: \boxed{\text{dropped}}. excellent exam-style threshold question. 5.27.19 why use a script threshold? because a sentence can technically pass language identification while still being dominated by another script. for example: indic-language words + english terminology + transliteration could produce a misleadingly mixed corpus. the script threshold therefore improves: \boxed{ \text{language-pure text quality} }. that is the purpose described by the slide. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.20 step 7 — punctuation-based cleaning now punctuation is stripped from each sentence. then the system asks: \boxed{ \text{how many words remain?} } if the resulting content is shorter than: \boxed{10\text{ words}} the document is discarded entirely. (source: indicxtreme-slides) notice the granularity: sentence-level punctuation stripping, document-level discard condition. that's easy to miss. 5.27.21 why strip punctuation? because punctuation and formatting can contribute noise to corpus statistics. the deck's pipeline uses this cleaning stage before deciding whether the remaining textual content is substantial enough. the specific 10-word threshold is source-derived. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.22 numerical example — 10-word threshold suppose after punctuation stripping a document contains: 8 remaining words. since: 8<10, it is: \boxed{\text{discarded}}. if it contains: 10 words: 10<10 is false. therefore: \boxed{\text{it survives this particular threshold}} assuming it passes the other filters. 5.27.23 why is this not just sentence filtering? because the slide explicitly says: if what remains is shorter than 10 words, the document is discarded entirely. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a useful exam trap. do not accidentally write: \text{discard sentence if <10 words}. the stated operation is: \boxed{ \text{discard document if remaining content <10 words} }. 5.27.24 step 8 — offensive-content filtering now comes another important cleaning stage. web-crawled indic text can contain offensive material. the deck uses two blacklists . blacklist a — in-house list native annotators create an in-house list covering: \boxed{17\text{ languages}} with about: \boxed{90\text{ words/phrases per language}} and including some borderline expressions identified as contextually offensive by native speakers. (source: indicxtreme-slides) blacklist b — nllb list a second independently released blacklist covers: \boxed{209\text{ languages}}. this is merged with the in-house list to widen coverage. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.25 why use two lists? because one list has: \boxed{\text{deep native/context coverage}} for the 17 languages, while the other provides: \boxed{\text{much wider language coverage}}. thus: \boxed{ \text{local expertise} + \text{broad external coverage} } produces a stronger filtering mechanism. that interpretation follows the stated purposes of the two lists. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.26 how is the offensive filter applied? the deck says: for a blacklisted word remove the sentence if the word occurs. for a blacklisted phrase remove the sentence if the whole phrase appears verbatim . so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{blacklisted word} \rightarrow \text{remove sentence} } and: \boxed{ \text{blacklisted phrase appears verbatim} \rightarrow \text{remove sentence} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.27 the surprising scale effect before this offensive-content filter: \boxed{23.1\text{b tokens}} after: \boxed{20.9\text{b tokens}}. reduction: 23.1-20.9 = \boxed{2.2\text{b tokens}}. percentage reduction: \frac{2.2}{23.1}\times100 \approx \boxed{9.52\%} which the deck reports as: \boxed{9.5\%}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.28 exam question — filtering percentage question: a corpus contains 23.1b tokens before filtering and 20.9b after filtering. what percentage was removed? \frac{23.1-20.9}{23.1}\times100 = \frac{2.2}{23.1}\times100 \approx \boxed{9.52\%} so the reported: \boxed{9.5\%} is mathematically consistent. 5.27.29 step 9 — deduplication after the cleaning pipeline, the resulting corpus is deduplicated . this matters because web crawling often finds the same material multiple times. for example: d_1=d_2 could happen because: multiple urls mirror the same article, syndication duplicates content, crawlers encounter repeated copies. if duplicated text remains, a language model effectively sees: \boxed{ \text{same evidence repeatedly} } which inflates the apparent dataset size. the deck reports the final corpus as de-duplicated . (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.30 final corpus after these steps: \boxed{ 20.9\text{b tokens} } remain across: \boxed{ 24\text{ languages} }. this is indiccorp v2. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.31 compare with indiccorp v1 indiccorp v1: \boxed{ 8.79\text{b tokens} } across: \boxed{ 12\text{ languages} }. indiccorp v2: \boxed{ 20.9\text{b tokens} } across: \boxed{ 24\text{ languages} }. so the token-scale ratio is: \frac{20.9}{8.79} \approx \boxed{2.38\times}. the deck states that the paper rounds this to approximately: \boxed{2.3\times}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.32 and language coverage doubled v1: 12 languages. v2: 24. so: \frac{24}{12} = \boxed{2\times}. this is a simple but useful observation from the reported figures. so the improvement is not merely: \boxed{\text{more text}} but also: \boxed{\text{broader language coverage}}. 5.27.33 hindi growth the deck reports that hindi alone grew: \boxed{3.28\times} from v1 to v2, with the paper rounding it to: \boxed{3.3\times}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this shows why simply saying “the corpus grew 2.38×” is incomplete. different languages experienced different growth. 5.27.34 low-resource tail this is an extremely important observation. the bottom: \boxed{11} lowest-resource languages together contribute only: \boxed{1.08\text{b tokens}}. the deck explicitly contrasts this with hindi alone. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so even within a corpus described as “indic”: \boxed{ \text{data distribution remains highly unequal} } 5.27.35 numerical interpretation of the low-resource tail the 11-language tail contributes: 1.08\text{b} out of: 20.9\text{b}. fraction: \frac{1.08}{20.9} \approx 0.0517. therefore: \boxed{\approx5.17\%} of the total corpus is contributed by those bottom 11 languages. this is our derived calculation from the deck's reported numbers. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.36 why this is important for the later benchmark results this connects directly to what we'll eventually see. even after creating a massive indic corpus: 20.9\text{b tokens} the data is still not evenly distributed. therefore we should expect: \boxed{ \text{resource-rich languages} > \text{resource-poor languages} } in many downstream tasks. and indeed, later in the deck, the lowest-resource languages show sharp performance drops. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so the data-construction section isn't isolated. it explains the benchmark results we will study later. 5.27.37 complete indiccorp pipeline now memorize the architecture: frequent-language words │ ▼ news repositories / web search │ ▼ candidate urls │ ▼ human url verification │ ▼ verified sources │ ▼ web crawling │ ▼ raw crawled text │ ├──► language id │ cld3 + langdetect │ ├──► native-script threshold │ >= 0.75 │ ├──► punctuation stripping │ document must retain >= 10 words │ ├──► offensive-content filtering │ in-house + nllb lists │ ▼ deduplication │ ▼ 20.9b-token indiccorp v2 the major stages and thresholds are directly from the supplied deck. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.38 what is human and what is automatic? this is another exam-important classification. human \boxed{ \text{source url verification} } and: \boxed{ \text{creation of the in-house offensive blacklist} } automatic \boxed{ \text{web crawling} } \boxed{ \text{lid} } \boxed{ \text{script filtering} } \boxed{ \text{punctuation/length filtering} } \boxed{ \text{blacklist filtering} } \boxed{ \text{deduplication} } the in-house blacklist itself comes from human annotators, while its application to text is automatic. 5.27.39 the underlying engineering philosophy indiccorp v2 follows a pattern: \boxed{ \text{human judgment where semantic quality is difficult} } and: \boxed{ \text{automation where scale is essential} }. humans are good at answering: “is this website actually a trustworthy source in the language?” machines are good at applying: \text{millions/billions of repetitive filtering operations}. that hybrid architecture is one of the most important lessons from the corpus-construction section. 5.27.40 exam-style level 5 problem suppose a hypothetical crawl produces: 10\text{b tokens}. after: lid filtering: 85% remain script filtering: 80% of the previous stage remains punctuation/length filtering: 90% remain offensive filtering: 90% remain deduplication: 95% remain then final size is: 10 \times0.85 \times0.80 \times0.90 \times0.90 \times0.95 = \boxed{5.2334\text{b tokens approximately}}. this is an illustrative multi-stage filtering problem, not an indiccorp reported statistic. the exam lesson is: \boxed{ \text{successive percentages multiply; they do not simply add} } 5.27.41 another exam trap suppose: 23.1\text{b} becomes: 20.9\text{b}. do not say: “the corpus lost 2.2%.” it lost: 2.2\text{b tokens} and the percentage loss is: \boxed{9.5\%}. always distinguish: \boxed{\text{absolute reduction}} from: \boxed{\text{relative percentage reduction}}. 5.27.42 another exam trap: 0.75 threshold the rule is: \text{drop if native-script fraction}<0.75. so: 0.749 \rightarrow \boxed{\text{drop}} but: 0.750 \rightarrow \boxed{\text{keep under this particular rule}}. because the inequality is strictly less than . 5.27.43 final mental model you should now visualize indiccorp v2 as: \boxed{ \text{discovery} } find candidate sources. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{human quality gate} } verify sources before crawling. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{web crawl} } collect massive raw text. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{automatic linguistic cleaning} } lid + script + length. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{safety/quality filtering} } offensive-content filtering. \downarrow \boxed{ \text{deduplication} } remove repeated material. \downarrow \boxed{ 20.9\text{b tokens / 24 languages} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.27.44 the deepest lesson the most important thing about indiccorp is not: \boxed{20.9\text{b}} it is the pipeline philosophy : \boxed{ \text{more data is not automatically better data} } a useful pretraining corpus must optimize: \boxed{ \text{coverage} + \text{quality} + \text{language correctness} + \text{script purity} + \text{safety} + \text{deduplication} } while still operating at billion-token scale. and there is a fundamental tension: \boxed{ \text{corpus-wide scale} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{low-resource language balance} } the final 20.9b-token corpus is much larger than v1, but the deck makes clear that its language distribution is still highly uneven. (source: indicxtreme-slides) step 5.27 checkpoint for an exam, you should be able to reproduce this without the slides: \boxed{ \text{search} \rightarrow \text{human url verification} \rightarrow \text{crawl} \rightarrow \text{lid} \rightarrow \text{script }(0.75) \rightarrow \text{length }(10\text{ words}) \rightarrow \text{offensive filter} \rightarrow \text{deduplicate} } and remember: \boxed{ 23.1b\rightarrow20.9b = 2.2b\text{ removed} = 9.5\%\text{ reduction} } \boxed{ 20.9/8.79\approx2.38\times } \boxed{ 24\text{ languages in indiccorp v2} } \boxed{ \text{bottom 11 languages}=1.08b\text{ tokens} } (source: indicxtreme-slides)

(source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.1 first understand why there are multiple tasks suppose a model gets: 90\% on sentiment. does that mean the model understands an indic language? not necessarily. it could be good at: \text{classification} but weak at: \text{ner} or: \text{question answering} or: \text{retrieval} or: \text{causal reasoning}. so indicxtreme intentionally evaluates multiple capabilities. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{language ability} \approx \text{many different downstream capabilities} } this is why the benchmark is a task suite , not one single test. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.2 the 9 tasks the benchmark table gives: classification — 5 \boxed{\text{indicsentiment}} \boxed{\text{indicxnli}} \boxed{\text{indiccopa}} \boxed{\text{indicpara}} \boxed{\text{m-intent}} structure prediction — 2 \boxed{\text{naamapadam}} \boxed{\text{m-slotfill}} qa — 1 \boxed{\text{indicqa}} retrieval — 1 \boxed{\text{flores}} (source: indicxtreme-slides) let's understand them sequentially. step 5.28.3 task 1 — indicsentiment the first task is: \boxed{\text{indicsentiment}} its purpose is sentiment classification. the model receives a review and predicts its sentiment category. for example: "the product looks excellent and works perfectly." the model might predict: \boxed{\text{positive}} while: "the material is poor and the product broke quickly." might be: \boxed{\text{negative}}. the benchmark table lists: 13 languages, 1,000 test examples, accuracy as the metric, product reviews as the domain. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.4 why is sentiment useful? sentiment appears simple, but multilingual sentiment is not merely: \text{translate english words} \rightarrow \text{predict polarity}. a model has to understand the actual indic-language input. the deck's later creation slide also deliberately makes indicsentiment harder than ordinary polarized review datasets by constructing reviews around specific product aspects rather than using only strongly positive/negative generic reviews. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.5 important creation detail the supplied deck says indicsentiment was built by: curating products from 15 popular categories on amazon, flipkart, and myntra; identifying product aspects; asking annotators to write positive/negative reviews around particular aspects; translating the english reviews into 13 indic languages manually. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is important because it attempts to create a more nuanced sentiment task. 5.28.6 metric: accuracy for classification: \boxed{ \text{accuracy} = \frac{\text{correct predictions}} {\text{total predictions}} } suppose: n=1000 test examples. if the model gets: 850 correct: \text{accuracy} = \frac{850}{1000} = \boxed{85\%}. 5.28.7 exam numerical a model gets 920 correct out of 1,000 indicsentiment examples. \frac{920}{1000}\times100 = \boxed{92\%}. very straightforward, but this type of calculation should be automatic for you. step 5.28.8 task 2 — indicxnli next: \boxed{\text{indicxnli}} this is the natural language inference (nli) task. the input is typically: \boxed{ \text{premise} + \text{hypothesis} } and the model determines their relationship. conceptually, the classes are: \boxed{ \text{entailment} } \boxed{ \text{contradiction} } \boxed{ \text{neutral} } the benchmark table lists: \boxed{12\text{ languages}} and: \boxed{5010\text{ test examples}}. the table marks its construction as machine-translated (mt), while the later deck explains that the resulting test set is being manually re-verified and corrected. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.9 example of nli premise: “rahul went to the market and bought vegetables.” hypothesis: “rahul bought vegetables.” then: \boxed{\text{entailment}} because the premise supports the hypothesis. hypothesis: “rahul did not buy anything.” then: \boxed{\text{contradiction}}. hypothesis: “rahul went to the market on sunday.” then: \boxed{\text{neutral}} unless the premise supplies that information. 5.28.10 why is indicxnli interesting for multilingual evaluation? because the original xnli-style setup is based on cross-lingual transfer. the important benchmark question becomes: \boxed{ \text{can a model learn the inference task from english and transfer it to an indic language?} } that question becomes central to the zero-shot evaluation protocol we'll study later. 5.28.11 metric again: \boxed{\text{accuracy}} suppose 5,010 test cases exist and the model gets 3,758 correct. then: \frac{3758}{5010}\times100 \approx \boxed{74. \! \ \text{?}} let's calculate carefully: 3758/5010\approx0.7501. so: \boxed{\approx75.0\%}. 5.28.12 task 3 — indiccopa now we get to a much more reasoning-oriented task: \boxed{\text{indiccopa}} copa stands for: \boxed{\text{choice of plausible alternatives}} it tests causal commonsense reasoning . the model receives: \boxed{\text{premise}} and two possible alternatives. it must choose which alternative is the more plausible: \boxed{\text{cause}} or: \boxed{\text{effect}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.13 example premise: “the road became extremely slippery.” question: what was the likely cause? options: a. it had rained heavily. b. the shop opened late. correct: \boxed{a} the model needs causal commonsense rather than simple keyword matching. 5.28.14 how indiccopa was constructed the deck gives a very interesting anti-bias procedure. the english copa test set is manually translated into: \boxed{18\text{ indic languages}}. but before translation: \boxed{ \text{premise + option 1 + option 2} } are randomized and reassigned across translators. that means one translator does not see the entire original item. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.15 why randomize the pieces? suppose a translator sees the whole item. they might unconsciously preserve: \text{sentence length} or: \text{word choice} or: \text{stylistic cues} that reveal the answer. then the benchmark could contain a translation artifact. the bias-guard procedure attempts to prevent this. so: \boxed{ \text{randomization} \rightarrow \text{reduced translation leakage} } this is directly from the dataset-construction description. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.16 important training detail copa itself has no training split. therefore fine-tuning uses: \boxed{\text{english social iqa}} according to the slide. this is another example of the benchmark's cross-lingual transfer idea. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.17 task 4 — indicpara next: \boxed{\text{indicpara}} this is a paraphrase/equivalence classification task. the question is: \boxed{ \text{do two sentences express essentially the same meaning?} } the benchmark table lists: \boxed{10\text{ languages}} and: \boxed{2002\text{ test instances}}. metric: \boxed{\text{accuracy}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.18 example sentence a: “the boy fell and injured himself.” sentence b: “the boy was hurt when he fell.” these can be: \boxed{\text{paraphrase}} because the meaning is substantially equivalent. but: “the girl pushed the boy and he fell.” is not equivalent. 5.28.19 how indicxparaphrase was created the deck says: \boxed{1001} english sentences of at least 10 words were machine-translated into: \boxed{10\text{ languages}}. annotators then: verified/corrected translations, wrote one paraphrase, wrote one non-paraphrase. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.20 the important anti-shortcut rule for paraphrases, annotators were instructed to minimize word overlap. they could use: \text{synonyms} \text{active/passive changes} \text{temporal phrase restructuring}. for non-paraphrases, they could change things like: \text{named entities} \text{pronouns} \text{adjectives} \text{adverbs}. the goal is: \boxed{ \text{meaning} > \text{surface word overlap} } the deck explicitly contrasts this construction with paws-x and says it did not use back-translation or noisy alignment to manufacture non-paraphrases. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.21 task 5 — m-intent the fifth classification task is: \boxed{\text{m-intent}} this is intent classification over spoken/user-query data. the benchmark table lists: \boxed{7\text{ languages}} with: \boxed{2974\text{ test examples}} and: \boxed{\text{accuracy}} as the metric. its domain is: \boxed{\text{spoken queries}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.22 example of intent classification suppose the user says: “set an alarm for seven tomorrow morning.” possible intents: \text{weather} \text{alarm} \text{music} \text{navigation}. correct: \boxed{\text{alarm}} this tests whether the model can map multilingual natural-language input to the correct user intent. 5.28.23 why does this task matter? because intent recognition tests a practical capability: \boxed{ \text{understand what the user wants} } rather than just: \boxed{ \text{understand what the sentence literally says} }. it is particularly relevant to spoken-agent systems. the dataset comes from the massive resource, whose 7-language indic subset is taken as-is according to the deck. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.24 now classification is complete we have: \boxed{ \text{indicsentiment} } sentiment. \boxed{ \text{indicxnli} } inference. \boxed{ \text{indiccopa} } causal commonsense reasoning. \boxed{ \text{indicpara} } semantic equivalence. \boxed{ \text{m-intent} } intent recognition. so the five tasks probe very different abilities. 5.28.25 numerical classification-bank suppose we get: task correct total sentiment 920 1000 nli 3758 5010 copa 410 500 paraphrase 1750 2002 intent 2600 2974 their individual accuracies are: sentiment 92.0\%. nli 75.01\%\approx75.0\%. copa 82.0\%. paraphrase \frac{1750}{2002}\times100 \approx \boxed{87.4\%}. intent \frac{2600}{2974}\times100 \approx \boxed{87.4\%}. these numbers are illustrative calculations, not reported model results. step 5.28.26 category 2 — structure prediction now classification ends. we move to: \boxed{\text{structure prediction}} there are: \boxed{2\text{ tasks}} in this category: \boxed{\text{naamapadam}} and: \boxed{\text{m-slotfill}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) the fundamental difference is: classification one label for the whole example. x\rightarrow y structure prediction labels are assigned to parts of the input. x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n \rightarrow y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n. this is a major conceptual shift. 5.28.27 task 6 — naamapadam naamapadam is the: \boxed{\text{named entity recognition (ner)}} task. suppose: aniket studies at bits pilani. the model should identify entities such as: \boxed{\text{aniket}} and: \boxed{\text{bits pilani}}. this is not one label for the sentence. instead, we assign a label to each relevant token/span. 5.28.28 iob2 representation the deck says naamapadam uses: \boxed{\text{iob2 format}} after projecting tags and then having annotators verify/correct them. (source: indicxtreme-slides) iob2 means: b=\text{beginning of entity} i=\text{inside entity} o=\text{outside entity}. example: aniket b-per studies o at o bits b-org pilani i-org so: \boxed{ \text{token sequence} \rightarrow \text{structured label sequence} } 5.28.29 how naamapadam is constructed the deck describes this pipeline: \boxed{ \text{english sentence} \rightarrow \text{off-the-shelf ner} } then: \boxed{ \text{project tags onto indic sentence using word alignment} } then: \boxed{ \text{human verification + correction} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a classic example of: \boxed{ \text{automatic generation} + \text{human quality control} } rather than blindly trusting projection. 5.28.30 metric: f1 because ner is structured prediction, the benchmark uses: \boxed{f1} rather than simple accuracy. recall: precision= \frac{tp}{tp+fp} recall= \frac{tp}{tp+fn} and: \boxed{ f1= \frac{2pr}{p+r} } where p is precision and r is recall. 5.28.31 numerical ner example suppose: tp=80,\quad fp=20,\quad fn=10. then: p=\frac{80}{80+20}=0.8. r=\frac{80}{80+10} = 0.8889. therefore: f1= \frac{2(0.8)(0.8889)} {0.8+0.8889} \approx \boxed{0.8421} or: \boxed{84.21\%}. this is an exam-style f1 calculation. 5.28.32 task 7 — m-slotfill the second structure-prediction task is: \boxed{\text{m-slotfill}} it comes from the massive family and evaluates slot filling. think: \boxed{ \text{intent} + \text{slot values} } for example: “play arijit singh songs tomorrow evening.” potential structure: \text{intent}=\text{play music} \text{artist}=\text{arijit singh} \text{time}=\text{tomorrow evening}. the model must identify spans and assign slot types. the benchmark table lists: \boxed{7\text{ languages}} and evaluates it with: \boxed{f1}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.33 why f1 again? because a slot-filling system can: miss an entity, produce an incorrect span, assign the wrong slot. accuracy would be a poor fit because the output is structured. so: \boxed{ \text{precision + recall} \rightarrow f1 } is more appropriate. step 5.28.34 category 3 — question answering now: \boxed{\text{qa}} has one task: \boxed{\text{indicqa}}. its task type is: \boxed{\text{span extraction}} and its metric is: \boxed{f1}. the table lists: \boxed{11\text{ languages}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.35 what is span extraction? suppose context says: “rabindranath tagore was born in kolkata.” question: where was rabindranath tagore born? the answer is a span from the context: \boxed{\text{kolkata}}. so the model must identify: \boxed{ [start,end] } of the answer span. this is fundamentally different from classification. 5.28.36 indicqa was built differently this is a particularly important dataset-construction idea. the deck says indicqa was created from scratch , without an english-source translation pipeline. (source: indicxtreme-slides) the researchers first identify topics connected to indic: \text{history} \text{monuments} \text{authors} \text{politicians} \text{festivals} etc. they then rank topics according to the number of indic-language wikipedia articles available and remove topics whose articles average fewer than 10 sentences. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.37 why is this important? because the benchmark is trying to test: \boxed{ \text{actual indic-language reading comprehension} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{translation of an english qa task} }. that is a crucial benchmark-design distinction. 5.28.38 the clever anti-leakage trick indicqa has a two-phase process. phase 1 — write question the context is split into: \boxed{\text{larger first part}} and: \boxed{\text{smaller second part}} of 2–3 sentences. these are machine-translated into english, and the annotator writes indic-language questions from the english translation. phase 2 — mark answer a different annotator sees only the original indic first part and marks the answer span. questions based on the withheld second part become naturally: \boxed{\text{unanswerable}} for the visible context. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a very clever way of generating both: \boxed{\text{answerable}} and: \boxed{\text{unanswerable}} questions. 5.28.39 indicqa annotation rules the deck specifies: \boxed{\ge 2\text{ questions per paragraph}} answer span: \boxed{\le5\text{ continuous words}} and: answer must be in one sentence; never use an entire sentence as an answer; never use a pronoun; minimize phrase overlap; choose the relevant occurrence if the answer string appears more than once. (source: indicxtreme-slides) these constraints are designed to make the 11 independently annotated languages comparable. 5.28.40 numerical qa example suppose the gold answer span is: [\text{kolkata}] and the model outputs: [\text{kolkata city}]. token overlap: 1 of: 1 gold token. precision: p=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 recall: r=\frac{1}{1}=1. therefore: f1= \frac{2(0.5)(1)}{0.5+1} = \boxed{0.667}. so: \boxed{66.7\%}. the benchmark's reported metric is f1, though the exact implementation details of tokenization/normalization are not specified on this slide. step 5.28.41 category 4 — retrieval the final category is: \boxed{\text{retrieval}} with: \boxed{\text{flores}}. the task is: \boxed{\text{sentence retrieval}} with: \boxed{1012} test sentences and: \boxed{18\text{ indic languages}}. the table lists: \boxed{\text{accuracy}} as the metric. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.42 what does sentence retrieval mean? conceptually, suppose we have: q a query sentence. and a collection: d=\{d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_n\}. the model must find the correct corresponding sentence: \boxed{ d^* } for the query. a retrieval system therefore computes some notion of: \text{similarity}(q,d_i) and selects the best candidate. the exact retrieval model architecture is not specified by this slide; this is the general retrieval formulation. 5.28.43 why flores is useful the deck says flores is already an: \boxed{n\text{-way parallel, human-translated dataset}} and the benchmark directly incorporates it for sentence-retrieval evaluation. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so unlike some newly constructed datasets: \boxed{ \text{no new translation creation pipeline is required here} } because the resource already exists. 5.28.44 complete task-suite map now we can finally see the whole benchmark: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} } classification \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\text{indicsentiment}\\ &\text{indicxnli}\\ &\text{indiccopa}\\ &\text{indicpara}\\ &\text{m-intent} \end{aligned} } structure prediction \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\text{naamapadam}\\ &\text{m-slotfill} \end{aligned} } qa \boxed{ \text{indicqa} } retrieval \boxed{ \text{flores} } (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.45 why the metrics differ this is very important for the exam. classification \boxed{\text{accuracy}} because the output is a class. ner / slot filling / qa \boxed{f1} because outputs involve structured spans/tags. retrieval \boxed{\text{accuracy}} in the benchmark table because the correct retrieval target is evaluated as a discrete outcome. thus: \boxed{ \text{metric depends on output structure} } not simply on whether the task is “hard” or “easy.” 5.28.46 human annotation vs machine translation another key table dimension is: \boxed{ha=\text{human annotated}} and: \boxed{mt=\text{machine translated}}. the benchmark table marks, for example: \text{indicsentiment}\rightarrow ha \text{indicxnli}\rightarrow mt \text{indiccopa}\rightarrow ha and other tasks accordingly. (source: indicxtreme-slides) but don't misinterpret mt . it does not mean: \boxed{ \text{“no humans involved.”} } the later slide explicitly emphasizes: \boxed{ \text{every indicxtreme evaluation set contains a human-supervision step} } through translation, post-editing, creation, verification, or correction. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.47 the four construction pathways the deck summarizes four broad paths: \boxed{\text{translated from scratch}} \boxed{\text{built without any english source}} \boxed{\text{machine-translated then verified}} \boxed{\text{tag-projected then corrected}} yet all retain human supervision. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a fundamental benchmark-quality principle. 5.28.48 why benchmark construction itself matters suppose benchmark translations contain systematic artifacts. then a model can exploit: \boxed{\text{translation artifacts}} instead of: \boxed{\text{actual language understanding}}. therefore benchmark design is itself part of model evaluation. this is why indicxtreme spends so much attention on: \text{human verification} \text{bias guards} \text{anti-overlap rules} \text{natural indic-language content}. the individual examples of these mechanisms are documented across the dataset-construction slides. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.49 numerical benchmark-total question suppose the benchmark has: 5 classification tasks, 2 structure tasks, 1 qa task, 1 retrieval task. then: 5+2+1+1 = \boxed{9}. exactly as stated by the deck. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.50 another exam numerical there are: 105 evaluation sets in total. of these: 52 are brand-new contributions. then reused/adapted evaluation sets: 105-52 = \boxed{53}. so approximately: \frac{52}{105}\times100 = \boxed{49.5\%} of the evaluation sets are new. the 105 and 52 figures are source-derived; the percentage is our calculation. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.51 the key structural difference among tasks this is an excellent way to organize the material: \boxed{ \text{classification} } asks: which label? x\rightarrow y \boxed{ \text{structure prediction} } asks: what label/span belongs to each piece? x_1,\ldots,x_n \rightarrow y_1,\ldots,y_n \boxed{ \text{qa} } asks: which span answers the question? (q,c)\rightarrow[a,b] \boxed{ \text{retrieval} } asks: which candidate is the correct match? q\rightarrow d^*. this is the conceptual framework to remember. 5.28.52 why indicxtreme is more than a leaderboard the benchmark is simultaneously testing: \boxed{ \text{semantic understanding} } \boxed{ \text{reasoning} } \boxed{ \text{sequence labeling} } \boxed{ \text{reading comprehension} } \boxed{ \text{retrieval} } across languages with different resource levels. so a model's performance is a profile , not a single scalar capability. 5.28.53 master table for memorization category task main capability metric classification indicsentiment sentiment accuracy classification indicxnli nli accuracy classification indiccopa causal reasoning accuracy classification indicpara paraphrase/equivalence accuracy classification m-intent intent accuracy structure naamapadam ner f1 structure m-slotfill slot filling f1 qa indicqa span extraction f1 retrieval flores sentence retrieval accuracy (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.28.54 the deeper lesson indicxtreme isn't designed merely to ask: \boxed{ \text{“can a model process hindi?”} } instead it asks: \boxed{ \text{“can a model transfer multiple nlp capabilities into many indic languages?”} } that is a much more demanding question. and this is why the benchmark must combine: \boxed{ \text{many tasks} + \text{many languages} + \text{careful data construction} + \text{controlled transfer protocol} }. the final piece— controlled transfer protocol —is what we study next. step 5.28 checkpoint you should now know: \boxed{9\text{ tasks}} across: \boxed{4\text{ categories}}. and you should remember: \boxed{ 5\text{ classification} + 2\text{ structure} + 1\text{ qa} + 1\text{ retrieval} } with: \boxed{ \text{accuracy for classification/retrieval} } and: \boxed{ \text{f1 for ner/slot-filling/qa} }. most importantly, don't memorize the task names independently. understand what each probes: \boxed{ \text{sentiment} \rightarrow \text{nli} \rightarrow \text{causal reasoning} \rightarrow \text{paraphrase} \rightarrow \text{intent} } then: \boxed{ \text{ner} \rightarrow \text{slot filling} } then: \boxed{ \text{reading comprehension} } then: \boxed{ \text{cross-lingual retrieval} }.
