core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.28 — indicxtreme benchmark architecture this lesson: step 5.29 — indicxtreme zero-shot fine-tuning protocol source references: indicxtreme-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.29 — indicxtreme zero-shot fine-tuning protocol plan node: i10 · chat order #70 now we reach one of the most important experimental-design concepts in the indicxtreme material. we already know: \boxed{\text{indicxtreme has many indic-language test sets}} but that alone does not tell us whether the benchmark is measuring: \boxed{\text{cross-lingual transfer}} or simply: \boxed{\text{ordinary supervised learning in each indic language}}. the solution is the benchmark's zero-shot fine-tuning protocol . (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.1 first understand the problem imagine a model is trained directly on hindi data. then we test it on hindi. suppose it gets: 90\%. what have we learned? the model is good at hindi. but we have not learned whether it can transfer knowledge from another language into hindi. now consider: \boxed{ \text{english training} \rightarrow \text{hindi testing} } if the model succeeds, that is evidence of: \boxed{ \text{cross-lingual transfer} }. that is what indicxtreme is designed to evaluate. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.2 what does “zero-shot” mean here? it means the model receives no indic-language training examples for the target benchmark task . the supplied slide is very explicit: \boxed{ \text{indic-language training data = none} } instead: \boxed{ \text{training data = english} } and the target evaluation is performed directly on indic-language test data. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.3 the exact pipeline the deck gives three steps. step 1 — fine-tune on english for each task: \boxed{ \text{pretrained lm} \rightarrow \text{english task training data} } this is done independently for the task. for example: \text{english sentiment training} for indicsentiment. or: \text{english nli training} for indicxnli. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.4 step 2 — select hyperparameters using english development data suppose we test: \text{learning rate}\in \{10^{-5},2\times10^{-5},5\times10^{-5}\} and: \text{weight decay}\in \{0,0.01\}. we evaluate candidate configurations on the: \boxed{\text{english development set}} and choose the best one. crucially: \boxed{ \text{indic test data is not used for model selection} } according to the protocol. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.5 step 3 — evaluate directly on indic test sets after selecting the model/configuration: \boxed{ \text{english-trained model} \rightarrow \text{indic-language test set} } no indic-language examples were used during the task training or model-selection process. so if we write: \theta^* = \arg\max_\theta \text{score}_{en-dev}(\theta), then evaluation is: \boxed{ \text{score}_{indic-test}(\theta^*) } this equation is a conceptual formalization of the protocol; the source states the three-stage procedure rather than presenting this exact notation. 5.29.6 why is this powerful? suppose: \text{english training accuracy}=95\% and: \text{hindi test accuracy}=85\%. the model has transferred: \boxed{ \text{task knowledge from english to hindi} }. the benchmark is therefore asking: does the multilingual pretrained representation allow knowledge learned in english to transfer into an indic language? that is the fundamental scientific question. 5.29.7 why not train on hindi too? because then we would be measuring something different. consider: setup a \text{english + hindi training} \rightarrow \text{hindi test}. setup b \text{english training} \rightarrow \text{hindi test}. setup a measures: \boxed{ \text{in-language supervised performance} } while setup b measures: \boxed{ \text{zero-shot cross-lingual transfer} }. indicxtreme is specifically interested in setup b. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.8 the most important anti-leakage condition the deck states: \boxed{ \text{no indic data is seen during training or model selection} } this prevents a hidden source of information. suppose the model is allowed to see 1000 hindi development examples. then choosing hyperparameters based on them could indirectly adapt the model to hindi. the resulting performance would no longer represent a clean zero-shot evaluation. so the protocol creates: \boxed{ \text{training language} \neq \text{evaluation language} } 5.29.9 numerical example: why leakage matters imagine two configurations. model a english dev: 82\% hindi dev: 77\%. model b english dev: 80\% hindi dev: 85\%. if we select using english dev: \boxed{\text{model a wins}} because: 82>80. if we select using hindi dev: \boxed{\text{model b wins}} because: 85>77. thus using hindi development data changes model selection. that would introduce target-language information into the process. the actual deck uses english development selection specifically to avoid that issue. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.10 a subtle point: zero-shot does not mean zero training this is a common exam trap. zero-shot here does not mean: \boxed{\text{the model receives no fine-tuning}} instead: \boxed{ \text{the model is fine-tuned} } but: \boxed{ \text{not on the target indic language} }. so: \boxed{ \text{zero-shot target-language transfer} } is more precise. 5.29.11 example: indicsentiment suppose the english training set contains: 100,000 english reviews. we fine-tune the multilingual model using those reviews. then: \boxed{\text{no hindi reviews}} are used for training. finally: \boxed{\text{hindi reviews}} are used only for evaluation. if the model gets: 88\% on hindi, that result is evidence of transfer. 5.29.12 example: indicxnli english training: \text{premise + hypothesis} \rightarrow \text{english nli labels} then hindi test: \text{hindi premise + hypothesis} \rightarrow \text{prediction}. the model has to carry the nli capability across languages. 5.29.13 why task-specific hyperparameter tuning matters the deck makes another methodological point. many earlier approaches reused one fixed hyperparameter configuration across tasks. indicxtreme instead performs a: \boxed{ \text{task-specific grid search} } for: \boxed{ \text{learning rate} } and: \boxed{ \text{weight decay} }. this is done for every model and task. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.14 why is this fairer? suppose: task a works best with: lr=10^{-5}. task b works best with: lr=5\times10^{-5}. if we force both to use: lr=10^{-5}, task b may be artificially weakened. then we'd be measuring: \boxed{ \text{quality under a poor hyperparameter choice} } rather than: \boxed{ \text{quality of the underlying model} }. so task-specific tuning makes the comparison more informative. the source explicitly motivates this as part of fair comparison. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.15 but doesn't hyperparameter tuning introduce target information? the benchmark avoids that by selecting configurations on: \boxed{\text{english development data}} rather than the target indic test data. so the target language remains hidden from model selection. this is a crucial experimental-design principle. 5.29.16 full experimental pipeline keep this picture in your head: multilingual pretrained lm │ ▼ english task training │ ▼ english development │ hyperparameter selection │ ▼ final model θ* │ ▼ ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ hindi test tamil test bengali test │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ zero-shot zero-shot zero-shot transfer transfer transfer no indic-language training data enters before evaluation. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.17 now comes the interesting extension the researchers ask: does using an in-language development set help model selection? at first, the benchmark says: \boxed{\text{english dev}} is used. but they investigate alternatives. this produces an important distinction: \boxed{ \text{in-language} } versus: \boxed{ \text{in-family} } versus: \boxed{ \text{english} }. 5.29.18 what is an in-language dev set? suppose we're evaluating: \boxed{\text{bengali}}. an in-language dev set is: \boxed{\text{bengali development data}}. this gives direct feedback about the target language. but using it changes the strict zero-shot protocol because the target language now influences model selection. 5.29.19 what is an in-family dev set? this is a very interesting intermediate idea. the deck uses: \boxed{\text{hindi}} as a representative language for: \boxed{\text{indo-european}} and: \boxed{\text{tamil}} as a representative language for: \boxed{\text{dravidian}}. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so instead of having bengali-specific dev data, one can potentially select using a related language. conceptually: \boxed{ \text{hindi dev} \rightarrow \text{select for other indo-european languages} } and: \boxed{ \text{tamil dev} \rightarrow \text{select for other dravidian languages} }. 5.29.20 why might that work? suppose two languages share some useful linguistic structure. then a model configuration that works well on: l_1 may also work reasonably well on: l_2 within the same family. this can provide a compromise: \boxed{ \text{better than english-only selection} } without needing a separate development set for every target language. the source reports that these in-family dev sets perform on par with true in-language dev sets and clearly ahead of english-only selection. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.21 let's inspect the reported table the slide compares: english development selection, in-language development selection, in-family development selection. the table shows that for the reported tasks, in-family selection tends to be close to actual in-language selection and better than english-only selection. (source: indicxtreme-slides) for example, on indicsentiment , the table reports approximately: \text{mbert: }72.9 for in-language and: 72.9 for in-family, compared with a smaller english-dev-selected result. for indicbert, the reported numbers similarly show in-family selection tracking in-language performance closely. (source: indicxtreme-slides) we should interpret the pattern rather than memorize every table cell. 5.29.22 what does this tell us? there appears to be a useful hierarchy: \boxed{ \text{english dev} < \text{related-language dev} \approx \text{target-language dev} } for the reported experiments. the key lesson is: \boxed{ \text{language-aware model selection can matter} } even when actual target-language training remains absent. the precise numerical gains are task/model dependent; the deck's broad conclusion is the important point. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.23 why is hindi particularly interesting? now the deck goes one step further. it asks: what happens if hindi itself becomes the transfer language? the slide reports: \boxed{\text{hindi is a better transfer language than english}} for the evaluated tasks. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this is a major observation. 5.29.24 “gold zero-shot” the deck defines: \boxed{\text{gold zero-shot}} as using real hindi training data for the tasks. so instead of: \text{english training} \rightarrow \text{indic test}, we have: \boxed{ \text{hindi training} \rightarrow \text{other indic-language test} }. this is not strict zero-shot with respect to hindi, because the model sees hindi training data. it is better understood as cross-indic transfer from hindi . the slide explicitly uses the term “gold zero-shot” for this setup. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.25 “silver zero-shot” the deck also constructs: \boxed{\text{silver zero-shot}} by machine-translating the english training set into hindi. so: \text{english training} becomes: \boxed{ \text{machine-translated hindi training} } and then the model transfers from hindi to the other indic languages. this provides: \boxed{ \text{hindi-language supervision without manually creating hindi data} } although translation errors can be introduced. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.26 reported hindi transfer gains the deck reports that switching the transfer language from english to hindi in the evaluated setup lifts: \boxed{\text{ner by }+3.5} \boxed{\text{intent by }+3.1} \boxed{\text{slot-filling by }+10.6} percentage points. (source: indicxtreme-slides) these are source-derived results. 5.29.27 why might hindi help? the deck's result supports the idea that: \boxed{ \text{english is not necessarily the optimal transfer language for indic targets} } because hindi may share more useful linguistic properties with other indic languages than english does. we should be careful, though: \boxed{ \text{hindi} \neq \text{equally close to every indic language} } and the source does not establish a universal rule that hindi must always be the best transfer language. the conclusion is specific to the experiments reported. 5.29.28 gold vs silver transfer here is the distinction: gold zero-shot \boxed{ \text{real hindi task training data} } silver zero-shot \boxed{ \text{machine-translated hindi task training data} } the silver approach is cheaper/easier to construct, but introduces translation errors. the deck reports that silver transfer helps: \boxed{ \text{sentiment} } \boxed{ \text{xnli} } \boxed{ \text{paraphrase} } similarly, but hurts: \boxed{ \text{indiccopa} } and: \boxed{ \text{indicqa} }. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.29 why would translation hurt copa and qa? the source explicitly attributes this to the sensitivity of these tasks to small translation errors. (source: indicxtreme-slides) this makes intuitive sense. for causal reasoning: \boxed{ \text{one subtle wording change} } can alter which cause is plausible. for qa: \boxed{ \text{small translation error} } can change: \text{answer span} or: \text{question/context relationship}. so: \boxed{ \text{translation noise} \rightarrow \text{task-dependent degradation} } is the important lesson. 5.29.30 numerical example — transfer improvement suppose a baseline ner score is: 70.0. the reported hindi-transfer improvement is: +3.5. then: 70.0+3.5 = \boxed{73.5}. for slot filling, suppose: 60.0 baseline. then: 60.0+10.6 = \boxed{70.6}. these are illustrative starting scores; the actual source provides the gains, not these hypothetical baselines. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.31 a very important conceptual distinction don't confuse these three experiments. strict indicxtreme zero-shot \boxed{ \text{english train} \rightarrow \text{indic test} } gold hindi transfer \boxed{ \text{hindi train} \rightarrow \text{other indic test} } silver hindi transfer \boxed{ \text{machine-translated hindi train} \rightarrow \text{other indic test} } all are evaluating transfer, but they answer different scientific questions. 5.29.32 why the benchmark starts with english because english is the conventional high-resource transfer language. so the baseline question is: \boxed{ \text{can multilingual pretraining transfer task knowledge from english into indic languages?} } then the hindi experiments ask a deeper question: \boxed{ \text{would a linguistically closer indic transfer language work better?} } that is a much more sophisticated benchmark study. 5.29.33 exam-style numerical question suppose: \text{english transfer score}=65.0 and hindi transfer gives: +10.6. then: 65.0+10.6 = \boxed{75.6}. relative improvement: \frac{10.6}{65.0}\times100 \approx \boxed{16.31\%}. again, the +10.6 is source-derived for slot filling; 65.0 is hypothetical. 5.29.34 another exam question: strict zero-shot a student says: “the model was fine-tuned on english and hindi before being evaluated on bengali, so this is zero-shot bengali.” under the deck's strict protocol, that statement is: \boxed{\text{incorrect}} because hindi-language training data was used. strict zero-shot requires: \boxed{ \text{no target indic-language training data} } and the benchmark's main protocol uses english training only. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.35 another exam question: model selection suppose there are three learning rates: 10^{-5},\;2\times10^{-5},\;5\times10^{-5}. their english-dev accuracies are: 80,\;84,\;82. choose: \boxed{2\times10^{-5}}. then test this configuration on hindi. suppose hindi accuracy is: 78. you must not go back and select the learning rate because another learning rate gave: 82 on hindi test. that would contaminate the evaluation. this is exactly why model selection is restricted to english development data. 5.29.36 why this protocol is experimentally clean the sequence: \boxed{ \text{train on english} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{choose using english dev} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{freeze the choice} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{test on indic} } means the target-language test set is truly an unseen evaluation environment. this reduces the chance that the benchmark score is inflated by target-language adaptation. 5.29.37 but there is still a deeper question suppose english is a very different language from hindi. then perhaps: \boxed{ \text{english transfer} } is simply a poor experimental baseline for indic languages. the hindi experiments investigate exactly that. if hindi is a better transfer language, then the problem isn't necessarily: \text{multilingual model failure}. it may partially be: \boxed{ \text{choice of source/transfer language} }. this is one of the most interesting implications of the deck's later analysis. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.38 complete conceptual picture we started with: \boxed{ \text{english} \rightarrow \text{indic} } and discovered that transfer is imperfect. then we tested: \boxed{ \text{in-language dev} } and: \boxed{ \text{in-family dev} } and found that in-family selection can approach in-language selection in the reported experiments. (source: indicxtreme-slides) then we tested: \boxed{ \text{hindi} \rightarrow \text{other indic} } and found substantial gains on some tasks. (source: indicxtreme-slides) so the experiment evolves from: \boxed{ \text{can english transfer?} } to: \boxed{ \text{does language-aware model selection help?} } to: \boxed{ \text{is a related indic language a better transfer source?} } that is the logic of the entire section. 5.29.39 exam-ready summary strict indicxtreme protocol \boxed{ \text{english train} \rightarrow \text{english dev for model selection} \rightarrow \text{indic test} } why? to measure: \boxed{ \text{zero-shot cross-lingual transfer} } without indic-language training or model selection contamination. (source: indicxtreme-slides) hyperparameters task-specific search over at least: \boxed{ \text{learning rate + weight decay} } using english development data. (source: indicxtreme-slides) in-family selection \boxed{ \text{hindi for indo-european} } \boxed{ \text{tamil for dravidian} } performed close to in-language selection and ahead of english-only selection in the reported study. (source: indicxtreme-slides) hindi transfer reported gains: \boxed{ ner:+3.5 } \boxed{ intent:+3.1 } \boxed{ slotfill:+10.6 } percentage points. (source: indicxtreme-slides) 5.29.40 final mental model the most important equation from this whole section is: \boxed{ \underbrace{ \text{english supervision} }_{\text{task learning}} \rightarrow \underbrace{ \text{indic evaluation} }_{\text{language transfer}} } that lets us separate: \boxed{ \text{“does the model know the task?”} } from: \boxed{ \text{“can the model transfer that knowledge across languages?”} } and the later hindi experiment adds a third question: \boxed{ \text{“which language is the best source for cross-lingual transfer?”} } that is the central experimental logic of indicxtreme's zero-shot section. (source: indicxtreme-slides)

core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.28 — indicxtreme benchmark architecture this lesson: step 5.31 — indicgenbench: why a second indic benchmark is needed source references: indicgenbench-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.31 — indicgenbench: why a second indic benchmark is needed plan node: i11 · chat order #72 we now enter the indicgenbench material. this is the natural continuation after indicxtreme. the key distinction is: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme asks: “can the model understand/classify indic text?”} } while: \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench asks: “can the model actually generate useful indic text?”} } the supplied deck explicitly frames indicgenbench as a benchmark for generation capabilities such as summarization, translation, and question answering, in contrast to indicxtreme's classification/nlu emphasis. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.1 start with the problem suppose an llm performs well on an indic classification task: \text{hindi sentence}\rightarrow\text{positive}. that tells us something about: \boxed{\text{understanding}} but a real user often wants the model to produce language . for example: \text{english article} \rightarrow \text{hindi summary} or: \text{english sentence} \rightarrow \text{tamil translation} or: \text{hindi question} \rightarrow \text{hindi answer}. these are generation problems. so the benchmark needs to test: \boxed{ \text{can the model produce correct, faithful, fluent indic-language output?} } 5.31.2 the motivation slide gives a striking result the deck says that singh et al. built indicgenbench to expose a large generation gap: on every one of five generation tasks , even the best model scores far below its own english performance. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{english capability} > \text{indic generation capability} } across all five reported generation tasks. this is important because a multilingual model can appear strong globally while still having a substantial target-language generation deficit. 5.31.3 why is generation harder to evaluate than classification? consider classification: x\rightarrow y where y might be: \{\text{positive, negative}\}. evaluation is easy: \boxed{ \hat y=y? } generation is different. suppose the gold summary is: “the mission launched successfully after several delays.” the model writes: “after multiple delays, the mission was finally launched successfully.” are these equivalent? yes, semantically. but exact string matching would say: \boxed{\text{different}} even though the generation is good. therefore generation benchmarks need metrics capable of handling: \boxed{ \text{multiple valid ways of expressing the same meaning} }. that is why indicgenbench's metric design becomes important. 5.31.4 scope of indicgenbench the deck defines: \boxed{29\text{ indic languages}} across: \boxed{13\text{ scripts}} and: \boxed{4\text{ language families}}. the 29 languages are divided into three resource tiers: \boxed{9\text{ higher}} \boxed{7\text{ medium}} \boxed{13\text{ low}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is already a major difference from our previous benchmark discussion. indicgenbench explicitly makes resource level a central experimental variable. 5.31.5 “higher-resource” does not mean high-resource globally this is an important source-specific warning. the deck gives hindi as an example: \boxed{\sim160,000\text{ wikipedia articles}} versus: \boxed{6.6\text{m+ for english}}. so “higher” means: \boxed{ \text{higher relative to other indic languages} } not: \boxed{ \text{high-resource by global standards} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this prevents a very common misinterpretation. 5.31.6 why classify languages into resource tiers? because we want to ask: \boxed{ \text{does generation quality decline as language resources decline?} } so instead of reporting only one average: \text{average performance}=x, we can investigate: \boxed{ \text{higher} \rightarrow \text{medium} \rightarrow \text{low} } and observe whether performance follows the same direction. the later results slide says it does: performance drops from high to medium to low across every task. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.7 the five generation tasks indicgenbench contains five generation tasks. the deck describes them as: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} cross-lingual summarization, \boxed{\text{flores-in}} machine translation, \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} multilingual qa, and two versions of: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in}} cross-lingual qa. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so: \boxed{ 1+1+1+2=5 } generation tasks. 5.31.8 why does the benchmark mostly translate existing datasets? this is one of the most important design decisions in the deck. instead of creating every benchmark entirely from scratch, the researchers start with existing english-source benchmarks: \boxed{\text{crosssum}} \boxed{\text{flores-200}} \boxed{\text{xquad}} \boxed{\text{xor-tydi}}. then they add professional human translations into indic languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) at first this may seem like a weakness: why not create everything directly in indic languages? the deck gives three explicit reasons . 5.31.9 reason 1 — multi-way parallel data suppose we start from the same source example: x and create: y_{\text{hindi}}, y_{\text{tamil}}, y_{\text{bengali}}, \ldots all corresponding to the same source. now comparisons become much cleaner. we can ask whether a model's performance difference comes from: \boxed{\text{language}} rather than: \boxed{\text{different underlying task content}}. this is exactly why the deck values multi-way parallel data . (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.10 example suppose the source is one english sentence: x=\text{“the satellite launched successfully.”} create translations into: \text{hindi} \text{tamil} \text{bengali} and so on. because every language began with the same x , comparisons become: \boxed{ \text{same task} + \text{same underlying content} + \text{different target language} } which is very useful for studying cross-lingual generalization. 5.31.11 reason 2 — clean source text may not exist in low-resource languages suppose researchers want to build a fresh qa dataset in a very low-resource language. they need: \text{clean documents} + \text{questions} + \text{answers} + \text{quality control}. but high-quality source material may not exist at sufficient scale. the deck specifically points out that some low-resource languages do not have clean knowledge corpora such as wikipedia at the level needed for fresh dataset construction. (source: indicgenbench-slides) translation provides a way around that. instead of: \boxed{ \text{find huge clean indic source corpus} } we can: \boxed{ \text{start from already-developed english benchmark} } and translate it. 5.31.12 reason 3 — reuse existing quality control existing datasets have already gone through substantial: \text{design} \text{validation} \text{quality control}. so indicgenbench can inherit that work and focus additional effort on: \boxed{ \text{high-quality human indic translation} }. the deck explicitly lists this as its third motivation. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.13 this is an important benchmark-design tradeoff translation-based construction gives: \boxed{ \text{comparability} + \text{scalability} + \text{reusable task design} } but introduces another possible problem: \boxed{ \text{translation artifacts/errors} }. and the deck later demonstrates exactly that translation quality matters, especially for some tasks. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the design tradeoff is: \boxed{ \text{clean common source} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{native-language authenticity} } and the benchmark tries to balance the two through professional human translation. 5.31.14 human translators the deck says the translators were: \boxed{\text{professional data labelers}} working through the authors' organization and an external vendor. they were paid competitively according to the labor laws and prevailing market rates of each region. (source: indicgenbench-slides) one reported detail is particularly interesting: \boxed{2.80\text{ usd/hour}} for pashto versus: \boxed{15.90\text{ usd/hour}} for tibetan. that is a: \frac{15.90}{2.80} \approx \boxed{5.68\times} difference, which the slide summarizes as a: \boxed{5.7\times} pay range across languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.15 why is this mentioned in a technical lecture? because dataset construction is not just: \boxed{\text{nlp algorithm}} it is also: \boxed{ \text{human annotation process} + \text{labor practices} + \text{quality control} }. the quality of a benchmark depends on the people producing and validating its data. 5.31.16 first major task: crosssum-in now we begin the individual task architecture. \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} is cross-lingual summarization . the source benchmark is: \boxed{\text{crosssum}} which itself comes from: \boxed{\text{xl-sum}} and is based on bbc news articles and summaries across languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the generation task is: \boxed{ \text{article} \rightarrow \text{summary in target language} } 5.31.17 why is this “cross-lingual” summarization? the source article and target summary can involve different languages. in the benchmark's construction, the deck starts from english article-summary pairs and creates target-language summaries. the key requirement is that the model should generate the summary: \boxed{ \text{directly in the target language} } rather than: \text{source} \rightarrow \text{english intermediate} \rightarrow \text{target}. the example slide explicitly emphasizes faithful compressed generation directly in the target language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.18 crosssum-in construction for each language, the dataset uses: \boxed{ 100\text{ train} + 100\text{ dev} + 500\text{ test} } examples. thus: 100+100+500 = \boxed{700} examples per language. there are: \boxed{29\text{ languages}}. therefore: 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300} examples total. the deck explicitly reports this number and confirms it by direct arithmetic. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.19 numerical exam question given: 29\text{ languages} and: 700\text{ examples/language}, compute total examples: 29\times700 = \boxed{20,300}. then: training examples: 29\times100 = \boxed{2,900}. development: 29\times100 = \boxed{2,900}. test: 29\times500 = \boxed{14,500}. check: 2900+2900+14500 = \boxed{20,300}. 5.31.20 second major task: flores-in the next task is: \boxed{\text{flores-in}} for machine translation. the source dataset is: \boxed{\text{flores-200}}. unlike crosssum, flores already contains high-quality human-annotated multilingual parallel data. so indicgenbench reuses as much as possible and translates into languages not already covered. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.21 flores split structure the source flores-200 split has: \boxed{997\text{ dev}} \boxed{1012\text{ devtest}} \boxed{992\text{ test}} but the deck says the non-public test is not used for this construction. therefore: 997+1012 = \boxed{2009} sentences per language. for: 29 languages: 2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261} examples. the slide reports approximately: \boxed{58.2k}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.22 important exception the deck says flores-in is: \boxed{\text{the only task with no training split}} in indicgenbench. why? because this is fundamentally a benchmark of translation over an established parallel evaluation set, and the source flores structure is reused directly rather than creating a new task-specific training split for the benchmark. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.23 what does flores-in actually ask the model to do? very simply: \boxed{ \text{source sentence} \rightarrow \text{target-language sentence} } no question. no long context. no multiple-choice alternatives. just translation. the deck emphasizes that the same source sentence is represented across all target languages, making the dataset n-way parallel . (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.24 why is n-way parallelity valuable? suppose: x_{\text{english}} has translations: y_{\text{hindi}}, y_{\text{tamil}}, y_{\text{punjabi}}, y_{\text{bengali}}, \ldots then each language is being tested against the same semantic source. thus: \boxed{ \text{language comparison becomes cleaner} } because the underlying content is held constant. 5.31.25 third task: xquad-in the next task is: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} for multilingual reading comprehension / qa. the source is: \boxed{\text{xquad}} which itself derives from: \boxed{\text{squad}} and contains english wikipedia passages and short-span questions/answers. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the generation problem is: \boxed{ \text{context + question} \rightarrow \text{answer} } in the target language. 5.31.26 fourth and fifth tasks: xorqa-in this is particularly interesting because one underlying translation effort produces two tasks . the source is: \boxed{\text{xor-tydi}}. the original data has: \boxed{\text{non-english question}} paired with: \boxed{\text{english evidence passage}} and an answer. (source: indicgenbench-slides) indicgenbench expands this into: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-en}} and: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-xx}}. we will study the exact distinction in the next step. 5.31.27 why two variants? because the model can be asked to: variant 1 read a target-language question, retrieve evidence from english, and answer in: \boxed{\text{english}}. variant 2 read the same kind of cross-lingual setup but generate the answer in: \boxed{\text{the target language}}. so these test different abilities. 5.31.28 first major metric: chrf for: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} and: \boxed{\text{flores-in}}, the benchmark uses: \boxed{\text{chrf}} or character-level f-score . the deck specifically chooses character-level scoring because token-based metrics such as: \boxed{\text{rouge}} and: \boxed{\text{bleu}} can be unreliable for low-resource languages, where tokenization itself may be problematic. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.29 why character-level evaluation? suppose a tokenizer splits one word into: 5 subword pieces in one language but only: 1 piece in another. then a token-level metric can become sensitive to tokenizer behavior. character-level comparison is less dependent on the model's subword segmentation. so conceptually: \boxed{ \text{tokenization artifact} \downarrow } when moving from token-level to character-level evaluation. the source specifically motivates chrf on this basis. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.30 second metric family: token f1 for: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} and both: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in}} variants, the benchmark uses: \boxed{\text{token-overlap f1}}. this is inherited from the squad-style qa literature. (source: indicgenbench-slides) recall: precision=\frac{tp}{tp+fp} recall=\frac{tp}{tp+fn} and: \boxed{ f1= \frac{2pr}{p+r} }. 5.31.31 so the benchmark has two metric families \boxed{ \text{generation of free text} \rightarrow \text{chrf} } for: \text{summary} and: \text{translation}. while: \boxed{ \text{short-span qa} \rightarrow \text{token f1} } because the answer is expected to overlap a gold answer span. this is an important exam distinction. 5.31.32 numerical chrf intuition the source does not give the underlying chrf formula on this slide, so we should not invent a full implementation equation and pretend it comes from the deck. the safe understanding is: \boxed{ \text{chrf compares character-level n-gram overlap using an f-score formulation} } which reduces sensitivity to subword/tokenization differences. that is the benchmark-design lesson supported by the source. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.33 indicgenbench vs indicxtreme now the distinction should be crystal clear. indicxtreme indicgenbench primarily nlu primarily generation classification-heavy summarization/translation/qa accuracy/f1 chrf/token f1 9 tasks 5 generation tasks tests understanding/transfer tests output generation 20-language contribution scope stated in deck 29-language scope the first five columns are conceptual descriptions grounded in the supplied decks. the language counts come directly from their respective slides. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.34 the important conceptual relationship we should not think: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme vs indicgenbench} = \text{same benchmark twice} } instead: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} = \text{can the model understand?} } and: \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench} = \text{can the model generate?} } a model can be strong at one and weak at the other. 5.31.35 why is that scientifically important? imagine a model with: 90\% classification performance. but when asked to generate an indic summary, its chrf is poor. then: \boxed{ \text{understanding capability} \not\rightarrow \text{generation capability} } this is one of the central gaps that indicgenbench is designed to expose. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.36 numerical exam bank question 1 crosssum-in: 100+100+500=700 per language. for 29 languages: 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300}. question 2 flores-in: 997+1012 = \boxed{2009}. for 29 languages: 2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) question 3 translator wage ratio: 15.90/2.80 \approx \boxed{5.68\times}. rounded: \boxed{5.7\times}. question 4 five generation tasks: \boxed{ 1\text{ crosssum} + 1\text{ flores} + 1\text{ xquad} + 2\text{ xorqa} = 5 } 5.31.37 exam-style conceptual question question: why does indicgenbench translate established benchmarks instead of constructing every dataset from scratch? the deck gives three reasons: \boxed{ \text{multi-way parallel data} } for separating task knowledge from language effects and measuring cross-lingual generalization, \boxed{ \text{lack of clean source data for many low-resource languages} } and: \boxed{ \text{reuse of existing benchmark quality control} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.38 exam-style conceptual question question: why does indicgenbench use chrf for summarization and translation rather than simply bleu/rouge? because the deck argues that token-level metrics can be unreliable for low-resource languages where tokenization itself is a weak link. character-level f-score reduces this dependence. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.31.39 the deeper lesson indicgenbench is not merely “another multilingual benchmark.” it addresses a different failure mode: \boxed{ \text{a model can understand an indic language without being able to generate it well.} } therefore the evaluation chain becomes: \boxed{ \text{indiccorp} \rightarrow \text{pretraining resources} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} \rightarrow \text{understanding/nlu evaluation} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench} \rightarrow \text{generation evaluation} } together they give a much more complete view of multilingual indic capability. 5.31.40 final mental model remember: \boxed{ \text{indicxtreme} = \text{understand} } \boxed{ \text{indicgenbench} = \text{generate} } indicgenbench covers: \boxed{29\text{ languages}} \boxed{13\text{ scripts}} \boxed{4\text{ families}} \boxed{3\text{ resource tiers}} and: \boxed{5\text{ generation tasks}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) its construction philosophy is: \boxed{ \text{existing high-quality benchmark} \rightarrow \text{professional human translation} \rightarrow \text{parallel indic evaluation} } rather than rebuilding the entire task ecosystem from scratch. and the first major warning is already visible: \boxed{ \text{even the best models perform substantially worse in indic generation than in english} } across all five generation tasks in the benchmark's reported analysis. (source: indicgenbench-slides)

core explanation mark read ← previous lesson · next lesson → prerequisites, purpose, and source status before this: step 5.31 — indicgenbench: why a second indic benchmark is needed this lesson: step 5.32 — indicgenbench: task-by-task dataset construction source references: indicgenbench-slides original katex syntax checked; claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.32 — indicgenbench: task-by-task dataset construction plan node: i11 · chat order #73 now we go through how each indicgenbench task is actually constructed . the four construction ideas we just established are now going to become concrete: \boxed{ \text{reuse} + \text{translate} + \text{preserve parallel structure} + \text{human quality control} } we will go in the exact task order of the supplied deck: \boxed{ \text{crosssum-in} \rightarrow \text{flores-in} \rightarrow \text{xquad-in} \rightarrow \text{xorqa-in} } with xorqa then splitting into two evaluation tasks. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.1 task 1 — crosssum-in start with: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} this is the cross-lingual summarization task. its source is: \boxed{\text{crosssum}} which itself derives from: \boxed{\text{xl-sum}} and contains bbc news articles paired with summaries in another language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the model's task is ultimately: \boxed{ \text{article} \rightarrow \text{compressed summary in target language} } 5.32.2 step 1 — start from english article-summary pairs the benchmark first samples: \boxed{700} english article-summary pairs. the split is: 100\text{ train} 100\text{ dev} 500\text{ test}. therefore: 100+100+500 = \boxed{700}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.3 step 2 — what about languages already covered by crosssum? crosssum already has: \boxed{9} of the target languages. for those 9 languages, the benchmark does not simply translate another 700 english pairs. instead, it resamples: \boxed{100/100/500} from the existing crosssum data. the reason is straightforward: \boxed{ \text{keep every language at the same dataset size} } so one language does not receive many more evaluation examples merely because an existing resource happened to be larger. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.4 step 3 — what about the remaining 20 languages? there are: 29-9 = \boxed{20} remaining target languages. for these, professional human translators translate the english summaries into the target language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the construction is: \boxed{ 9\text{ languages} \rightarrow \text{reuse existing crosssum examples} } while: \boxed{ 20\text{ languages} \rightarrow \text{new human translation} } 5.32.5 total size every language receives: 700 examples. there are: 29 languages. therefore: 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300} total examples. this is explicitly confirmed in the supplied slide. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.6 exam numerical training: 100\times29 = \boxed{2,900}. development: 100\times29 = \boxed{2,900}. test: 500\times29 = \boxed{14,500}. total: 2900+2900+14500 = \boxed{20,300}. 5.32.7 what does a crosssum-in example look like? conceptually: input: long news article output: short summary in hindi the target is not another full article. it is: \boxed{ \text{compressed preservation of the important information} } the deck's example highlights alignment between article information such as “nasa,” “problem,” “launch,” “spacecraft,” and “scheduled” and corresponding content in a hindi summary. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.8 why does the deck emphasize “never via an intermediate english summary”? because a poor multilingual system might conceptually do: \text{article} \rightarrow \text{english summary} \rightarrow \text{target language}. but the benchmark is testing whether the model can directly produce: \boxed{ \text{article} \rightarrow \text{target-language summary} } this matters because an intermediate-language step can hide weaknesses in direct target-language generation. the supplied example specifically emphasizes direct target-language generation rather than an english intermediary. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.9 crosssum-in metric crosssum-in uses: \boxed{\text{chrf}} because it is a free-form generation task and the benchmark wants a character-level metric less dependent on tokenization. (source: indicgenbench-slides) we will later derive why chrf is particularly useful for low-resource languages. 5.32.10 task 2 — flores-in now: \boxed{\text{flores-in}} is the machine-translation task. its source is: \boxed{\text{flores-200}} from the nllb work. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the important feature here is that flores-200 already contains: \boxed{ \text{human-annotated multi-way parallel translation data} } for many languages. therefore indicgenbench follows: \boxed{ \text{reuse where possible} } and: \boxed{ \text{translate where necessary}. } 5.32.11 what does “multi-way parallel” mean? suppose one english sentence is: x. it has translations: y_{\text{hindi}}, y_{\text{tamil}}, y_{\text{punjabi}}, y_{\text{bengali}}, \ldots all corresponding to the same x . so: \boxed{ x \rightarrow \{y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_k\} } where each y_i belongs to a different language. this gives direct comparability across languages. 5.32.12 flores-in source coverage the source slide says flores-200 already covers: \boxed{22\text{ of the 29 target languages}}. therefore: 29-22 = \boxed{7} languages still need new human translations. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.13 flores splits the source dataset has: \boxed{997\text{ dev}} \boxed{1012\text{ devtest}} and: \boxed{992\text{ non-public test}}. the benchmark uses: 997+1012 = \boxed{2009} sentences per language. it does not use the non-public test set in this construction. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.14 total flores-in size there are: 2009 sentences per language and: 29 languages. therefore: 2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261}. the deck reports this as approximately: \boxed{58.2k}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.15 exam calculation check: 2009\times30 = 60,270. subtract one language: 60,270-2,009 = \boxed{58,261}. useful mental-math approach. 5.32.16 important special case: no training split the supplied deck explicitly says: \boxed{ \text{flores-in is the only task with no training split}. } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is important to memorize because the other generation tasks have training/dev/test structures in the benchmark. 5.32.17 what does a flores-in example look like? it is extremely simple: \boxed{ \text{source sentence} \rightarrow \text{target-language sentence} } there is: \text{no question} and: \text{no context passage}. it is sentence-level translation. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.18 why is flores-in especially useful experimentally? suppose english sentence x is translated independently into: 29 target languages. because all outputs correspond to the same source sentence: \boxed{ \text{content is controlled} } while: \boxed{ \text{language changes}. } this makes flores-in particularly useful for comparing generation quality across languages. 5.32.19 task 3 — xquad-in now we move to: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}}. this tests multilingual reading comprehension. its source is: \boxed{\text{xquad}} which itself derives from: \boxed{\text{squad}}. the original structure is: \boxed{ \text{passage} + \text{question} \rightarrow \text{short answer span} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.20 step 1 — reuse existing xquad data the benchmark starts from: \boxed{240\text{ passages}} containing: \boxed{1190\text{ qa pairs}}. these are already human-translated into: \boxed{10\text{ higher-resource languages}} and hindi is the only indic language among them. these are reused as the test component. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.21 step 2 — create train/dev data the benchmark additionally selects: \boxed{20\text{ passages}/100\text{ qa pairs}} from squad's training set, and: \boxed{20\text{ passages}/100\text{ qa pairs}} from squad's development set. thus: 20+20 = \boxed{40\text{ new passages}} and: 100+100 = \boxed{200\text{ new qa pairs}} for the train/dev construction. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.22 total xquad-in source material so overall: 240+20+20 = \boxed{280\text{ passages}} and: 1190+100+100 = \boxed{1390\text{ qa pairs}}. this is exactly what the slide reports. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.23 step 3 — human translation into indic languages all: 280 passages and: 1390 qa pairs are professionally translated into: \boxed{12\text{ indic languages}}. therefore: 280\times12 = \boxed{3360} passage-language instances. and: 1390\times12 = \boxed{16,680} qa-language instances. the deck reports these as approximately: \boxed{3.3k\text{ passages}} and: \boxed{16.6k\text{ qa pairs}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.24 important distinction: passage count vs qa count do not confuse: \boxed{3360} with: \boxed{16,680}. the first counts: \text{passage × language} while the second counts: \text{qa pair × language}. there can be multiple questions per passage. this is a classic exam-data-counting trap. 5.32.25 what makes xquad-in “multilingual”? suppose: \text{passage}=\text{punjabi} \text{question}=\text{punjabi} \text{answer}=\text{punjabi}. then: \boxed{ \text{everything matches in one language} } for that example. the deck emphasizes that this is what “multilingual” means here: the model handles one language at a time, repeated across 12 languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is important because the next xorqa task is deliberately different. 5.32.26 xquad-in versus xorqa-in xquad-in \boxed{ \text{question: target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage: target language} } \boxed{ \text{answer: target language} } everything is within one language. xorqa-in \boxed{ \text{question: target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage: english} } \boxed{ \text{answer: english or target language} } that distinction is crucial. 5.32.27 task 4/5 — xorqa-in now we reach the most conceptually interesting construction. \boxed{\text{xorqa-in}} comes from: \boxed{\text{xor-tydi}}. the original source contains: \boxed{\text{non-english question}} paired with: \boxed{\text{english evidence passage}} and an answer. its purpose already involves cross-lingual retrieval. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.28 initial indic coverage the original xor-tydi source covers two indic languages: \boxed{\text{bengali}} with: 302 examples, and: \boxed{\text{telugu}} with: 237 examples. so total original indic examples: 302+237 = \boxed{539}. this is a useful source-derived numerical calculation. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.29 the problem with pairwise translation suppose there are: 29 target languages. if you independently translated every language pair, you'd face roughly: 29\times28 = 812 directed language pairs. or: \frac{29\times28}{2} = 406 undirected pairs. that becomes a huge translation-routing problem. the source therefore uses a clever pivot. 5.32.30 stage 1 — normalize through english first: \boxed{ \text{bengali/telugu question} \rightarrow \text{english} } professional translators translate the original question into english. now every source question has a common english representation. 5.32.31 stage 2 — fan out from english then: \boxed{ \text{english question} \rightarrow \text{all target languages} } and independently: \boxed{ \text{english answer} \rightarrow \text{all target languages} }. this is far more scalable than pairwise translation among every language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.32 the pivot architecture think of english as a hub: english / / | \ / / | \ hindi tamil telugu bengali ... instead of: hindi ↔ tamil ↔ telugu ↔ bengali ↔ ... the hub-and-spoke architecture dramatically simplifies the translation workflow. 5.32.33 why is this called normalization? because all original questions are first mapped into the same intermediate representation: \boxed{\text{english}} before being expanded outward. so: q_{\text{bengali}} \rightarrow q_{\text{english}} \rightarrow q_{\text{hindi}},q_{\text{tamil}},\ldots and: q_{\text{telugu}} \rightarrow q_{\text{english}} \rightarrow q_{\text{hindi}},q_{\text{tamil}},\ldots this creates a consistent multilingual source for the later benchmark variants. 5.32.34 now the clever part: one dataset becomes two tasks the same stage-2 translations provide: \boxed{\text{question in every target language}} and: \boxed{\text{answer in every target language}}. these are recombined into two different evaluation tasks. 5.32.35 xorqa-in-en in: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-en}} we have: \boxed{ \text{question = target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage = english} } \boxed{ \text{answer = english} } so the model must understand a target-language question and find/produce the relevant answer using english evidence. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.36 xorqa-in-xx in: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-xx}} we have: \boxed{ \text{question = target language} } \boxed{ \text{passage = english} } but: \boxed{ \text{answer = target language} }. so now the model must perform both: \boxed{ \text{cross-lingual comprehension} } and: \boxed{ \text{target-language generation} }. this makes xorqa-in-xx harder in a different way than xorqa-in-en. 5.32.37 why is xorqa-in-xx particularly interesting? consider: \text{telugu question} \rightarrow \text{english evidence} \rightarrow \text{telugu answer}. the model must: interpret telugu; retrieve relevant information from english; map the information back into telugu; generate the answer correctly. so it combines: \boxed{ \text{cross-lingual understanding} + \text{cross-lingual retrieval} + \text{target-language generation} }. the deck explicitly contrasts this with xorqa-in-en, where the answer is generated in english. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.38 compare all three qa designs xquad-in \boxed{ l_q=l_c=l_a } where all three are the same target language. xorqa-in-en \boxed{ l_q\neq l_c,\quad l_a=l_c=\text{english} } xorqa-in-xx \boxed{ l_q=l_a\neq l_c } where l_c is english. this is a very useful symbolic way to memorize the difference. 5.32.39 coverage across languages the deck says: crosssum-in \boxed{29\text{ languages}} flores-in \boxed{29\text{ languages}} xquad-in \boxed{11\text{ languages}} xorqa-in \boxed{28\text{ languages}} with: \boxed{\text{nepali excluded}} from the latter due to not being translated. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.40 why does xquad-in have fewer languages? the slide says its coverage is constrained by: which languages already had xquad translations; the three medium-resource languages selected for extension. therefore it reaches only: \boxed{11}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is another example of why benchmark coverage depends partly on the availability of usable source resources. 5.32.41 numerical coverage comparison crosssum/flores: 29/29 = \boxed{100\%} of the target language set in this benchmark. xquad: 11/29 \approx \boxed{37.9\%}. xorqa: 28/29 \approx \boxed{96.6\%}. these percentages are our calculations from the deck's reported language counts. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.42 why are the benchmark tasks not equally broad? because the source datasets are different. crosssum has a route to 29 languages. flores already has broad multilingual coverage. xquad has more constrained existing translation coverage. xor-tydi starts from only certain source-language questions and then expands them. therefore: \boxed{ \text{benchmark coverage is constrained by source-resource structure} } not just by the researchers' desired language count. 5.32.43 complete dataset-construction table task source what is generated languages crosssum-in crosssum / xl-sum target-language summaries 29 flores-in flores-200 target-language translations 29 xquad-in xquad / squad target-language qa 11 xorqa-in-en xor-tydi target-language question + english answer 28 xorqa-in-xx xor-tydi target-language question + target-language answer 28 (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.44 exact numerical bank crosssum-in 700\times29 = \boxed{20,300}. flores-in (997+1012)\times29 =2009\times29 = \boxed{58,261}. xquad-in (240+20+20)\times12 = 280\times12 = \boxed{3,360\text{ passages}}. qa pairs: (1190+100+100)\times12 = 1390\times12 = \boxed{16,680}. original indic xor-tydi 302+237 = \boxed{539} examples. all of these are directly derived from the deck's reported figures. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.45 the deepest construction idea the most interesting thing about indicgenbench is that the researchers are not merely increasing: \boxed{\text{number of languages}} they are trying to control the experimental variables . for example: crosssum same underlying article/task structure, different output languages. flores same source sentence, many target languages. xquad same passage/question structure, translated consistently into target language. xorqa same evidence language, different question/output-language configurations. therefore: \boxed{ \text{language} } can be varied while holding much of the underlying task constant. that is exactly what makes these datasets scientifically useful for cross-lingual comparison. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.46 one final conceptual comparison imagine these two systems. system a \text{english question} \rightarrow \text{english answer}. system b \text{telugu question} \rightarrow \text{english evidence} \rightarrow \text{telugu answer}. system b requires much more than ordinary generation. it requires: \boxed{ \text{language understanding} + \text{cross-lingual information retrieval} + \text{target-language generation} }. this is why xorqa-in-xx is an especially valuable task conceptually. 5.32.47 exam-ready master structure memorize this: \boxed{ \text{crosssum-in} = \text{summarization} } \boxed{ \text{flores-in} = \text{translation} } \boxed{ \text{xquad-in} = \text{same-language qa} } \boxed{ \text{xorqa-in-en} = \text{target-question + english-evidence + english-answer} } \boxed{ \text{xorqa-in-xx} = \text{target-question + english-evidence + target-answer} } and the key language counts are: \boxed{ 29,\ 29,\ 11,\ 28,\ 28 } respectively. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.32.48 final mental model the construction can be summarized as: \boxed{ \text{existing benchmark} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{reuse existing multilingual data where possible} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{professionally translate missing indic languages} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{preserve parallel correspondence} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{evaluate generation across resource levels} } this is the core engineering philosophy of indicgenbench. and the most important distinction between the tasks is: \boxed{ \text{xquad-in keeps question, context, and answer in the same language} } while: \boxed{ \text{xorqa-in deliberately separates the question language from the evidence language} } and then tests both english and target-language answer generation. (source: indicgenbench-slides)

claim-by-claim source/mathematical review pending. original teaching retained; independent depth scoring pending. step 5.33 — indicgenbench: metrics, resource gaps, directionality, and in-context learning plan node: i11 · chat order #74 we now move from how indicgenbench was constructed to: \boxed{ \text{how do we score generation quality, and what do the results reveal?} } this step contains some of the most important insights in the indic material because the benchmark does more than rank models. it exposes why generation quality breaks down for lower-resource indic languages . the major chain is: \boxed{ \text{metric choice} \rightarrow \text{model comparison} \rightarrow \text{resource-tier gap} \rightarrow \text{translation asymmetry} \rightarrow \text{few-shot behavior} \rightarrow \text{tokenizer bottleneck} } 5.33.1 first: why ordinary accuracy is not enough for classification we had: x\rightarrow y so accuracy was natural. but generation looks like: x\rightarrow \hat y where many different outputs can be valid. suppose gold: the mission launched after several delays. model: after being delayed several times, the mission finally launched. the strings are different, but the meaning is very similar. therefore: \boxed{ \text{exact string equality is too strict} } for most generation tasks. indicgenbench therefore uses two major metric families: \boxed{\text{chrf}} for summarization/translation, and: \boxed{\text{token-level f1}} for qa. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.2 chrf — character-level f-score the deck uses: \boxed{\text{chrf}} for: \boxed{\text{crosssum-in}} and: \boxed{\text{flores-in}}. the important idea is: \boxed{ \text{compare character-level n-gram overlap rather than token overlap} } the deck specifically motivates this because token-level metrics such as bleu and rouge can be unreliable for low-resource languages when tokenization itself is problematic. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.3 why character-level evaluation helps suppose the same word is tokenized differently. language a: w\rightarrow[t_1] language b: w\rightarrow[t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4]. a token-level metric now depends partly on the tokenizer. at the character level, we instead compare something closer to: \text{c-a-t} against another string's character sequence. thus: \boxed{ \text{evaluation becomes less tied to subword segmentation} } the deck calls this important because tokenization is itself a weakness for some low-resource languages. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.4 why not say chrf is “perfect”? we should be careful. the deck says character-level scoring sidesteps the tokenization problem. it does not claim that chrf perfectly captures semantics. two sentences can have high character overlap but different meanings, or low overlap while expressing the same meaning. so the correct lesson is: \boxed{ \text{chrf reduces one important low-resource evaluation problem} } not: \boxed{ \text{chrf completely solves generation evaluation} }. that stronger statement is not supported by the slide. 5.33.5 token-f1 for qa for: \boxed{\text{xquad-in}} and: \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-en}} \boxed{\text{xorqa-in-xx}}, the benchmark uses squad-style: \boxed{\text{token-overlap f1}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) recall: p=\frac{tp}{tp+fp} r=\frac{tp}{tp+fn} and: \boxed{ f1=\frac{2pr}{p+r} }. 5.33.6 numerical qa example suppose: p=0.8 and: r=0.6. then: f1= \frac{2(0.8)(0.6)}{0.8+0.6} = \frac{0.96}{1.4} = \boxed{0.6857}. so: \boxed{68.57\%}. 5.33.7 why f1 is appropriate for short answers suppose gold answer: [\text{new delhi}] and prediction: [\text{delhi}] the model is partially correct. accuracy would force a binary: 0\text{ or }1. f1 can reflect partial overlap. that makes it much more useful for span-based qa. the exact normalization/tokenization details are not specified on this deck page, so we shouldn't invent them. 5.33.8 now: do bigger models actually do better? the benchmark asks: \boxed{ \text{does indicgenbench distinguish model quality?} } the answer from the deck is: \boxed{\text{yes}} and several patterns emerge. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.9 pattern 1 — larger models within a family generally perform better the deck states: \boxed{ \text{larger models within a family consistently do better} } the reported comparison includes models such as: \text{palm-2-xxs} \text{palm-2-xs} \text{palm-2-s} \text{palm-2-l} and llama variants. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is a classic scaling observation. 5.33.10 why is the family comparison useful? suppose: m_1<m_2<m_3 in model size. if performance consistently follows: p(m_1)<p(m_2)<p(m_3), then the benchmark has some sensitivity to model capability. that doesn't prove size is the only factor, because architecture, training data, and training procedure can also differ. but within one model family, size comparisons become more informative. 5.33.11 palm-2-l the deck reports that: \boxed{\text{palm-2-l wins on 4 of the 5 tasks}} among the listed comparisons. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so the largest model in that family is very strong, but notably: \boxed{ \text{not necessarily the winner on all five} }. again: \text{larger} \not\rightarrow \text{automatic universal dominance}. 5.33.12 llama result the slide reports that open-source llama models lag substantially in this benchmark setup. it even notes that: \boxed{ \text{llama-65b underperforms the smallest palm-2-xxs} } in the reported comparisons. (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is extremely important. it tells us: \boxed{ \text{parameter count alone does not determine multilingual generation quality} } because a much larger model can still underperform a smaller model from another training family. 5.33.13 bloomz the deck reports: \boxed{\text{bloomz wins 3 of 5 tasks}} among the listed models. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the deck describes bloomz as: \boxed{ \text{instruction-tuned + broad multilingual pretraining} }. so multilingual training and instruction tuning can be particularly valuable for this benchmark. again, this doesn't establish a universal ranking outside the reported benchmark. 5.33.14 the biggest result: indic performance trails english the most important sentence on that results slide is: \boxed{ \text{every model, even the best, trails its own english performance by 20+ points.} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is a very strong diagnosis. the benchmark isn't merely showing: \text{different models behave differently}. it is showing: \boxed{ \text{the same model is substantially weaker when generating indic languages than when generating english} }. 5.33.15 numerical illustration suppose a model scores: 85\% on english. if it trails english by 22 points on an indic task: 85-22 = \boxed{63\%}. the source says the gap is 20+ points across the reported models; 22 is just an illustrative example. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.16 now the resource-tier analysis the next question is: is this degradation uniform across all indic languages? no. the deck reports a clear ordering: \boxed{ \text{high resource} > \text{medium resource} > \text{low resource} } across every task . (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is one of the central findings. 5.33.17 what is being measured? for every task, the benchmark groups languages into: \boxed{h=\text{higher}} \boxed{m=\text{medium}} \boxed{l=\text{low}}. then it computes performance by tier. so rather than one number: p_{\text{all}} we look at: \boxed{ p_h,\quad p_m,\quad p_l }. the reported pattern is: p_h>p_m>p_l. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.18 why is this stronger than one overall average? suppose: p_h=70 p_m=60 p_l=40. overall average could still look respectable: \frac{70+60+40}{3} = \boxed{56.7}. but that average hides the fact that the lowest-resource languages are far weaker. this is why resource-tier breakdown is much more revealing. 5.33.19 translation direction changes the story now comes one of the strongest findings in the entire deck. consider: \boxed{\text{flores-in}}. the benchmark evaluates translation in both directions. for palm-2-l: english → target language high: 56.9 low: 41.9. so the drop is: 56.9-41.9 = \boxed{15.0\text{ points}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.20 now reverse the direction target language → english high: 68.2 low: 62.6. drop: 68.2-62.6 = \boxed{5.6\text{ points}}. so: \boxed{ 15.0\text{ points} } vs: \boxed{ 5.6\text{ points} }. that is a huge difference. 5.33.21 calculate the ratio \frac{15.0}{5.6} \approx \boxed{2.68}. so the resource-tier degradation reported for palm-2-l is roughly 2.7 times larger in the: \boxed{ \text{english}\rightarrow\text{target} } direction than in: \boxed{ \text{target}\rightarrow\text{english} }. this ratio is our calculation from the source numbers. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.22 this reveals a major asymmetry the deck's interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{current llms are better at understanding low-resource languages than generating them} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) think about the direction: understanding low-resource language \text{low-resource language} \rightarrow \text{english} the model receives the difficult language and produces english. generating low-resource language \text{english} \rightarrow \text{low-resource language} now the model has to produce target-language text. the second is much more fragile. 5.33.23 why is generation harder? the source reports the empirical asymmetry, but does not give a single definitive mathematical cause. a reasonable interpretation is: \boxed{ \text{understanding requires recognizing patterns} } whereas generation requires: \boxed{ \text{reliably producing those patterns} }. the model may have enough representation to understand some low-resource input but insufficient learned generation statistics to produce fluent target-language output. this explanatory distinction is model reasoning/inference, not a direct formula from the slide. 5.33.24 exam question: directionality suppose: p_{h}^{en\rightarrow indic}=60 p_{l}^{en\rightarrow indic}=40. drop: 20. for reverse direction: p_h^{indic\rightarrow en}=70 p_l^{indic\rightarrow en}=65. drop: 5. then: \boxed{ \text{generation-side resource sensitivity is }4\times\text{ larger} } because: 20/5=4. this is an illustrative exam problem modeled on the directionality finding. 5.33.25 now the few-shot question suppose the model receives: 0 examples. that is: \boxed{\text{zero-shot}}. what happens if we give: 1 worked example? the deck reports that: \boxed{ \text{every model family improves monotonically as in-context examples increase} } and the biggest jump is often: \boxed{0\rightarrow1\text{ shot}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.26 the striking example for palm-2-xxs on flores-in: \boxed{0\text{-shot}=0.8} and: \boxed{1\text{-shot}=24.0}. improvement: 24.0-0.8 = \boxed{23.2\text{ points}}. relative increase: \frac{23.2}{0.8}\times100 = \boxed{2900\%}. this enormous percentage is mathematically correct, but because the original score is tiny, the more meaningful source-friendly statement is: \boxed{+23.2\text{ points}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.27 why does one example help so much? the source reports the phenomenon but does not claim a single mechanism. a reasonable interpretation is that one example gives the model: \boxed{ \text{task format} + \text{translation style} + \text{expected output structure} }. so the model does not need to infer the entire task from instructions alone. this is an inference from general in-context learning, not a statement explicitly established as a theorem by the slide. 5.33.28 but “more examples” has a limit the slide title is: \boxed{ \text{more in-context examples help — up to a point} } why does the improvement stop being straightforward? because every example consumes context. and for indic languages: \boxed{ \text{tokenization itself can become the bottleneck} }. that takes us to the tokenizer section. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.29 language-specific exemplars now the benchmark asks: which language should the in-context examples be written in? the reported ordering is: \boxed{ \text{test language} > \text{hindi} > \text{english} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this is a very elegant result. 5.33.30 why is the ordering interesting? suppose the test language is punjabi. then the model benefits most from: \boxed{\text{punjabi examples}} then: \boxed{\text{hindi examples}} then: \boxed{\text{english examples}}. the deck says this matches the order of linguistic relatedness to the test language. (source: indicgenbench-slides) so: \boxed{ \text{similar-language demonstration} > \text{distant-language demonstration} } in the reported experiments. 5.33.31 especially important for smaller models the deck says: \boxed{ \text{for smaller models, hindi exemplars can come extremely close to, and sometimes beat, test-language exemplars} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this suggests that hindi can function as a useful bridge language in prompting. again, that is a reported empirical finding, not a universal guarantee for every indic language. 5.33.32 numerical example suppose a model scores: 50 with english exemplars, 56 with hindi exemplars, and: 60 with test-language exemplars. then: \boxed{ 60>56>50 } matching the reported ordering. 5.33.33 now the biggest hidden bottleneck: tokenizer fertility this is one of the most important technical concepts in the entire indicgenbench deck. the slide defines: \boxed{ \text{fertility} = \text{average number of subword tokens per word} } (source: indicgenbench-slides) this connects directly to everything we learned earlier about tokenization. 5.33.34 example of fertility suppose a language has 100 words. after tokenization, those words become: 500 subword tokens. then: \text{fertility} = \frac{500}{100} = \boxed{5}. so on average: \boxed{5\text{ tokens per word}}. 5.33.35 reported fertility values the deck says: \boxed{\text{english}\approx1} and among indic languages: \boxed{\text{pashto}=4.1} while: \boxed{\text{tibetan}=19.9}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the important consequence is: one tibetan word can consume roughly 20 tokens under the evaluated tokenizer. 5.33.36 why is this not a statement about the language itself? the slide makes this explicit. high fertility is: \boxed{ \text{a tokenizer artifact} } and is not a measure of intrinsic language complexity. so: \boxed{ \text{language is not “hard” because fertility is high} } rather: \boxed{ \text{the chosen tokenizer represents the language inefficiently} }. this distinction is extremely important. 5.33.37 context-window mathematics suppose the model has a context budget: b=1920 tokens. for english: f_e\approx1. suppose an example requires: 100 words. approximate token cost: 100\times1 = 100. now suppose a target language has: f=10. the same 100 words consume approximately: 100\times10 = \boxed{1000} tokens. so the same semantic amount of text consumes: \boxed{10\times} more context. this is a conceptual calculation directly based on the fertility definition. 5.33.38 why does this hurt few-shot prompting? suppose each demonstration has: 200 words. for a language with fertility: f=1, rough estimate: 200\text{ tokens}. five examples: 5\times200 = 1000. easy to fit in: 1920. now fertility: f=8. each example costs: 200\times8 = 1600. even one demonstration consumes most of the budget. so: \boxed{ \text{high fertility} \rightarrow \text{fewer demonstrations fit} }. that is the central mechanism highlighted by the deck. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.39 the actual 1920-token result at: \boxed{1920\text{ tokens}} of context budget: english the deck reports that english still fits: \boxed{5\text{ in-context examples}} for more than: \boxed{80\%} of its test set. oriya and punjabi the deck reports that these high-fertility languages fall to nearly: \boxed{0\%} of test cases being able to fit the required examples by only: \boxed{2-3\text{ examples}}. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.40 this creates a hidden disadvantage suppose two languages have identical model reasoning capability. language a can fit: 5 examples. language b can fit: 1 example. then even if the model would benefit equally from demonstrations, language b receives less usable prompting support. so: \boxed{ \text{measured performance} = \text{model capability} + \text{context/tokenizer effects} } conceptually. the second equation is a general inference; the source's direct point is that fertility causes some languages to fit fewer worked examples. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.41 why this changes how we interpret low-resource performance earlier we might conclude: low-resource language models perform poorly because they understand the language poorly. the tokenizer analysis adds another layer: \boxed{ \text{they may also receive fewer effective in-context examples} } because their text consumes more tokens. so the gap may contain both: \boxed{\text{representation/understanding difficulty}} and: \boxed{\text{context-budget inefficiency}}. the deck explicitly connects the high-fertility result to the low-resource in-context performance gap. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.42 numerical exam question — fertility a language has: f=4.1. a document contains: 500 words. approximate token cost: 500\times4.1 = \boxed{2050\text{ tokens}}. if the context budget is: 1920, the document alone exceeds the budget under this simplified calculation. this is an illustrative estimate using the source's fertility concept and pashto value; real token counts vary from word to word. 5.33.43 numerical exam question — tibetan suppose: f=19.9 and: 200 words need to be included. approximate token count: 200\times19.9 = \boxed{3980}. so a 1920-token context cannot even hold that 200-word text under this average-based approximation. this illustrates why fertility can become a severe practical bottleneck. 5.33.44 the full causal chain now becomes visible we began with: \boxed{ \text{low-resource language} } then: \downarrow \boxed{ \text{less training data} } then: \boxed{ \text{weaker learned generation} } but there is another path: \boxed{ \text{high tokenizer fertility} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{same content consumes more tokens} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{fewer in-context examples fit} } \downarrow \boxed{ \text{less prompting support} } thus the low-resource challenge isn't only a data quantity problem. 5.33.45 another surprising result: fine-tuning vs few-shot the deck compares: \boxed{\text{mt5}} and: \boxed{\text{palm-2}} under fine-tuning and few-shot prompting. (source: indicgenbench-slides) the reported pattern is: qa mt5 performs very strongly because it is purpose-built for short-span generation. crosssum palm-2 performs better on the longer-form generation task. and: \boxed{ \text{palm-2-xs few-shot} \approx \text{or exceeds its fine-tuned performance on qa} } while: \boxed{ \text{fine-tuning remains clearly better for long-form generation} }. (source: indicgenbench-slides) 5.33.46 why is this distinction useful? it tells us: \boxed{ \text{there is no universally best adaptation method} } the task structure matters. for short-span qa: \boxed{\text{few-shot prompting can be surprisingly competitive}} for long-form summarization: \boxed{\text{additional training data is more valuable}} in the reported experiments. 5.33.47 exam-style conceptual question question: why can few-shot prompting beat fine-tuning on some qa tasks but not on long-form summarization? the reported benchmark suggests that short-span qa can be performed very effectively through in-context examples, while long-form generation benefits more strongly from task-specific fine-tuning. the result is task-dependent rather than a universal rule. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.3 the key observation for causal decoding:  oxed{ k_i,v_i } for an old token do not change merely because a new token arrived. so why recompute them? we can calculate: k_i=x_iw_k and: v_i=x_iw_v once. then store them. that is the:  oxed{	ext{kv cache}}. 5.36.4 kv cache idea at generation step t :  oxed{ k_{\le t},v_{\le t} } are stored. when token t+1 arrives, we calculate only its new: k_{t+1} and: v_{t+1}, then append them to the cache. so: k_{	ext{cache}} \leftarrow [k_{	ext{cache}};k_{t+1}] and: v_{	ext{cache}} \leftarrow [v_{	ext{cache}};v_{t+1}]. the book explicitly describes the cache as being maintained independently at each layer and attention head. (source: build a deepseek model (from scratch)) 5.36.5 why this speeds up generation without kv caching:  oxed{ 	ext{recompute old k/v every step} } with caching:  oxed{ 	ext{compute old k/v once, reuse thereafter} } so the repeated historical projection work disappears. the book gives an actual gpt-2 experiment: 	ext{100 generated tokens} without cache:  oxed{30.9818	ext{ s}} with cache:  oxed{6.1630	ext{ s}}. reported speedup:  rac{30.9818}{6.1630} \approx  oxed{5.03	imes}.
