read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 02.10. original source image and extract follow. slide 11 — beam search isn't a cure for open-ended generation slide text (extracted) beam search isn't a cure for open-ended generation beam search finds a higher-probability sequence than greedy — but higher probability is not the same as higher quality. holtzman et al. (2020) found beam search text is often just as repetitive as greedy, and additionally tends toward generic, bland phrasing: maximizing probability pulls toward whatever is safest, not what a person would actually write. where beam search shines vs. where it doesn' t tasks with one (or a few) essentially "correct" output — translation, summarization, code — reward finding the single best sequence, and beam search is standard there. open-ended generation — chat, stories, brainstorming — has many equally valid continuations; relentlessly maximizing probability actively hurts it.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 02.16. original source image and extract follow. slide 17 — min-p sampling slide text (extracted) min-p sampling nguyen et al. (2024) scale the cutoff by the top token's own probability, rather than fixing it in advance: pmax = max qθ (v), ​ ​ v∈v ​ pscaled = pbase × pmax , ​ ​ ​ v min = {v : qθ (v) ≥ pscaled } ​ ​ pbase ∈ (0, 1] — a fixed hyperparameter, typically 0.05–0.1; the actual threshold pscaled rises and falls automatically with the model's own confidence pmax . ​ ​ p s c a l e d = 0.10 × p m a x ​ d i st r i b u ti o n pmax peaked 0.8062 0.0806 france only flat 0.2181 0.0218 all 6 tokens ​ ​ ​ to k e n s k e p t when the model is very confident, min-p's threshold rises with it and prunes aggressively — here down to a single token. when the model is unsure, the threshold stays low and nearly everything plausible survives.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 02.17. original source image and extract follow. slide 18 — three truncation rules, side by side slide text (extracted) three truncation rules, side by side ru l e o n t h e p e a k e d d i st r i b u ti o n o n t h e f l at d i st r i b u ti o n top-k always keep exactly k 3 tokens (fine here) 3 tokens (cuts off 2 nearly-as-likely ones) top-p keep until cumulative ≥ p 3 tokens 5 tokens (adapts to the flatness) min-p keep while qθ ≥ pbase × pmax 1 token (very aggressive when sure) 6 tokens (very permissive when unsure) ​ ​ ​ all three exist for the same reason: a single fixed number of tokens is the wrong knob to turn, because how many tokens are actually plausible changes at every single step. top-p and min-p each adapt to that in a different way — top-p from the shape of the cumulative curve, min-p from the model's own peak confidence.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 02.18. original source image and extract follow. slide 19 — repetition penalty slide text (extracted) repetition penalty keskar et al. (2019, ctrl) penalize tokens the model already used, directly at the logit level, before the softmax: qi = ​ exp(zi /(t ⋅ ii )) ​ ​ ∑j exp(zj /(t ⋅ ij )) ​ ​ ​ , ​ θ i already generated ii = { 1 otherwise ​ ​ ​ θ > 1 — the penalty strength; dividing an already-used token's logit by θ before the softmax pulls its probability down without touching any other token directly. to k e n the cat (already used) s at ag a i n logit 1.2 0.8 2.0 0.3 logit after ÷θ=1.5 1.2 0.5333 2.0 0.3 p before penalty 0.2324 0.1558 0.5173 0.0945 p after penalty 0.2412 0.1238 0.5369 0.0981 "cat" drops from 15.58% to 12.38%, and every other token's share rises slightly to compensate — a direct, tunable nudge away from repeating what's already been said.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 02.19. original source image and extract follow. slide 20 — further decoding & sampling strategies slide text (extracted) further decoding & sampling strategies the methods above cover the standard toolkit; several others target the same problems from different angles: typical sampling contrastive search meister et al. (2022) keep tokens whose information content is close to the distribution's own conditional entropy — neither surprising nor overly predictable — rather than just su et al. (2022) pick the next token by balancing model confidence against how similar its representation is to recently generated tokens, directly discouraging near-repeats. the highest-probability ones. mirostat combining methods basu et al. (2021) adaptively tune the truncation threshold every step to hold the generated text's perplexity near a chosen target value, avoiding both repetitive ("bored") and incoherent ("confused") extremes. in practice, temperature, top-k, and top-p are commonly applied together in sequence — reshape with temperature, truncate the tail with top-k and/or top-p, then sample from what remains.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 04.03. original source image and extract follow. slide 4 — decoding a float: a worked example slide text (extracted) decoding a float: a worked example take the fp16 bit pattern below and recover the number it encodes, one field at a time: st e p co m p u tati o n r e s u lt sign s = 0 ⇒ (−1)0 +1 exponent e = 100002 = 16, bias = 24 − 1 = 15 16 − 15 = 1 mantissa bits 1001001000 ⇒ 2−1 + 2−4 + 2−7 0.5703125 value (+1) × 21 × (1 + 0.5703125) 3.140625 ​ t h i s i s π , to t h e p r e c i s i o n f p 1 6 a l low s the true value π = 3.14159265 … gets rounded to the nearest representable fp16 value, 3.140625 — an error of about 0.00097, purely from having only 10 mantissa bits to work with.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 04.04. original source image and extract follow. slide 5 — where a format's min and max come from slide text (extracted) where a format's min and max come from the largest and smallest representable magnitudes follow directly from how many bits go to the exponent and mantissa. the all-ones exponent is reserved for ±∞/nan, so the largest usable stored exponent is 2e − 2; the smallest is 1 (stored exponent 0 is reserved for zero/subnormals): max magnitude min normal magnitude 1.0 × 2 1−bias e (2 − 2−m ) × 2 (2 −2)−bias all mantissa bits zero, smallest usable exponent. all mantissa bits set (closest to 2), largest usable exponent. fo r m at s i g n + e x p + m a n ti ss a bias max min (normal) fp32 1 + 8 + 23 127 3.4028 × 1038 1.1755 × 10−38 fp16 1 + 5 + 10 15 6.5504 × 104 6.1035 × 10−5 bf16 1+8+7 127 3.3895 × 1038 1.1755 × 10−38 r a n g e i s e x p o n e n t- d o m i n at e d, n o t e x p o n e n t- o n ly min normal has zero mantissa-dependence: it's always 1.0 × 21−bias , mantissa forced to all-zero. max does depend on the mantissa a little, through the (2 − 2−m ) term above — that's exactly why the table shows bf16's max (3.3895 × 1038 ) isn't bit-identical to fp32's (3.4028 × 1038 ) despite sharing all 8 exponent bits. but (2 − 2−m ) only ever ranges between 1 and 2 — at most a 2× difference — dwarfed by the exponent's contribution: 2127 vs 215 is a factor of 2112 . so the mantissa can nudge the max by less than 1 bit's worth of magnitude, while the exponent moves it by 112 bits' worth — which is the precise sense in which range is set by the exponent, and fp16's 3-bits-narrower exponent (not its mantissa) is why its max is 65504, not 1038 .

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 04.05. original source image and extract follow. slide 6 — the max, bit by bit slide text (extracted) the max, bit by bit concretely, which bit pattern is fp16's max? all mantissa bits set, largest usable exponent, exactly as the previous slide's formula describes: st e p co m p u tati o n r e s u lt sign s = 0 ⇒ (−1)0 +1 exponent e = 111102 = 30 (all-1s, 11111, is reserved for ∞/nan — so the largest usable pattern is one less) 30 − 15 = 15 mantissa all 10 bits set: 1111111111 ⇒ 1023/1024 0.9990234375 value (+1) × 215 × (1 + 0.9990234375) 65504 ​ this is exactly the 6.5504 × 104 from the previous slide's table — not a separately quoted constant, but this specific bit pattern, decoded with the same formula used for every other value. one exponent step higher would need the reserved all-1s pattern, which is why 65504 is the ceiling.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 04.06. original source image and extract follow. slide 7 — subnormal numbers: the other reserved exponent slide text (extracted) subnormal numbers: the other reserved exponent just as all-1s exponent bits are reserved (for ±∞/nan), all-0s exponent bits are reserved too — for numbers smaller than any normal number can represent. when e = 0, the format switches formulas: the implicit leading 1 disappears, and the exponent freezes at the smallest normal's value instead of continuing to shrink: normal (e ≠ 0) subnormal (e = 0, f ≠ 0) (−1)s × 21−bias × f (−1)s × 2e−bias × (1 + f ) f — the mantissa read as a plain fraction (f = ∑ fk 2−k , no added 1). dropping the implicit 1 is what lets these values shrink past the normal floor — each step ​ down the mantissa halves the value instead of barely denting it, so precision degrades gracefully instead of the format jumping straight from its smallest normal number to exactly 0 (gradual underflow). if e = 0 and f = 0 too, the value is exactly 0. b it pat t e r n ( s e f ) co m p u tati o n va lu e 0 00000 1000000000 21−15 × (512/1024) 3.0518 × 10−5 0 00000 0000000001 21−15 × (1/1024) 5.9605 × 10−8 (smallest subnormal) 0 00001 0000000000 21−15 × (1 + 0) 6.1035 × 10−5 (smallest normal) so fp16's true floor isn't 6.1 × 10−5 — it's 5.96 × 10−8 , once subnormals are counted. a value can still be too small even for that: 1.8 × 10−42 , coming up shortly, is far below even this subnormal floor, which is why it underflows all the way to 0.0 rather than landing on a subnormal. s u b n o r m a l s a r e n ot " e v e ry t h i n g b e low 1 " almost all of (0, 1) — 0.5, 0.1, 0.001, down to about 6.1 × 10−5 — is still normal, just with a negative exponent (0.1 = 2−4 × 1.6, e.g.). subnormals only take over in the last, extremely thin sliver right before zero.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 04.31. original source image and extract follow. slide 32 — why not skip dequantizing — the next layer just requantizes anyway? slide text (extracted) why not skip dequantizing — the next layer just requantizes anyway? two independent reasons the real values have to reappear, even briefly. first: yint32 isn't in any usable unit on its own — it's scaled by this layer's joint scale sx ⋅ sw , ​ ​ ​ and whatever sits between two matmuls (gelu, softmax, layernorm, a residual add) needs real, comparable numbers to compute correctly, not raw accumulator values in an arbitrary per-layer scale. va lu e yint32 (raw accumulator, one entry) 12614 joint scale sx ⋅ sw (this layer only) 4032.25 y = yint32 /(sx sw ) — the real value 3.128 ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ second, even for two matmuls with nothing in between: the next layer's dynamic quantization still has to measure α = max ∣y ∣ to build its own fresh scale. max ∣yint32 ∣ = 12614 alone is useless for that — it still carries the old joint scale baked in. getting max ∣y ∣ = 3.128, the number the next scale actually gets ​ calibrated from, requires that same division. some form of dequantization is what produces the next layer's calibration input — it can't be skipped just because a requantization follows it.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 04.39. original source image and extract follow. slide 40 — gptq: does this actually help? slide text (extracted) gptq: does this actually help? at realistic scale — a 64-weight row, calibration activations with realistic feature correlation, int4 — sequential quantize-and-compensate vs. naive independent rounding, measured on the loss gptq actually optimizes, e⊤ he (the real output-reconstruction error, not raw weight error): method e ⊤ he ( o u t p u t e r ro r ) naive independent rounding 151.4 gptq (sequential + compensation) 71.8 v e r i f i e d : 5 2 . 6 % low e r o u t p u t e r r o r — b u t n ot low e r w e i g h t e r r o r plain unweighted weight mse tells the opposite story here: naive = 0.00067 vs. gptq = 0.00137 — gptq's weights are individually less accurate on average. that's not a bug: gptq deliberately pushes weights further from their true values in directions h says the output barely notices, in exchange for staying accurate in directions the output is sensitive to. it optimizes what the layer actually computes, not how close the weights look on paper.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 04.52. original source image and extract follow. slide 53 — bitnet: recovering an fp16 output slide text (extracted) bitnet: recovering an fp16 output ydequantized = y ⋅ ​ α⋅β 2b−1 ​ α — the weight-quantization scale from a few slides back; β — the activation-quantization scale just used. multiplying by both undoes both roundings at once, handing the next (ordinary, fp16) layer a normal-looking activation.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.10. original source image and extract follow. slide 11 — word-level kd vs. seqkd: two approximations slide text (extracted) word-level kd vs. seqkd: two approximations forward kld wants two things at once: y sampled from the teacher's own generation, and the student matching the teacher's full distribution at every step. neither practical method gets both — they trade off in opposite directions: co n t e x t y < t co m e s f ro m p e r-to k e n ta rg e t word-level kd real, ground-truth data teacher's full soft distribution (exact) seqkd the teacher itself (exact) one-hot on the teacher's own sampled token ​ word-level kd keeps the soft, per-token target exact, but evaluates it on real sequences instead of teacher-generated ones — the paper's "approximately," since real data only matches teacher-generated contexts once the teacher is strong. seqkd keeps the sampling source exact — a real teacher-generated sequence — but then discards the teacher's actual probabilities and trains on that one sample as ordinary one-hot ground truth, losing the dark knowledge every other slide has been carrying.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.11. original source image and extract follow. slide 12 — why not sample from the teacher and keep the soft target? slide text (extracted) why not sample from the teacher and keep the soft target? nothing rules this out mathematically — sample y from the teacher, then match the teacher's full distribution at every step of that same y . that is exactly the unapproximated forward-kld objective from three slides ago. each practical method drops it for its own documented reason: s e q k d : t h e e x a c t ta r g e t i s a n i n t r a c ta b l e s u m the true sequence-level target sums over every possible response, weighted by how likely the teacher is to produce it: − ∑y∈y p(y∣x) log qθ (y∣x) — ​ ​ exponentially many terms. kim & rush's original seqkd approximates p(y∣x) by a single point, the teacher's most likely response y ^ (found via beam search). ​ collapsing the teacher's distribution down to one response is exactly what removes the soft target — the loss becomes plain − log qθ (y ^∣x), with nothing soft ​ ​ left to keep. w o r d - l e v e l k d : r e a l d ata i s a l r e a d y t h e r e scoring the teacher's per-token distribution on an already-written sequence takes one parallel forward pass. generating a new response from the teacher instead takes t sequential decoding steps per example, repeated across the whole training set — so word-level kd keeps using the real dataset it already has. s e l f - s t u d y: o n - p o l i c y d i s t i l l at i o n later work (agarwal et al., 2024) shows this combination — a generated sequence plus the teacher's per-token soft distribution along it — is a real option, but works better when the sequence comes from the student, not the teacher: that is what the student needs to get right at inference time, the same reason minillm samples y from qθ on the next slide. ​

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.12. original source image and extract follow. slide 13 — why forward kld hurts open-ended generation slide text (extracted) why forward kld hurts open-ended generation forward kld forces qθ to place probability everywhere p does — if p(y∣x) > 0 but qθ (y∣x) → 0 anywhere, log(p/qθ ) → ∞ and the loss explodes. for a small ​ ​ ​ number of classes (text classification), this is harmless: both distributions have few modes anyway. t e x t g e n e r at i o n h a s t o o m a n y m o d e s f o r a s m a l l s t u d e n t an llm's response space is enormous and multi-modal — many different phrasings are all individually plausible. a small student lacks the capacity to represent every mode p does, so forced coverage makes it spread probability onto void regions of p — places the teacher finds implausible — producing lowquality, hallucinated generations at free-run time.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.13. original source image and extract follow. slide 14 — a worked example: forward kld spills into the void slide text (extracted) a worked example: forward kld spills into the void context "the cat ___", a 4-token vocabulary. the teacher genuinely likes two different continuations — "sat" and "ran" — and almost never says "purred" or "flew": to k e n s at purred flew ran teacher p 0.49 0.01 0.01 0.49 suppose the student is capacity-limited to a single "bump" of confidence across these four tokens — it can commit to one coherent continuation shape, not two unrelated ones at once. fitting that one bump by forward vs. reverse kld gives very different students: forward kld: arg minq kl[p ∥ q ] reverse kld: arg minq kl[q ∥ p] q = [0.03, 0.47, 0.47, 0.03] — the bump lands between the two real q = [0.80, 0.20, 0.00, 0.00] — the bump commits to one real mode, "sat", modes, the only place a single bump gets partial credit for both. 94% of the student's probability lands on "purred"/"flew". and stays close to it. only 20% spills onto the neighboring void token, none onto the far one. ​ ​ same teacher, same student family — minimizing forward kld produces a student that mostly says implausible things; minimizing reverse kld produces one that says a real thing, just not always the same real thing.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.14. original source image and extract follow. slide 15 — minillm's objective: reverse kld slide text (extracted) minillm's objective: reverse kld minillm instead minimizes the reverse kld — the same two distributions, with the direction flipped: p(y∣x) θ = arg min kl[qθ ∥ p] = arg min [ − ex∼px , y∼qθ log ] θ θ qθ (y∣x) ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ same p, qθ , x as before — but now y is sampled from the student's own distribution qθ , not the teacher's. this one change — whose distribution y comes from — is ​ ​ what turns the training signal from "cover everything the teacher might say" into "get good at what you already tend to say."

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.15. original source image and extract follow. slide 16 — forward vs. reverse kld: a numeric example slide text (extracted) forward vs. reverse kld: a numeric example kl divergence is not symmetric — kl[p∥q] ≠ kl[q∥p] in general. take p = [0.70, 0.25, 0.05] and q = [0.40, 0.40, 0.20] over 3 outcomes: y p q p log(p/q ) q log(q /p) 1 0.70 0.40 0.3917 −0.2238 2 0.25 0.40 −0.1175 0.1880 3 0.05 0.20 −0.0693 0.2773 kl[p‖q] = 0.2049 kl[q‖p] = 0.2414 sum same two distributions, two genuinely different numbers — forward and reverse kld are not interchangeable objectives; minimizing one does not minimize the other.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.16. original source image and extract follow. slide 17 — why: which mistake each direction punishes slide text (extracted) why: which mistake each direction punishes look at what each term does when p and q disagree in different ways: q spends probability where p is tiny (q = 0.20, p = 0.01) q ignores a region p likes (q = 0.001, p = 0.30) reverse term q log(q/p) = 0.20 log(20) = 0.599 — big penalty. forward term p log(p/q) = 0.30 log(300) = 1.711 — big penalty. forward term p log(p/q) = 0.01 log(0.05) = −0.030 — negligible. reverse term q log(q/p) = 0.001 log(0.0033) = −0.006 — negligible. forward kld is severely punished for under-covering any mode p has — mode-covering. reverse kld is severely punished for wandering into regions p dislikes, but barely cares about ignoring modes — mode-seeking. this asymmetry is the entire reason the two objectives train such differently-behaved students.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.17. original source image and extract follow. slide 18 — seeing it directly: fitting a single gaussian slide text (extracted) seeing it directly: fitting a single gaussian fit one gaussian q to a multi-modal target p (a gaussian mixture) by minimizing each kld direction: forward kld (orange) spreads itself thin trying to cover every mode at once, ending up low and wide — reasonably present everywhere, confidently right nowhere. reverse kld (green) picks the single largest mode and matches it closely, ignoring the smaller ones entirely — exactly the mode-seeking behavior from the previous slide, now visible on an actual distribution.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.18. original source image and extract follow. slide 19 — what this means for training slide text (extracted) what this means for training sequence-level kd samples y from the teacher and trains the student to match those exact samples — forward kld, forcing memorization of everything the teacher might generate. minillm samples y from the student itself and asks the teacher to grade it — reverse kld, improving the text the student already tends to produce rather than forcing it to reproduce the teacher's.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.19. original source image and extract follow. slide 20 — why this needs policy gradient slide text (extracted) why this needs policy gradient kl[qθ ∥p] is an expectation over y ∼ qθ — the distribution being optimized is also the one doing the sampling. ordinary backprop can't differentiate through a ​ ​ sampling step directly. this is exactly the situation reinforcement learning solves: treat the student as a policy choosing tokens, use the policy gradient theorem to get a usable gradient anyway. the rl framing state = the prompt plus tokens generated so far, (x, y<t ). action = the next token yt , chosen from the vocabulary. reward = how much more the teacher likes ​ each generated token than the student already does. ​

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.20. original source image and extract follow. slide 21 — the gradient, qualitatively slide text (extracted) the gradient, qualitatively the policy gradient theorem gives an update rule with the shape every policy-gradient method shares: push up the probability of an action in proportion to a reward signal, push it down otherwise. here, at each generated token yt , the reward is rt — how much more the teacher likes the rest of this response, from this ​ ​ point on, than the student itself currently expects. t h e p r e c i s e m e c h a n i c s c o m e l at e r this deck hasn't covered rl for llms / rlhf yet, so the full derivation of rt and the gradient formula is deliberately left qualitative here — worth revisiting in ​ detail once that foundation is in place. the idea to hold onto for now: reward = teacher-relative quality of what follows, and the gradient just does ordinary policy-gradient credit assignment with that reward.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.21. original source image and extract follow. slide 22 — three problems, three fixes slide text (extracted) three problems, three fixes plain policy gradient on this reward is unstable in practice. the paper identifies three specific failure modes and a fix for each — the mechanics are rl-specific and worth returning to once rl for llms is covered properly; the ideas themselves are simple: high variance reward hacking length bias early-token errors compound across a whole sampled sentence. fix: compute the immediate next-step quality sampling purely from the student can find degenerate text (repeated phrases) that the teacher scores well. fix: summing reward over more remaining tokens mechanically favors short or empty responses. fix: exactly (summed over the vocabulary) instead of estimating it from one noisy rollout. sample from a mix of teacher and student, so training rarely wanders into those degenerate regions in the first place. normalize the reward by how many tokens remain, so it reflects average quality, not raw length.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.22. original source image and extract follow. slide 23 — training minillm: two phases slide text (extracted) training minillm: two phases 1. phase 1 — sft initialization. fine-tune the student on the labeled instruction-response dataset d , standard supervised training. this gives policy gradient a reasonable starting point instead of a random one. 2. phase 2 — minillm refinement. continue training with the combined gradient from the three fixes above (single-step + teacher-mixed + length-normalized), alongside a language-modeling loss on a separate pretraining corpus dpt to preserve the student's general capabilities. ​ the overall pipeline mirrors rlhf: an sft phase followed by a policy-optimization phase — except the reward here comes directly from the teacher's own output distribution, not a separately-trained reward model.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.23. original source image and extract follow. slide 24 — experimental setup slide text (extracted) experimental setup instruction-following as the task — models learn to produce a response given an instruction, evaluated with rouge-l against ground truth, human judgment, and gpt-4 feedback. teacher / student pairs data & evaluation gpt-2-1.5b → gpt-2 125m/340m/760m gpt-j 6b / opt 13b → opt 1.3b/2.7b/6.7b trained on databricks-dolly-15k (~12.5k examples). evaluated on 5 instructionfollowing sets: dolly, selfinst, vicuna, s-ni, unni. llama 13b → llama 7b baselines: sft w/o kd (no distillation at all), kd (word-level, forward kld), seqkd (sequence-level, trains directly on teacher-generated text).

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.24. original source image and extract follow. slide 25 — does it work? the headline result slide text (extracted) does it work? the headline result average rouge-l vs. student size, three independent teacher/student families. minillm (solid) beats seqkd (dashed) at every size tested, and the gap holds as student capacity scales from 100m to 6.7b — approaching, and at the largest sizes nearly matching, the teacher's own score (dashed grey line).

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.25. original source image and extract follow. slide 26 — the full results table slide text (extracted) the full results table minillm is the best or tied-best student almost everywhere, across every family and every size. on several datasets (vicuna, s-ni, unni) it even exceeds the teacher's own score — attributed to exposure bias: the teacher was fine-tuned with plain teacher-forcing, which itself has a training/inference mismatch that policy-gradient training doesn't share (next slide).

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.26. original source image and extract follow. slide 27 — lower exposure bias slide text (extracted) lower exposure bias teacher-forced training only ever sees ground-truth prefixes, never its own mistakes — at free-run inference, small errors compound as generation gets longer (exposure bias). minillm trains on the student's own generated rollouts (reverse kld samples y ∼ qθ ), so it already sees, and corrects for, its own mistakes during ​ training — the excess error (exaccerr) stops growing past ~150 tokens, while the baselines keep drifting.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.27. original source image and extract follow. slide 28 — better calibration slide text (extracted) better calibration expected calibration error (ece) — how well a model's confidence matches its actual accuracy — on two zero-shot classification tasks. forward-kld baselines (kd, seqkd) are dramatically worse calibrated than the teacher; minillm narrows that gap substantially, consistent with reverse kld avoiding the void-region overconfidence forward kld introduces.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.28. original source image and extract follow. slide 29 — human preference slide text (extracted) human preference head-to-head human comparisons, llama-7b student vs. llama-13b teacher. minillm wins outright against every baseline more often than it loses, and even against the teacher itself it's competitive — wins or ties in roughly two-thirds of comparisons.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.29. original source image and extract follow. slide 30 — bigger teachers make better students slide text (extracted) bigger teachers make better students fix the student (gpt-2-125m) and grow only the teacher. prior work has found this doesn't always help — a bigger teacher can even hurt naive distillation. minillm instead improves monotonically with teacher size, while seqkd stays flat — reverse kld keeps extracting more signal from a stronger teacher instead of just inheriting its blind spots.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.30. original source image and extract follow. slide 31 — the advantage grows with response length slide text (extracted) the advantage grows with response length for short expected responses (≤ 5 tokens) the output space is small enough that any method covers it — forward and reverse kld perform similarly. for longer responses, the teacher's true distribution has far more modes than a small student can represent, and that's exactly where minillm's margin over standard kd widens the most.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.31. original source image and extract follow. slide 32 — does mode-seeking hurt diversity? slide text (extracted) does mode-seeking hurt diversity? reverse kld is mode-seeking by design — a natural worry is that it makes generations repetitive. measured directly with distinct-4-grams (dist-4, higher = more diverse vocabulary) and language-modeling loss on held-out text: minillm's dist-4 and loss stay close to the teacher's and the other baselines' — mode-seeking within one response does not collapse diversity across different prompts or different sampling seeds.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 05.33. original source image and extract follow. slide 34 — what the outputs actually look like slide text (extracted) what the outputs actually look like minillm produces the most complete, correctly-formatted answer — a full bulleted list of valid substitutions. without teacher-mixed sampling, the same architecture degenerates into a near-empty response ("we to know") — a direct, visible instance of the reward hacking the ablation on the previous slide measured numerically.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 06.28. original source image and extract follow. slide 29 — why the kl term can backfire slide text (extracted) why the kl term can backfire adding a naive kl term to real grpo training caused the run to collapse shortly after step 50 — the model started outputting non-sensical text and random tokens. two compounding causes: 1. it scales with sequence length 2 . i t c a n b e c o m e t h e o n ly g r a d i e n t the kl term is computed on summed log-probabilities, so longer responses automatically produce a larger-magnitude kl term — incentivizing everlonger outputs and destabilizing training. once rewards collapse to all-zero, advantages are all zero and the policy gradient loss vanishes entirely — leaving the kl term as the sole remaining signal, which then pushes the model toward near-uniform, effectively random output.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 06.29. original source image and extract follow. slide 30 — the common recommendation: skip kl for math rl slide text (extracted) the common recommendation: skip kl for math rl several possible fixes exist — length-normalizing the kl and policy-ratio terms, lowering kl_coeff , reweighting the kl term via importance sampling, or adding a small format reward so advantages don't collapse to exactly zero. b u t t h e m o r e c o m m o n f i x : d r o p i t e n t i r e ly multiple independent lines of work — dr. grpo, olmo 3, and deepseek v3.2 — report training better without a kl term when training on math data. this also simplifies the implementation and removes the need to keep an extra copy of the reference model in memory during training.

read the teaching bridge for this source page · syllabus 07.09. original source image and extract follow. slide 10 — a negative result worth keeping: arxiv papers don't help slide text (extracted) a negative result worth keeping: arxiv papers don't help arxiv papers are a standard ingredient in prior math corpora (proof-pile-2, minerva, mathpile) on the assumption that formal mathematical writing teaches formal mathematical reasoning. training deepseek-llm 1.3b and deepseek-coder-base-v1.5 7b on arxiv-only corpora (mathpile, arxiv-redpajama) shows no improvement, and sometimes deterioration, across gsm8k, math, mmlu-stem, and formal theorem proving (minif2f). why this is worth reporting, not just discarding the authors explicitly flag this as preliminary — untested at larger scale, and untested combined with other data types. a clearly-scoped negative result is still useful: it means "arxiv papers = better math reasoning" should not be assumed without evidence.
